case_title: United India Insurance Company Ltd vs Neelam Devi And Others
court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh
core_facts: On 21.11.2013 at about 10:00 P.M., Munish Kumar and friends Ram Niwas, Sultan and Sunil were travelling from Narwana to Vrindavan in a Maruti Car (HR-99-QMTP-3245) which was struck by a Truck/Tanker (HR-38-F-4365), causing deaths of Munish Kumar, Sultan Singh and Ram Niwas and injuries to Sunil.
FIR No. 938 dated 22.11.2013 was registered under Sections 279, 337, 338 and 304-A IPC at Police Station City Jind.
The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Jind passed a common award dated 30.10.2017 awarding compensation in four MACP cases totalling over Rs. 38 lacs.
United India Insurance Company filed four appeals (FAOs 1113, 1114, 1119, 1120 of 2018) challenging the award.

Driver Sandeep's license (Ex.R-2) was valid for MC, LMV, HGV, HTV but lacked the special endorsement required under Rule 9 of Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 for driving a vehicle carrying dangerous or hazardous goods.
Claimants in FAO-1119-2018 filed cross-objections seeking enhancement of compensation for death of Munish Kumar, supported by Income Tax Returns showing gross annual income of Rs. 2,40,380/-.
Insurer challenged income assessment at DC Rate instead of Minimum Wages Act and questioned awards for consortium and funeral expenses.
legal_issues: Whether Sandeep's driving license was valid for driving a Tanker carrying dangerous or hazardous goods under Rule 9 of Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989
Whether absence of special endorsement constitutes a breach of insurance policy conditions enabling the insurer to recover from the owner
Whether insurer can escape liability despite policy breach, or must pay and recover from the owner
Quantum of compensation including future prospects, income assessment and consortium
outcome: Four appeals by the insurer partly allowed. Driver Sandeep found to lack the special endorsement required for driving a Tanker carrying hazardous goods under Rule 9 of Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, constituting a policy breach; Tribunal findings on Issue No. 3 reversed giving insurer the right to recover from the insured. Insurer nonetheless directed to pay compensation. Compensation recalculated upward in FAO-1114-2018 and FAO-1119-2018 with 40% future prospects applied; cross-objections in FAO-1119-2018 accepted, compensation for Munish Kumar's death enhanced to Rs. 40,60,400/-. All four appeals and cross-objections disposed of.
key_holdings: A driver of a vehicle carrying dangerous or hazardous goods requires a special endorsement on the driving license under Rule 9 of Central Motor Vehicles Rule, 1989; absence of such endorsement is a breach of insurance policy conditions.
Despite the policy breach, the insurer cannot escape liability to third-party claimants and must pay compensation, retaining the right to recover from the insured.
There is no fixed rule that the income of a deceased must be assessed only as per minimum wages; the facts and circumstances of each case must be evaluated.
Future prospects must be added to income for compensation calculation as mandated by National Insurance Company Limited v. Pranay Sethi and Others.

key_passages.label: license_breach_defence
key_passages.quote: there is no such endorsement on the driving license of Sandeep. Therefore, he was not competent to drive Truck/Tanker and there is clear cut violation of the terms and conditions of insurance policy.

key_passages.label: pay_and_recover
key_passages.quote: the insurance company cannot escape its liability to make payment of compensation awarded in favour of the claimants. Once the payment is made, the insurance company has right to recover the same from the insured.

key_passages.label: income_determination
key_passages.quote: there cannot be any fixed rule in all the situations where there is no documentary evidence regarding income of the deceased nor there is any fixed rule that income of the deceased has to be taken only as per minimum wages revised from time to time.

key_passages.label: compensation_enhancement
key_passages.quote: the future prospects have to be considered in case of deceased Sultan, who was 22 years old, which is to the extent of 40%.

adverse_value: Insurer's pay-and-recover right affirmed: the court accepted the driving license breach defense (no special endorsement for hazardous goods tanker) and reversed the Tribunal on Issue No. 3, reserving the insurer's right to recover compensation from the owner. Insurers can cite this to establish policy breach and shift ultimate financial liability to the owner in similar tanker/hazardous goods cases.
summary: United India Insurance Company filed four appeals challenging a common award dated 30.10.2017 by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Jind, arising from a motor vehicle accident on 21.11.2013 in which a Truck/Tanker struck a Maruti Car, resulting in three deaths and one injury. The insurer contested the quantum of compensation and the validity of driver Sandeep's license for operating a Tanker transporting hazardous goods. The High Court upheld the income assessment method (rejecting the insurer's plea to restrict income to Minimum Wages Act) and applied 40% future prospects for the 22-year-old and 32-year-old deceased, and 25% for the 46-year-old deceased, as mandated by National Insurance Company Limited v. Pranay Sethi. On the license issue, the court reversed the Tribunal and held that a special endorsement under Rule 9 of Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 is required for driving a vehicle carrying dangerous or hazardous goods, which Sandeep lacked, constituting a policy breach. Nonetheless, the insurer was directed to pay the compensation with the right to recover from the insured. The cross-objections filed by claimants in FAO-1119-2018 were accepted and compensation for the death of Munish Kumar was substantially enhanced to Rs. 40,60,400/-. All four appeals and cross-objections were disposed of.

case_title: Liyakat Ali vs Smt Chunni Devi
court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
judge_or_bench: Hon'ble Devi Prasad Singh, J. and Hon'ble Dr. Satish Chandra, J.

claimants: Smt Chunni Devi (mother/heir of deceased Arvind Kumar)

core_facts: On 02.12.2000, deceased Arvind Kumar was travelling on a scooter when Tractor No. UP-35-B-1649 took a sharp turn and iron rods loaded in the trolley/trailer attached to the tractor struck him; he died on the spot.
The tractor was insured but the trolley/trailer was not separately insured; no premium was paid for the trolley.
The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Unnao awarded Rs. 1,18,850/- against the owner of the tractor (Liyakat Ali), holding the insurer not liable.
The tractor was insured only for agricultural use; at the time of accident it was carrying bricks and iron rods for construction of a room (pakki boring), not for agricultural purposes.
The owner admitted in paragraph 3 of his affidavit that the trolley was being used to carry iron rods and bricks for construction purposes.
legal_issues: Whether the trailer/trolley attached to the tractor is part of the tractor and covered under its insurance policy without separate premium
Whether using the tractor for non-agricultural purposes (construction) constitutes a breach of the insurance policy
Whether the insurer is liable to pay compensation or the owner of the tractor
outcome: Appeal dismissed for different reasons. While the court held that a trailer/trolley attached to a tractor is part of the tractor and covered by the tractor's insurance (not requiring separate premium), it found that the tractor was insured only for agricultural use and was carrying bricks and iron rods for construction — a non-agricultural purpose — constituting a breach of policy conditions. The insurer was therefore not liable and the owner of the tractor was held liable to pay the compensation of Rs. 1,18,850/-.
key_holdings: A trailer/trolley attached to a tractor is part of the tractor and need not be separately insured under Section 146 of the Motor Vehicles Act; if the prime mover (tractor) is insured and the driver's negligence is established, the insurer cannot escape liability merely because the trailer was not separately insured.

However, where the tractor was insured only for agricultural use and was being used for a non-agricultural purpose at the time of the accident, there is a breach of insurance policy conditions and the insurer is not liable; the owner must pay compensation.

key_passages.label: insurance_liability
key_passages.quote: the trailer/trolley, which is attached with the tractor is a part of the tractor, which was duly insured from the insurance company. Hence, the insurance company cannot escape from its liability to pay compensation by taking the plea that the trailer was not separately insured.

key_passages.label: policy_breach
key_passages.quote: Transportation of iron rods and bricks is certainly not an agricultural activity. The tractor was insured only for the purpose of agricultural activity. The tractor will have to be used only for agricultural purpose not for any other purpose including the construction of a room. Thus, there is a violation of the terms and conditions of the insurance policy.

key_passages.label: owner_liability
key_passages.quote: in the instant case, the insurance company is not liable to pay the compensation and the owner of the tractor will have to pay the compensation.

adverse_value: Directly adverse to claimants: the court exonerated the insurer from liability because the tractor was used for a non-agricultural purpose in breach of policy conditions. Claimants must recover from the owner (who may be less solvent) rather than the insurer.
summary: An appeal by the owner of a tractor (Liyakat Ali) against an award of Rs. 1,18,850/- by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Unnao, arising from the death of Arvind Kumar on 02.12.2000 when iron rods in the trolley attached to the tractor struck him as the tractor took a sharp turn near Hyderabad Paisara. The tractor was insured but the trolley was not separately insured. The court held that a trailer/trolley is part of the tractor and covered under the tractor's insurance, so the insurer could not escape liability merely for want of separate trailer insurance. However, the critical finding was that the tractor was insured only for agricultural use and was actually carrying bricks and iron rods for construction of a room — a non-agricultural purpose — constituting a breach of insurance policy conditions. Accordingly, the insurer was held not liable and the award was upheld against the owner of the tractor. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: United India Insurance Co Ltd vs Smt Parvathi Hebbar W/O Late Ramakrishna Hebbar
court: High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru

owner_or_driver: N. Chandrakantha Prabhu (owner/insured of Maruthi Omni KA-20/Z-3931)

core_facts: On 02-07-2008 at about 6.30 a.m., deceased Ramakrishna Hebbar was standing on the southern side mud portion of Udupi-Karkala Road when the driver of Maruthi Omni (KA-20/Z-3931) drove rashly and dashed against him; he succumbed to injuries on 16-07-2008.
The deceased was aged about 60 years and working as a Head Cook earning Rs. 15,000/- per month.
Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Kundapura awarded Rs. 2,45,000/- with interest at 6% p.a. fastening liability on the insurer.
The driving license of the driver of the Maruthi Omni had expired on 30-04-2008 (more than 30 days before the accident on 02-07-2008) and was renewed only on 04-07-2008, after the accident.
The insurer proved through evidence that as on the date of accident, the driver of offending Maruthi Omni was not holding a valid and effective driving license.
legal_issues: Whether a driving license which had expired more than 30 days before the accident and was renewed after the accident constitutes a breach of policy conditions under Section 15 of the Motor Vehicles Act
Whether the insurer can be exonerated from liability to third-party claimants or must pay and recover from the insured
outcome: Appeal allowed. Liability shifted from insurer to owner. The driving license expired on 30-04-2008 and the accident occurred on 02-07-2008; since renewal was applied for more than 30 days after expiry, the proviso to Section 15(1) operates and the license is valid only from the date of renewal (04-07-2008), not retrospectively. The driver was not holding a valid license on the date of the accident, constituting a policy breach. However, since third parties have a statutory right to recover compensation, the insurer was directed to pay the awarded sum and recover from the insured by applying the pay-and-recover principle.
key_holdings: Where a driving license has expired and an application for renewal is made more than 30 days after expiry, the proviso to Section 15(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act applies and the license is renewed only from the date of renewal, not from the date of expiry; hence the driver cannot be deemed to hold a valid license on the date of the accident.

Despite the policy breach, the insurer must pay the awarded compensation to the claimants (as third parties have a statutory right to recover) and then recover the same from the insured, applying the pay-and-recover principle.

key_passages.label: driving_license_validity
key_passages.quote: In the interregnum period i.e., from 30-04-2008 to 04-07-2008, the driver of offending Maruthi Omni was not holding valid and effective driving license and the accident had occurred on 2.7.2008.

key_passages.label: license_breach_defence
key_passages.quote: The liability fastened on the Insurance Company is contrary to law. The Tribunal ought to have fastened the liability on the owner of the vehicle, who entrusted the vehicle to a person, who did not possess valid and effective driving license as on the date of accident.

key_passages.label: pay_and_recover
key_passages.quote: the Insurance Company is directed to pay the awarded sum to the claimants and then to recover the said sum from the insured in the same proceedings by applying the principle of "Pay and Recover".

adverse_value: Directly adverse to claimants: the court accepted the insurer's defense of driving license breach (license expired more than 30 days before the accident and renewed only after) and shifted primary liability to the owner. The insurer pays only on a pay-and-recover basis, exposing claimants to collection risk if the owner cannot repay.
summary: United India Insurance Company challenged the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Kundapura's award of Rs. 2,45,000/- for the death of Ramakrishna Hebbar who was struck by a Maruthi Omni on 02-07-2008. The key dispute was whether the insurer was liable when the driver's license had expired on 30-04-2008 — more than 30 days before the accident — and was renewed only on 04-07-2008. The Karnataka High Court held that under the proviso to Section 15(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, where renewal is applied for more than 30 days after expiry, the license is renewed only from the date of renewal, not retrospectively from the date of expiry. Since the accident fell in the interregnum period when the driver lacked a valid license, there was a breach of policy conditions. The court reversed the Tribunal's finding and fastened liability on the owner. However, since it is the statutory right of third parties to recover compensation, the insurer was directed to pay the awarded compensation and then recover from the insured, applying the pay-and-recover principle established in National Insurance Company v. Swaran Singh and Manuara Khatun v. Rajesh Kr. Singh.

case_title: Oriental Insurance Company vs Soma Devi and Others
court: High Court of Himachal Pradesh at Shimla

claimants: Smt. Soma Devi (mother of deceased Harish Kumar)

core_facts: On Jun 19, 2010, deceased Harish Kumar (aged 21 years, born Jan 21, 1989) was riding a motorcycle (HP34A-9526) when it collided with a car (HP33B-2444) driven by Jai Ram near Bhangrotu Bridge; both riders of the motorcycle fell and sustained injuries; Harish Kumar died while being transported to IGMC Hospital Shimla.
FIR No. 219 dated Jun 20, 2010 was registered by Jai Ram (driver of the car) at Police Station-Balh, District Mandi, HP, alleging rash and negligent driving by the deceased motorcycle rider.
The mother Soma Devi filed a Claim Petition under Section 166 of MV Act claiming Rs. 15 lacs; she alleged her son earned Rs. 10,000/- per month working in M/s Sidharth Communications.

Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (1), Mandi, HP, vide award dated Aug 31, 2012 awarded total compensation of Rs. 4,00,000/- fastening liability on Oriental Insurance Company, treating income as Rs. 3,500/- per month (unskilled worker).
Oriental Insurance Company challenged the award arguing the car's driver Jai Ram was not at fault and the FIR was against the deceased motorcycle rider.
legal_issues: Whether the driver of the insured car was negligent or whether the accident was caused solely by the deceased motorcycle rider
Whether the FIR filed by the car driver and police investigation report against the deceased suffice to discharge the insurer's liability
Whether the court can enhance compensation beyond the claimed amount in the absence of cross-objections, to award just compensation
outcome: Appeal disposed of. Insurer's contention that the car's driver was not at fault was rejected; the FIR was found to be a one-sided version from the car driver, without independent investigation of the surviving occupant. Insurer's liability affirmed. Compensation enhanced from Rs. 4,00,000/- to Rs. 5,99,000/- by applying 40% future prospects on Rs. 3,500/- (self-employed, below 40 years per Pranay Sethi), 50% deduction for personal expenses (bachelor), multiplier 18 for age group 21-25 years (Sarla Verma), plus conventional heads: loss of estate Rs. 15,000/-, consortium Rs. 40,000/-, funeral expenses Rs. 15,000/-. Interest reduced from 7.5% to 6% p.a. from the date of filing of the petition.
key_holdings: A FIR recording a one-sided version from the surviving car driver, without corroboration or investigation of other eyewitnesses, cannot be accepted as conclusive proof of negligence by the deceased motorcycle rider.

Under Order 41 Rule 33 CPC and Section 168 MV Act, courts may enhance compensation beyond the amount claimed or awarded even in the absence of cross-objections, where the award is manifestly unjust to a poor claimant.
For a self-employed bachelor below 40 years, 40% future prospects applies (Pranay Sethi), 50% is deducted for personal expenses, and multiplier 18 applies for age 21-25 years (Sarla Verma).

key_passages.label: fir_credibility
key_passages.quote: What clinches the issue is the joint reply to the claim petition filed by the owner of the car and its driver. In response to paragraph No. 8, the respondent specifically pleaded that the accident took place due to rash and negligent driving of the driver of the motorcycle and hit his bike with the stationary car.

key_passages.label: insurance_liability
key_passages.quote: there is no illegality or infirmity in the award, and on the other hand, the same is well reasoned. This Court affirms the same, however, with the following modifications.

key_passages.label: just_compensation
key_passages.quote: the claimant had claimed an amount of Rs. 15 Lacs, whereas what she got was around one fourth of it.

key_passages.label: compensation_enhancement
key_passages.quote: Consequently, this Court modifies the compensation to the calculations mentioned in column no. 3 of paragraph 23.

summary: Oriental Insurance Company challenged the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Mandi's award of Rs. 4,00,000/- for the death of Harish Kumar (aged 21 years) in a road accident on Jun 19, 2010, in which his motorcycle collided with an insured car driven by Jai Ram. The FIR was registered against the deceased based on the car driver's version, and the police investigation concluded that the motorcycle was rash and negligent. The Himachal Pradesh High Court found the FIR to be a one-sided version from the surviving car driver; the joint reply filed by the car owner and driver in the claim petition contained an improvement over the FIR, undermining its credibility. The court affirmed liability on the insurer. Applying National Insurance Company Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi, the court calculated just compensation: 40% future prospects on Rs. 3,500/-, 50% personal expense deduction (bachelor), multiplier 18 for age 21, plus conventional heads as per Pranay Sethi. Total compensation was enhanced to Rs. 5,99,000/- with interest at 6% p.a. from the date of filing the petition.

case_title: L And T Insurance Co Ltd vs Bindudevi Samharu Yadav And Others
court: High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad
judge_or_bench: Honourable Mr. Justice Mool Chand Tyagi

appellants: L And T Insurance Co Ltd
claimants: Bindudevi Samharu Yadav and others (wife and dependants of deceased Sunil Samharu Yadav)
insurer: L And T Insurance Co Ltd
owner_or_driver: Respondent No. 5 (driver of dumper truck GJ-18-X-9452)

core_facts: On 19.05.2013 at about 1:00 p.m., deceased Sunil Samharu Yadav (aged 28 years, driver of tempo DN-09-K-9486 loaded with yarn) parked his tempo on the left side of National Highway No. 8 to change a punctured tyre; a dumper truck (GJ-18-X-9452) driven rashly by respondent No. 5 struck the tempo from behind, causing fatal injuries.

Claimants filed proceedings before the Workmen's Compensation Commissioner against the employer of the deceased and the insurer of the tempo (ICICI Lombard) and received compensation of Rs. 8,39,680/-.

Claimants also filed a claim petition under Section 166 of MV Act before Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (Auxiliary), Navsari against the driver, owner and insurer (L&T Insurance) of the offending dumper truck.
Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Navsari awarded Rs. 12,12,400/- with interest at 9% p.a. from the date of filing of claim petition till realization.

L&T Insurance challenged the award on two grounds: (1) bar of Section 167 MV Act due to prior Workmen's Compensation proceedings; and (2) that the driver of the dumper truck was holding a fake driving license.
legal_issues: Whether Section 167 of MV Act bars the claimants from filing a claim petition before the MACT after having received compensation under the Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923 from the employer, where the parties before both forums are entirely different
Whether the insurer can be exonerated from liability if the driver of the offending vehicle holds a fake driving license
Whether the insurer discharged the burden of proving by cogent evidence that the driving license was fake
outcome: Appeal dismissed. The bar of Section 167 of MV Act does not apply because the parties before the Workmen's Compensation Commissioner (employer of the deceased and ICICI Lombard as insurer of the tempo) and the parties before the MACT (driver, owner and L&T Insurance as insurer of the dumper truck) were entirely different; the two claims arose under different legal relationships. On the driving license issue, the insurer failed to prove by cogent evidence that the license was fake; merely relying on oral testimony of a legal officer without producing proper documentation from the RTO was insufficient. Award of Rs. 12,12,400/- maintained.
key_holdings: Section 167 of the Motor Vehicles Act bars dual proceedings only where the claimants seek compensation from the same employer/tortfeasor before both forums; where the parties before each forum are entirely different, the bar of Section 167 does not apply.

The liability under the Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923 is the statutory liability of the employer while the liability under Section 166 of the MV Act is tortious liability; claims against different parties under different instruments are not barred.

The insurer bears the burden of proving by cogent documentary evidence that the driving license was fake; mere oral evidence of its own legal officer without proper RTO documentation fails to discharge this burden.

key_passages.label: section_167_mv_act
key_passages.quote: The respondent nos.1 to 4 also filed the claim petition before the learned Tribunal under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act against the driver, owner and insurer of the dumper truck bearing registration no.GJ-18-X-9452, therefore, the parties before the Commissioner Workmen's Compensation and the parties before the learned Motor Accident Claims Tribunal are different.

key_passages.label: maintainability
key_passages.quote: the bar of Section 167 of MV Act is applied only where the claimants seek compensation under the Motor Vehicles Act from the employer and insurer. When the parties before the both forums are entirely different, the bar of Section 167 of the MV Act would not apply.

key_passages.label: fake_license
key_passages.quote: the Insurance Company could not prove, that the driving license in question was fake, by leading the cogent evidence on record.

summary: L&T Insurance Company appealed against a MACT award of Rs. 12,12,400/- arising from the death of Sunil Samharu Yadav (aged 28 years) on 19.05.2013 when a dumper truck struck his parked tempo while he was changing a punctured tyre on NH-8. The insurer raised two defenses: (1) Section 167 MV Act bars the claim since claimants had already received Rs. 8,39,680/- from the employer under the Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923; and (2) the dumper driver held a fake driving license. The Gujarat High Court dismissed both defenses. On Section 167, it held that the bar applies only where the claimants seek compensation from the same tortfeasor/employer in both forums; here, the Workmen's Compensation proceedings were against the employer (and ICICI Lombard as insurer of the tempo) while the MACT proceedings were against the tortfeasors (dumper truck driver, owner, and L&T Insurance) — different parties with different liabilities. On the fake license, the insurer failed to lead cogent documentary evidence to prove the license was fake; mere oral testimony of the legal officer was insufficient. The appeal was dismissed and the award maintained.

case_title: National Insurance Company Ltd. vs Smt. Meena And 4 Others
court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench

respondents: Sri Anil Kumar Gupta and Another (F.A.F.O. 123/2012)
owner_or_driver: Sri Anil Kumar Gupta (owner of Tanker UP32-T/6251)

core_facts: On 12.5.2006 at about 7.00 A.M., deceased Sundar Lal was riding a moped (UP-32-AB/8094) near Neelam Traders, Devpur Tara, Police Station Talkatora, Lucknow when a Tanker (UP32-T/6251) driven negligently collided with the moped; Sundar Lal died on 15.5.2006.
The deceased was a government servant with a monthly salary of Rs. 8,841/-; the MACT deducted Rs. 500/- towards VPF and Rs. 150/- towards festival advance while calculating income.
Eye-witness P.W.-2 (Ram Gopal, also riding a moped) testified that deceased was on the left side of the road, took further left to avoid the Tanker, and was not negligent.
The MACT applied 50% contributory negligence based on the police site plan (relied upon as showing head-on collision), awarding only 50% of the calculated compensation.
Valid driving license of the Tanker driver was not produced; MACT directed insurer to pay compensation with right to recover from the owner.
MACT awarded Rs. 4,26,880/- with 6% simple interest; two appeals filed: F.A.F.O. 123/2012 by claimants and F.A.F.O. 148/2012 by the insurer.
legal_issues: Whether the MACT was justified in applying 50% contributory negligence based on the site plan despite credible and unrebutted eye-witness testimony that the deceased was not negligent
Whether the insurer can avoid liability when the driver's valid driving license was not produced
Whether VPF contributions and festival advance are deductible from income when calculating compensation
Whether 30% future prospects must be added for a government servant aged between 40 and 50 years
outcome: Insurer's appeal (F.A.F.O. 148/2012) dismissed: following S. Iyyapan v. United India Insurance Company, even where the driver lacks a valid license, the insurer must pay compensation to claimants with right to recover from the owner. Claimants' appeal (F.A.F.O. 123/2012) partly allowed: 50% contributory negligence finding reversed; 100% negligence attributed to Tanker driver based on credible unrebutted eye-witness testimony; VPF and festival advance deductions restored to income; 30% future prospects added; interest increased from 6% to 7%; total compensation recalculated to Rs. 13,74,876/-; insurer directed to pay with right to recover from owner Anil Kumar Gupta.
key_holdings: Where there is consistent and credible testimony of an eye-witness that the deceased was not negligent, the Tribunal cannot discard that testimony and apply contributory negligence solely on the basis of a police site plan that does not clearly indicate a head-on collision.

Even where the driver of the offending vehicle does not possess a valid driving license, the insurer is liable to pay compensation to claimants and has a right to recover from the insured; this follows S. Iyyapan v. M/s. United India Insurance Company.
VPF contributions and festival advances form part of the deceased's gross income and cannot be deducted while calculating income available to dependent family members.
For a government servant aged between 40 and 50 years, 30% must be added to income towards future prospects as mandated by National Insurance Company Limited v. Pranay Sethi.

key_passages.label: contributory_negligence
key_passages.quote: once there was consistent testimony of the P.W.-2 before the learned Tribunal wherein he has categorically stated that deceased was not at all negligent while driving the moped, there was no occasion for the learned Tribunal to discard the testimony of P.W.-2 and hold the accident in question to be result of the contributory negligence on the basis of site plan/sketch

key_passages.label: compensation_enhancement
key_passages.quote: Thus the award dated 11.11.2011 passed by the learned Motor Accident Claims Tribunal in M.A.C.P. No. 190 of 2009 is modified and the Claim Petition is awarded for an amount of Rs. 13,74,876/- along with 7% simple interest from the date of filing of the Claim Petition till the date of actual payment.

key_passages.label: pay_and_recover
key_passages.quote: The insurer i.e. National Insurance Company Limited is directed to pay the entire compensation amount along with interest [after excluding the amount already paid (if any) ] to the claimants within three months from today. The insurer i.e. National Insurance Company Limited is also given right of recovery to recover the amount of compensation paid to the claimants from the owner of the vehicle i.e. Mr. Anil Kumar Gupta.

adverse_value: Insurer can cite the pay-and-recover direction: where the Tanker driver lacked a valid license, the court confirmed the insurer's right to recover the entire compensation from the owner (Anil Kumar Gupta). Insurers can use this precedent to shift ultimate financial liability to the vehicle owner.
summary: Two cross-appeals arose from the MACT award in M.A.C.P. No. 190 of 2009 relating to the death of Sundar Lal (a government servant) on 12.5.2006 when a Tanker collided with his moped in Lucknow. The MACT applied 50% contributory negligence based on a site plan and directed the insurer to pay with right to recover, as the Tanker driver's license was not produced. The Allahabad High Court (Lucknow Bench) dismissed the insurer's appeal: following S. Iyyapan, the insurer must pay even where the driver lacks a valid license, with a right to recover from the owner. The claimants' appeal was partly allowed: the 50% contributory negligence finding was reversed since eye-witness P.W.-2 gave consistent and unrebutted testimony that the deceased was on the left side of the road, and the site plan did not clearly indicate head-on collision. VPF and festival advance deductions were reversed; 30% future prospects added for the government servant aged 40-50; interest enhanced from 6% to 7%. Total compensation was enhanced from Rs. 4,26,880/- to Rs. 13,74,876/-.

case_title: National Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Harpreet Singh and Others
court: High Court of Jammu and Kashmir at Jammu
judge_or_bench: Hon'ble Mr. Justice Janak Raj Kotwal

owner_or_driver: Inderjit Singh Bali (owner and driver of car JK02D-9212)

core_facts: On 29.09.2007, deceased Amarjeet Singh was travelling from Kishtwar to Jammu in a car (JK02D-9212) owned and driven by Inderjit Singh Bali; the car met with an accident near Thathri, plunged into a trench, and Amarjeet Singh died.
The deceased was a Government servant serving as Manager QC in the Food Corporation of India with a monthly salary of Rs. 24,149/-; he was aged 54 years at the time of death.
Claimants Harpreet Singh (son, employed as clerk in Doordarshan, Central Government service) and Harbaksh Singh (son, MBA student) filed claim under Section 166 MV Act.
Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Jammu awarded Rs. 17,53,800/- treating family strength as 3 (deceased + 2 sons) with 1/3 deduction for personal expenses, multiplier 9.

Insurer challenged: Harpreet Singh being gainfully employed in Central Government service is not dependent on the deceased and should not be counted for loss of dependency; only Harbaksh Singh (MBA student) qualifies as a dependent.
legal_issues: Whether a legal representative of the deceased who is gainfully employed and not financially dependent on the deceased at the time of death is entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'
Whether the family strength for calculating 'loss of dependency' should include non-dependent claimants
Correct application of multiplier method under Sarla Verma for income, deduction for personal expenses, and selection of multiplier
outcome: Appeal allowed in part. key_holdings: A legal representative of a motor accident victim who was not financially dependent on the deceased at the time of death is not entitled to compensation under the head 'loss of dependency'; such a claimant is entitled only to compensation for loss to estate and the statutory minimum under Section 140 of the Motor Vehicles Act.

For calculating 'loss of dependency', only financially dependent claimants are counted to determine family strength and the applicable personal expense deduction; non-dependent legal representatives are excluded from this computation.

case_title: General Manager Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation vs Khatujabee
court: High Court of Karnataka (Full Bench)

appellants: General Manager, Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation

core_facts: Fatal motor accident involving Kashimsab (Blacksmith, aged 40) whose dependants claimed compensation before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal
Tribunal awarded Rs. 2,70,000 under 'loss of dependency' using multiplier of 30; appeal confirmed award with 20% deduction for life's uncertainties

Division Bench in Khatujabee's case (MFA 708/1990) held that the operative multiplier principle in Bhandary's case had ceased to be binding after SC decisions in Jyotsna Dey and Rajendra Kumari under Art. 141
A second Division Bench referred the question of whether Bhandary's case stood impliedly overruled to the Full Bench
Full Bench examined nature of ratio decidendi and binding precedent under Art. 141 with reference to multiple SC decisions
legal_issues: Whether the 'operative multiplier' principle in H.T. Bhandary v. Muniyamma was impliedly overruled by SC decisions in Jyotsna Dey v. State of Assam and Rajendra Kumari v. Shanta Trivedi
When do conclusions in an SC decision constitute 'law declared' under Article 141 of the Constitution
What is the appropriate method for determining the multiplier in fatal accident loss-of-dependency claims
outcome: Full Bench answered that H.T. Bhandary v. Muniyamma [ILR 1985(2) Karnataka 2337] does NOT stand overruled by the SC decisions in Rajendra Kumari v. Shanta Trivedi and Jyotsna Dey v. State of Assam [1987(1) ACJ 172]. The contrary view taken by the Division Bench in Khatujabee's case stands overruled. The operative multiplier principle (base multiplier 16, scaled down with age) remains binding on all Motor Accident Claims Tribunals in Karnataka.
key_holdings: The 'operative multiplier' principle elaborated in Bhandary's case constitutes law declared by the Karnataka High Court and is a binding precedent for Tribunals in the State.

SC decisions in Jyotsna Dey and Rajendra Kumari contain fact-specific conclusions reached in the setting of the particular cases before them and do not constitute 'law declared' under Art. 141 on the general question of multiplier selection.
A decision is binding as a precedent only with respect to the ratio or principle laid down therein, not because of its conclusion; an obiter cannot take the place of the ratio.

key_passages.label: operative_multiplier_principle
key_passages.quote: All these factors, cumulatively, may be taken to bring down the multiplier by 20% which would perhaps be a just measure of deduction for all the contingencies and considerations relevant to the matter in an average case. This brings down the basic-multiplier to the operative multiplier of 16. This multiplier of 16 would be the highest applicable.

key_passages.label: ratio_decidendi
key_passages.quote: A decision ordinarily is a decision on the case before the Court while the principle underlying the decision would be binding as a precedent in a case which comes up for decision subsequently. Hence, while applying the decision to a later case, the Court which is dealing with it should carefully try to ascertain the true principle laid down by the previous decision. A decision often takes its colour from the questions involved in the case in which it is rendered.

key_passages.label: holding_outcome
key_passages.quote: The decision of this Court in H.T. Bhandary v. Muniyamma [IL.R 1985(2) Karnataka 2337] does not stand overruled by the decisions of the Supreme Court in Rajendra Kumari v. Shanta Trivedi and in Jyotsna Dey and Ors. v. State of Assam and Ors. [1987(1) ACJ 172]. Contrary View taken in the Division Bench decision of this Court in General Manager, Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation v. Khatujabee stands over-ruled.

adverse_value: The operative multiplier principle caps the maximum multiplier at 16 for the youngest deceased and requires systematic reduction with age; insurers or owners could cite this older Karnataka Full Bench precedent to argue for lower multipliers than those in the Sarla Verma schedule, potentially reducing compensation awards.
summary: This 1990 Karnataka High Court Full Bench judgment resolved a reference question on whether the 'operative multiplier' principle established in H.T. Bhandary v. Muniyamma (ILR 1985(2) Karnataka 2337) was impliedly overruled by Supreme Court decisions in Jyotsna Dey v. State of Assam (1987 1 ACJ 172) and Rajendra Kumari v. Shanta Trivedi. The reference arose from a Division Bench in MFA No. 708/1990 where KSRTC appealed a Tribunal award applying a multiplier of 30 for a fatal accident involving a blacksmith. The Full Bench extensively examined the nature of binding precedent under Article 141 of the Constitution, holding that a Supreme Court decision is 'law declared' only with respect to the ratio and principle laid down therein—not mere conclusions reached on specific facts. Applying this test, the Full Bench found that the multiplier choices in Jyotsna Dey and Rajendra Kumari were factual determinations rather than legal principles of general application. Since those decisions laid down no general rule on multiplier selection, they could not have impliedly overruled Bhandary's carefully elaborated operative multiplier principle, which capped the base multiplier at 16 and provided a systematic framework for scaling it down with the deceased's age. The Full Bench answered the reference in favour of Bhandary's case and overruled the contrary view in Khatujabee's case.

case_title: Mohammed Aynuddin @ Miyam vs State of Andhra Pradesh
court: Supreme Court of India
judge_or_bench: R.P. Sethi and K.T. Thomas JJ. (Thomas, J. writing)
core_facts: On 17.12.1993 the appellant was driving an Andhra Pradesh Road Transport Corporation bus; passenger Agamma boarded the bus enroute, fell as the bus moved forward, and the rear wheel ran over her causing death
All three courts below (trial court, Sessions Court, and High Court in revision) convicted the appellant under Section 304A IPC and sentenced him to three months' imprisonment
The conductor (PW3) admitted only hearing the sound of the accident while the bus was in motion; the sole eyewitness (PW4) stated only that Agamma was boarding and the bus moved, causing her to fall
No witness, including the conductor, stated that the driver moved the bus before getting a signal from the conductor; the driver's version was that he was unaware of the accident
legal_issues: Whether the evidence on record was sufficient to establish criminal negligence of the bus driver under Section 304A IPC
Whether res ipsa loquitur applies to create a presumption of negligence where a passenger falls from a bus while boarding
The distinction between culpable rashness and criminal negligence for the purposes of Section 304A IPC
outcome: Appeal allowed. Conviction and sentence under Section 304A IPC set aside. Appellant acquitted. The Supreme Court held that the evidence was too scanty to establish criminal negligence and that res ipsa loquitur did not apply because the accident could have had multiple explanations other than negligent driving.
key_holdings: A presumption of negligence cannot be drawn merely because a passenger fell from a bus while boarding; negligence must be positively established by evidence that the driver moved the bus prematurely or without the conductor's signal.

Res ipsa loquitur applies only where the nature of the accident and attending circumstances reasonably lead to the belief that in the absence of negligence the accident would not have occurred and the thing causing injury was under the management and control of the accused.

Criminal negligence requires failure to exercise duty with reasonable and proper care and precaution; where no witness establishes that the driver moved without signal, the evidence is insufficient to convict under Section 304A IPC.

key_passages.label: no_presumption_of_negligence
key_passages.quote: It is a wrong proposition that for any motor accident negligence of the driver should be presumed. An accident of such a nature as would prima facie show that it cannot be accounted to anything other than the negligence of the driver of the vehicle may create a presumption and in such a case the driver has to explain how the accident happened without negligence on his part. Merely because a passenger fell down from the bus while boarding the bus no presumption of negligence can be drawn against the driver of the bus.

key_passages.label: criminal_negligence_defined
key_passages.quote: Culpable rashness lies in running the risk of doing an act with recklessness and with indifference as to the consequences. Criminal negligence is the failure to exercise duty with reasonable and proper care and precaution guarding against injury to the public generally or to any individual in particular.

key_passages.label: acquittal_outcome
key_passages.quote: The evidence in this case is too scanty to fasten him with criminal negligence. Some further evidence is indispensably needed to presume that the passenger fell down due to the negligence of the driver of the bus. Such further evidence is lacking in this case. Therefore, the court is disabled from concluding that the victim fell down only because of the negligent driving of the bus. The corollary thereof is that the conviction of the appellant of the offence is unsustainable. In the result, we allow this appeal and set aside the conviction and sentence and he is acquitted.

summary: This 2000 Supreme Court criminal appeal concerned the conviction of an APSRTC bus driver under Section 304A of the Indian Penal Code. On 17 December 1993, passenger Agamma boarded the appellant's bus enroute; as the bus moved forward she fell and the rear wheel ran over her, causing death. The trial court, Sessions Court, and High Court in revision all convicted the driver and sentenced him to three months' imprisonment. The Supreme Court (per Thomas, J.) allowed the appeal and set aside the conviction. The court held that criminal negligence cannot be presumed merely because a passenger fell from a boarding bus; the prosecution must establish positively that the driver moved the bus prematurely or without the conductor's signal to proceed. The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur applies only where the accident cannot be reasonably attributed to causes other than negligence within the accused's control; on the present facts, a passenger's fall while boarding admits of multiple explanations. No witness, including the conductor (PW3), said the driver moved the bus before getting the signal, and the sole eyewitness (PW4) only observed the fall itself. Finding the evidence too scanty to establish criminal negligence, the Supreme Court acquitted the appellant. The judgment provides important guidance on the higher standard of evidence required for criminal liability as distinct from civil negligence.

case_title: Shivlal and Ors vs Smt. Rukmabai and Ors
court: High Court of Madhya Pradesh
core_facts: On 24.04.1977 at about 11:30 AM, tractor MPU 5571 owned by Shivlal and Kanhaiyalal and driven by Shivlal turned turtle on the road between Bibdod and Ratlam near a culvert from Sagod
Laxminarayan (agriculturist and milk vendor, aged about 50 years), who was travelling in the tractor brought to his field for boring of a well, died instantly in the accident
Widow Rukmabai and minor sons Radheshyam and Jagdish filed Claim Case No. 16 of 1977 before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Ratlam
MACT awarded Rs. 32,000 to the claimants (annual dependency Rs. 2,000 with 15% deduction for lump-sum payment); owners' and insurer's appeals and claimants' cross-objections pending
Owners contended deceased had forcibly occupied a seat; insurer denied liability on the ground that its policy did not cover risk of gratuitous passenger in a goods vehicle (tractor)
legal_issues: Whether the accident was caused by negligence of the driver Shivlal (res ipsa loquitur)
Whether the insurer is liable for a gratuitous passenger who was not covered under the policy or under Section 95 of the Motor Vehicles Act
Whether the compensation of Rs. 32,000 awarded by the Tribunal was adequate
outcome: MA 26/81 (owners' appeal) dismissed: negligence of Shivlal established under res ipsa loquitur; tractor turning turtle without credible explanation raises a rebuttable presumption of negligent driving. MA 55/81 (insurer's appeal) allowed: insurer held NOT liable for gratuitous passenger not covered under Section 95 of the Motor Vehicles Act; award set aside as against insurer. Claimants' cross-objection for enhancement dismissed: Rs. 32,000 award held adequate.
key_holdings: A heavy vehicle (tractor) turning turtle without explanation attracts the maxim res ipsa loquitur; in the absence of credible rebuttal evidence, the presumption of negligence stands established.

Under Section 95(2) of the Motor Vehicles Act the insurer's liability is limited to the statutory minimum; a policy insuring a goods vehicle (tractor) is not required to cover risk to passengers who are not carried for hire or reward.
A gratuitous passenger in a goods vehicle is not covered under Section 95 of the Act; in the absence of policy terms covering such a passenger's risk, no liability can be fastened on the insurer.

key_passages.label: res_ipsa_loquitur_negligence
key_passages.quote: a heavy vehicle like the tractor had turned turtle and normally such a thing does not happen with a careful driving. The applicability of the maxim res ipsa loquitur is clearly, therefore, attracted in this case and there is no credible material to rebut the presumption of negligence.

key_passages.label: insurer_statutory_minimum
key_passages.quote: It is well settled that the insurer's liability is limited to the statutory minimum required by Section 95(2) of the Act.

key_passages.label: gratuitous_passenger_outcome
key_passages.quote: his risk was not required to be covered under Section 95 of the Act and the absence of any terms in the policy of insurance covering the risk of such a passenger, no liability can certainly be fastened on the insurance company.

adverse_value: Insurance company held not liable for death of a gratuitous passenger in a goods vehicle (tractor) where the policy does not cover such risk under Section 95(2) of the Motor Vehicles Act; directly usable by insurers to defeat compensation claims from families of persons who died while travelling as non-paying, non-employee passengers in goods vehicles.
summary: This 1985 Madhya Pradesh High Court judgment decided two appeals and cross-objections against a 1980 MACT Ratlam award in Claim Case No. 16 of 1977. On 24 April 1977, tractor MPU 5571 owned by Shivlal and Kanhaiyalal turned turtle on the Bibdod-Ratlam road, killing Laxminarayan (an agriculturist and milk vendor, aged about 50), who was travelling in the tractor brought to his field for boring of a well. The MACT awarded Rs. 32,000 to his widow Rukmabai and minor sons based on annual dependency of Rs. 2,000 with a 15% deduction for lump-sum payment. The owners appealed against liability (MA 26/81) and the insurer appealed against its liability (MA 55/81); the claimants cross-objected for enhancement. The court dismissed the owners' appeal: a tractor turning turtle without credible explanation attracted res ipsa loquitur, and neither the owners' witnesses nor any plausible alternative explanation rebutted the presumption of negligence. The insurer's appeal was allowed: applying Section 95(2) of the Motor Vehicles Act and the Supreme Court's decision in Pushpabai's case (AIR 1977 SC 1735), the court held that a goods vehicle (tractor) policy is not required to cover risk to gratuitous passengers; since the policy contained no such term, no liability could be fastened on the insurer. The claimants' cross-objection was dismissed, the Tribunal's Rs. 32,000 award being found adequate.

case_title: State of H.P. vs. Krishan Lal
court: High Court of Himachal Pradesh, Shimla
core_facts: On 30.08.2006 a vehicle bearing registration No. HP-01A-3243 driven by accused Krishan Lal alias Babli fell into a gorge at place Thachi due to alleged high speed and negligence.
Three persons (Yog Raj, Paras Ram and Besar Dutt) died on the spot; other occupants including Mohan Lal, Virender and Sanju sustained injuries.
The accused denied rash driving and claimed the accident occurred because the retaining wall (danga) on the road suddenly gave way.

Trial Court acquitted the accused under Sections 279, 337, 338 and 304-A IPC after finding the retaining wall collapse version plausible, supported by prosecution witnesses' own cross-examination admissions.
The State filed Cr. Appeal No. 189 of 2011 against the judgment of acquittal dated 31.07.2010.
legal_issues: Whether the accused drove the vehicle rashly and negligently or whether the accident was caused by the collapse of a retaining wall.
Whether the principle of res ipsa loquitur applies to criminal trials and whether its application can substitute cogent evidence of rashness.
Whether the High Court should interfere with an order of acquittal where two views are possible from the evidence on record.
outcome: Criminal appeal by State of H.P. dismissed. Acquittal of accused Krishan Lal upheld. High Court held the Trial Court's view was a plausible and reasonable view based on material on record, as prosecution witnesses admitted in cross-examination that the danga (retaining wall) on the road had collapsed, raising a reasonable alternative explanation. The accused was ordered released from custody.
key_holdings: When two views are possible from evidence in a criminal case, the one in favour of the accused must be accepted; the prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
Use of the term 'high speed' by lay witnesses is legally insufficient to establish rashness or negligence without ascertaining what the witness understood by that expression.
A witness may not depose as to whether a driver was negligent; negligence is an inference to be drawn by the court from proven facts.
An appellate court will not interfere with an order of acquittal unless the Trial Court's view is perverse, illegal or affected by an error of law or fact.

key_passages.label: two_views_theory
key_passages.quote: The "two-views theory" has been judicially recognised by the courts and it comes into play when the appreciation of evidence results in two equally plausible views. However, the controversy is to be resolved in favour of the accused.

key_passages.label: res_ipsa_loquitur_criminal
key_passages.quote: in a criminal trial, the burden of proving everything essential to the establishment of the charge against the accused always rests on the prosecution, as every man is presumed to be innocent until the contrary is proved

key_passages.label: high_speed_insufficient
key_passages.quote: Merely because the truck was being driven at a "high speed" does not bespeak either "negligence" or "rashness" by itself. None of the witnesses examined by the prosecution could give any indication, even approximately as to what they meant by "high speed".

key_passages.label: outcome_acquittal_upheld
key_passages.quote: the learned Trial Court had taken a reasonable view which could have been taken based on the material placed before it and no interference is required with the same while deciding an appeal against the acquittal.

summary: The State of Himachal Pradesh appealed against the acquittal of Krishan Lal alias Babli, who was charged under Sections 279, 337, 338 and 304-A IPC and Section 186 MV Act arising from a road accident on 30.08.2006 in which a vehicle fell into a gorge killing three persons and injuring others. The accused claimed the accident resulted from the sudden collapse of a retaining wall. The Trial Court acquitted him after prosecution witnesses themselves admitted in cross-examination that the 'danga' on the road gave way, the vehicle was not driven at high speed in rainy conditions, and the retaining wall had collapsed. The High Court, applying the parameters in Mallappa v. State of Karnataka, held that when two equally plausible views emerge from evidence the one favourable to the accused must be adopted. Witness statements that the accused was driving negligently were held inadmissible as expressions of opinion rather than depositions of fact. Bare reference to 'high speed' without any attempt to quantify or explain the term was held legally insufficient. The appeal was dismissed and the accused ordered released.

case_title: Chaina Ram vs. State of H.P.
court: High Court of Himachal Pradesh, Shimla
core_facts: On 11.03.2003, victim Akshay Kumar (PW-2) was boarding bus HP53-2713 at the old bus stand in Palampur when driver Chaina Ram started the bus.
Akshay Kumar fell and his left leg was crushed under the rear tyre of the bus, sustaining simple and grievous injuries.
Trial Court convicted accused under Sections 279, 337, 338 IPC and Section 181 MV Act; Appellate Court affirmed conviction.
In revision before the High Court, the accused argued no evidence showed he moved the bus without conductor's signal, and that absence of driving license does not constitute negligence.
Accused never produced any driving license before the Trial Court, Appellate Court, or High Court.
legal_issues: Whether starting a bus while a passenger is boarding constitutes rash and negligent driving under Sections 279/337/338 IPC.
Whether absence of a driving license per se constitutes rashness or negligence in driving.
Whether the revisional court can re-appreciate evidence and substitute its own view.
outcome: Revision partly allowed. Conviction and sentence under Sections 279, 337 and 338 IPC set aside; prosecution failed to prove accused moved the bus without receiving conductor's signal. Conviction under Section 181 MV Act upheld as accused never produced driving license before any court. Fine for Section 181 MV Act conviction maintained.
key_holdings: To fasten criminal liability on a bus driver for negligent driving when a passenger falls while boarding, there must be evidence that the driver moved the bus without getting a signal from the conductor.
Absence of a driving license does not per se constitute rashness or negligence in driving; liability under Section 181 MV Act is separate from criminal negligence under IPC.
No presumption of negligence can be drawn against a driver merely because a passenger fell from the bus while boarding.

In revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 CrPC, the High Court does not exercise appellate jurisdiction and should not re-appreciate evidence to reverse concurrent factual findings unless there is perversity, illegality, or a gross miscarriage of justice.

key_passages.label: negligence_standard_bus_boarding
key_passages.quote: to fasten the liability with the driver for negligent driving in such a situation, there should be evidence that he moved the bus suddenly before the passenger could get into the vehicle or that the driver moved the vehicle even before getting any signal from the rear side.

key_passages.label: no_signal_evidence
key_passages.quote: Learned Courts below proceeded on the basis that since the passenger had fallen, therefore, the accused was negligent, which is not a correct proposition of law. The prosecution was required to prove that the accused had moved the bus without getting the signal from the conductor, and nobody asserted any such fact.

key_passages.label: license_absence_not_negligence
key_passages.quote: There is no presumption in law that a person who possesses only a learner's licence or possesses no licence at all does not know driving.

key_passages.label: outcome
key_passages.quote: the present appeal is partly allowed and judgment of conviction and order of sentence passed by learned Trial Court convicting and sentencing the accused for the commissions of offences punishable under Sections 279, 337, 338 of IPC as affirmed by the learned Appellate Court are ordered to be set aside

adverse_value: Holding that driving without a valid license does not per se constitute rash or negligent driving can be cited by accused drivers to resist IPC negligence convictions based solely on license absence.
summary: Chaina Ram, a bus driver, was convicted by the Trial Court under Sections 279, 337, 338 IPC and Section 181 MV Act after passenger Akshay Kumar's leg was crushed under the rear tyre of bus HP53-2713 while boarding at Palampur bus stand on 11.03.2003. The conviction was affirmed in appeal. In revision before the Himachal Pradesh High Court, the Court applied the law laid down by the Supreme Court in Mohd. Aynuddin v. State of A.P. and held that to impose criminal liability for negligent driving in a bus-boarding scenario, the prosecution must specifically prove that the driver moved the bus without receiving a signal from the conductor. No prosecution witness deposed to this fact. One witness (PW-9) suggested the victim was pushed by other passengers. Accordingly, the conviction under Sections 279, 337, 338 IPC was set aside for insufficient proof. However, since the accused never produced any driving license before any court despite being given the opportunity, the conviction under Section 181 MV Act was upheld. The revision was partly allowed to this limited extent.

case_title: Sanjay vs. State of Haryana
court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh
judge_or_bench: Hon'ble Mr. Justice Vinod S. Bhardwaj

owner_or_driver: Sanjay (driver and registered owner of HR 44 E 0207)

core_facts: On 17.11.2016 at about 7:30 P.M. near Kabrel bus stand area, Hisar, a pick-up van bearing registration No. HR 44 E 0207 driven rashly and negligently by Sanjay struck Balbir who was near the khokha of Vikas on the roadside.
The offending vehicle also rammed into the khokha of PW-7 Vikas, causing property damage. Sanjay fled the spot.
Balbir succumbed to injuries on 09.12.2016 after continuous treatment at multiple hospitals; Section 304-A IPC was added.
Accused Sanjay was identified in court by eyewitnesses PW-6 Satish (son of deceased) and PW-7 Vikas; no Test Identification Parade was held.
Trial Court convicted and sentenced the accused; Additional Sessions Judge dismissed the criminal appeal. The offending vehicle was not insured.
legal_issues: Whether the death of Balbir was proximately caused by the accident or broken by subsequent shifts in medical treatment.
Whether identification of accused in court without prior Test Identification Parade is legally valid.
Whether sentence of 2 years RI under Section 304-A IPC is excessive given mitigating circumstances.
outcome: Revision petition partly allowed on sentence only. Conviction under all sections affirmed. Sentence under Section 304-A IPC reduced from 2 years rigorous imprisonment to 18 months rigorous imprisonment, considering petitioner is aged 44 years, is the sole breadwinner with four minor children and a deceased wife, and civil compensation of Rs. 11,76,509 has already been awarded under Section 166 MV Act. All other sentences and fine unchanged.
key_holdings: Continuous shifting of an injured person from one hospital to another does not break the causal nexus between the accident and death; the family cannot be attributed negligence for such transfers absent positive medical evidence of improper treatment.
Identification of an accused in court by natural witnesses who had adequate opportunity to observe the accused is valid even without a prior Test Identification Parade.

The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur applies where a vehicle crosses the entire width of a road and strikes a pedestrian standing off the road; no contributory negligence can be attributed to such a pedestrian.
Compensation awarded in a civil motor accident claim is a relevant mitigating factor while considering modification of sentence in a criminal revision.

key_passages.label: causation_medical_treatment
key_passages.quote: It is not in dispute that the deceased remained under continuous medical treatment from the date of the accident until his demise. The mere shifting of the injured from one hospital to another cannot, by itself, be construed as an act of negligence attributable to the family of the deceased.

key_passages.label: res_ipsa_loquitur
key_passages.quote: The site plan further fortifies the prosecution case. The deceased was standing towards the kuccha portion near PW-7's shop, away from the metalled road. The petitioner, while driving a pick-up vehicle, approached from village Dobhi, failed to negotiate the T-point, and crossed the entire width of the road before striking the deceased.

key_passages.label: identification_valid
key_passages.quote: identification of the accused in court is valid and admissible in law, and that it is not always mandatory that such identification must be preceded by a Test Identification Parade.

key_passages.label: outcome_sentence_modified
key_passages.quote: I am of the opinion that the compensation awarded under the M.V. Act, 1988 to the tune of Rs.11,76,509/- has already been awarded, the interest of justice would be well served in case, the sentence awarded by the Courts is modified

summary: Sanjay, the registered owner and driver of pick-up van HR 44 E 0207, was convicted by the Trial Court under Sections 279, 337, 304-A, 427 IPC and Sections 181 and 192 MV Act for rashly driving and causing the death of Balbir on 17.11.2016 near Kabrel bus stand, Hisar. The Additional Sessions Judge dismissed the criminal appeal. In the criminal revision before the Punjab and Haryana High Court, the petitioner challenged the conviction on three grounds: the causal chain was broken by repeated hospital transfers, in-court identification without TIP was unreliable, and the sentence was excessive. The High Court rejected all contentions on conviction. It held that continuous medical treatment linked the death to the accident, and no medical evidence suggested improper treatment or a break in causation. Identification by natural witnesses PW-6 and PW-7, who had opportunity to observe the accused and were not impeached in cross-examination, was held valid without TIP. The site plan demonstrating that the pick-up van crossed the entire road to strike a pedestrian standing off the road established res ipsa loquitur. On sentence, the Court granted partial relief under Section 304-A, reducing imprisonment from two years to eighteen months RI, considering the petitioner's age, family circumstances (sole breadwinner, four minor children), and the civil compensation already awarded.

case_title: The Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. vs. Smt. Rani And Others
court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench

appellants: The Oriental Insurance Company Ltd., Amethi Sultanpur
claimants: parents of deceased Shyam Lal and Dhanpata Devi
owner_or_driver: Dev Raj Singh (owner of Truck 44 AH/4081)

core_facts: On 22.06.2009 at about 3:00 p.m. deceased Ramhet was riding Motorcycle No. UP 42-G/2180 from village Umaradeeh to Jamo with father-in-law Shyam Lal and mother-in-law Dhanpata Devi as pillion riders.

Mini Truck No. 44 AH/4081 driven rashly and negligently by Ram Sumer collided with the motorcycle from the front side near Dharmshala of Jivnanandan Tiwari Ka Purwa; Ramhet died on the spot and pillion riders sustained severe injuries.
FIR No. 375/2009 was registered under Sections 338, 279, 427, 304-A IPC at Police Station Jamo, District Sultanpur.
MACT Sultanpur (MACP No. 232 of 2009) awarded Rs. 4,17,500 with 7% interest using multiplier 17 and notional income Rs. 3,000 per month for the 32-year-old deceased.

Oriental Insurance Company (insurer of the offending truck) filed FAFO No. 757 of 2011 challenging the award on grounds of excessive compensation, contributory negligence, and wrongful rejection of Section 170 application.
legal_issues: Whether the compensation award of Rs. 4,17,500 was excessive.
Whether the deceased motorcycle driver was contributorily negligent for carrying two pillion passengers.
Whether the Tribunal erred in rejecting the insurer's application under Section 170 MV Act, and whether such rejection restricts the insurer's right to contest on all grounds.
outcome: Appeal dismissed. MACT award of Rs. 4,17,500 with interest at 7% per annum confirmed. Insurer directed to pay entire compensation within one month from date of judgment.
key_holdings: In motor accident claims the standard of proof is preponderance of probability, not proof beyond reasonable doubt; the Tribunal is not a criminal court.

Where the insurer is already impleaded as a party respondent in the claim petition, it can contest on all available grounds without restriction to statutory defences under Section 149(2); a separate Section 170 application is unnecessary.
Contributory negligence must be proved by documentary or oral evidence; an unsubstantiated plea of negligence for carrying two pillion riders will fail in absence of such evidence.
An insurer of the offending vehicle is responsible to indemnify the third party where the insurance coverage was effective at the relevant date of accident.

key_passages.label: standard_of_proof_civil
key_passages.quote: in a road accident claim, the strict principles of proof in a criminal case are not attracted.......

key_passages.label: contributory_negligence_unproved
key_passages.quote: no documentary evidence has been produced on behalf of the appellant-Oriental Insurance Company or on behalf of the owner of the offending vehicle Truck no. 44 AH/4081 to prove the fact of negligence on the part of Motorcycle driver

key_passages.label: insurance_liability
key_passages.quote: as the offending vehicle was insured by the appellant and the insurance coverage was effective at the relevant date of accident, there is no doubt as to the responsibility of the Insurance Company to demnify the third party who suffered the risk.

key_passages.label: outcome
key_passages.quote: In view of the discussions made hereinabove, there is no need to interfere with the judgment and award of the learned court below. The appeal is liable to be dismissed and it is hereby dismissed.

adverse_value: Suggests that the insurer's failure to call the driver for cross-examination and not producing any evidence of contributory negligence is fatal; insurer must adduce positive evidence to successfully plead contributory negligence.
summary: The Oriental Insurance Company appealed against a MACT Sultanpur award of Rs. 4,17,500 at 7% interest, arising from the death of Ramhet whose motorcycle UP 42-G/2180 was hit from the front by Mini Truck No. 44 AH/4081 on 22.06.2009. The insurer argued the award was excessive, the deceased was contributorily negligent in carrying two pillion riders, the Section 170 application was wrongly rejected, and the driver was not examined. The Allahabad High Court held: (i) in MACT proceedings the standard is preponderance of probability, not proof beyond reasonable doubt, making the claim valid; (ii) the insurer produced no documentary or oral evidence to rebut eyewitness PW-2 Shyam Lal's account that the truck driver was on the wrong side; (iii) since the insurer was already impleaded as opposite party respondent, it was entitled to contest on all grounds and the Section 170 application was unnecessary; and (iv) the multiplier of 17 for age 32 and notional income Rs. 3,000 per month were in accord with Schedule Table of Section 163(A). The appeal was dismissed and the award confirmed.

case_title: Surendra Singh And Another vs. Vijay Singh And Another (with connected appeals)
court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad

respondents: The New India Assurance Co. Ltd. and Others
claimants: Surendra Singh (father of Kapil Singh, 16 yrs)
Mukthar Singh and Others (parents of Rakesh Kumar, 27 yrs)
Prabhu Narain Agarwal and Others (parents of Pankaj Agarwal, 23 yrs)
Ramjeet and Others (parents of Dharmendra, 20 yrs)

statutes: Code of Civil Procedure Order XLI Rule 33
core_facts: Four connected First Appeals from Orders all involved death of bachelor sons (ages 16, 27, 23 and 20) caused in separate motor vehicle accidents, with parents claiming compensation.
In FAFO 3484/2012: Kapil Singh (16 years) was hit by truck UP-78 BT-3985 on 22.07.2010; Tribunal applied multiplier 7 based on age of claimant parents, not the deceased.
In FAFO 1199/2016: Rakesh Kumar (27 years) died on 29.11.2003; Tribunal applied multiplier 11 based on parents' age instead of deceased's age, and denied future prospects.
In FAFO 1820/2002: Pankaj Agarwal (23 years) died on 08.09.1997; Tribunal applied multiplier 15 but did not award future prospects for fixed salary employee.

In FAFO 4230/2017: Dharmendra (20 years) died on 17.09.2010; Reliance Insurance appealed the award claiming higher deduction for personal expenses, but the correct multiplier (18) with future prospects results in higher total compensation.

After the judgment reserved on 21.09.2017, the Supreme Court's constitution bench in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi was pronounced on 31.10.2017; the case was re-listed and decided thereafter.
legal_issues: Whether the multiplier in motor accident death cases involving bachelor deceased should be based on the age of the deceased or the age of the claimant (parent).
Whether future prospects under Pranay Sethi apply to deceased who was self-employed or on a fixed salary.
Whether the High Court can enhance compensation in an insurer's appeal even where no cross-objection has been filed by the claimants.
outcome: FAFO Nos. 3484/2012, 1199/2016 and 1820/2002 (claimant appeals) allowed with substantially enhanced compensation. FAFO No. 4230/2017 (insurer appeal) also allowed on the ground of higher personal expense deduction (1/2 for bachelor), but total compensation enhanced to Rs. 5,83,500/- because the correct multiplier of 18 and 40% future prospects together yielded a higher overall figure.
key_holdings: The multiplier for computing compensation in motor accident death cases must be applied with reference to the age of the deceased (using the Sarla Verma table as approved in Pranay Sethi), not the age of the claimant parent.
Future prospects must be awarded for self-employed persons and persons on fixed salary: 40% if deceased was below 40 years, 25% if between 40-50 years, and 10% if between 50-60 years.
Future prospects cannot be awarded on notional income, since notional income is never actually earned and cannot constitute 'established income' within the meaning of Pranay Sethi.

In non-adversarial MACT proceedings, a court can enhance compensation in an insurer's appeal without cross-objection by the claimants, by applying the correct legal principle laid down by the Supreme Court, under Order XLI Rule 33 CPC.

key_passages.label: multiplier_age_of_deceased
key_passages.quote: the multiplier to be used should be as mentioned in Column (4) of the table above (prepared by applying Susamma Thomas, Trilok Chandra and Charlie), which starts with an operative multiplier of 18 (for the age groups of 15 to 20 and 21 to 25 years)

key_passages.label: future_prospects_self_employed_fixed_salary
key_passages.quote: when we accept the principle of standardization, there is really no rationale not to apply the said principle to the self-employed or a person who is on a fixed salary. To follow the doctrine of actual income at the time of death and not to add any amount with regard to future prospects to the income for the purpose of determination of multiplicand would be unjust.

key_passages.label: enhancement_in_insurer_appeal
key_passages.quote: The issue of determination of just and fair compensation has to be treated to be open for examination to offer correction at least on the basis of binding principle and/or formula laid down by the Supreme Court.

key_passages.label: outcome
key_passages.quote: Consequently, the First Appeal From Order Nos. 3484 of 2012, 1199 of 2016 and 1820 of 2002 are allowed. First Appeal From Order No. 4230 of 2017 is also allowed. However, the amount of compensation awarded in that case would also stand enhanced as above.

adverse_value: Establishes that future prospects cannot be awarded on notional income (income not actually earned), which insurers can cite to resist future prospects claims where the deceased had no established income.
summary: Four First Appeals from Orders were consolidated before the Allahabad High Court to resolve common questions of law: the correct multiplier in bachelor death cases and entitlement to future prospects for the self-employed and fixed salary deceased. Judgment was reserved in September 2017 but the matter was re-opened after the Supreme Court's Constitution Bench decision in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Pranay Sethi (31.10.2017). The Court held: (i) the multiplier must be applied with reference to the age of the deceased, following the Sarla Verma table as approved in Pranay Sethi, and not the age of the parent-claimant; (ii) future prospects at 40% must be added to established income of self-employed and fixed-salary deceased below 40 years; (iii) future prospects cannot be awarded where income is notional, not established; (iv) standardized non-pecuniary heads from Pranay Sethi (loss of estate Rs. 15,000, consortium Rs. 40,000, funeral Rs. 15,000 enhanced at 10% every 3 years) apply. All three claimant appeals were allowed with substantially enhanced awards. The insurer's appeal on personal expense deduction was also allowed but the net effect was a higher total award. The Court exercised its power under Order XLI Rule 33 CPC to enhance even in the insurer's appeal.

case_title: Yogeshkumar Badharsinh Baria vs. Dilipkumar Ranchhodbhai Damor And Another
court: High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad
judge_or_bench: Honourable Ms. Justice Nisha M. Thakore
core_facts: Original claimant Yogeshkumar Badharsinh Baria sustained amputation of right leg below knee in a motor accident caused by rash and negligent driving of respondent no. 1.
Claimant was 28 years old at time of accident and was engaged as a skilled worker in masonry and centering work; also earned from agriculture.
MACT (Auxiliary) & 6th Additional District Judge, Panchmahals at Godhra awarded Rs. 4,68,600 in MACP No. 695 of 2016 (judgment dated 08.02.2023).
Disability certificates showed 65% permanent disability (doctor opined 70% but conceded 35% as whole body disability in cross-examination); Tribunal applied 35% disability.
Tribunal also assessed income at Rs. 4,000 per month instead of minimum wages rate of Rs. 7,800 per month applicable to skilled workers for April-September 2016 period.
legal_issues: Whether functional disability for amputation below knee should be assessed at 50% per Schedule I Part II of Employees Compensation Act 1923 rather than 35% whole body disability accepted by Tribunal.
Whether income should be assessed at minimum wages for skilled workers (Rs. 7,800/month) rather than Rs. 4,000/month accepted by Tribunal.
Whether future prospects at 40% under Pranay Sethi were applicable.
Whether future medical expenses for prosthetic leg were omitted by the Tribunal.
outcome: Appeal allowed. Total compensation revised from Rs. 4,68,600 to Rs. 16,42,440 (enhanced by Rs. 11,73,840), with interest at 9% p.a. from date of filing of claim petition till actual realization. Respondents held jointly and severally liable. Enhanced amount to be deposited with concerned Tribunal within eight weeks.
key_holdings: Functional disability for amputation below knee must be assessed at 50% per Schedule I Part II of the Employees Compensation Act 1923 (Entry Nos. 20 and 21), which is the percentage of loss of earning capacity for such specific injury, particularly when the claimant's occupation requires physical mobility.
Income of a skilled worker should be assessed with reference to the prescribed minimum wages; for April-September 2016 the applicable rate was Rs. 7,800 per month.

Courts should not adopt a stereotypical or myopic approach in assessing disabilities and compensation; the functional impact of the injury on the claimant's earning capacity in their specific occupation is the relevant measure.
Future medical expenses including the cost of prosthetic limb and its periodic replacement must be awarded as a separate head; failure by the Tribunal to consider this is a material error.

key_passages.label: courts_functional_disability
key_passages.quote: Courts should not adopt a stereotypical or myopic approach, but instead, view the matter taking into account the realities of life, both in the assessment of the extent of disabilities, and compensation under various heads.

key_passages.label: amputation_below_knee_50_percent
key_passages.quote: On bare appreciation of Schedule-I appended to Employees Compensation, 1923, under part-II thereof specifies list of injuries which would be deemed to result in permanent partial disablement. The said list includes amputation below knee at Entry nos.20 and 21, wherein the percentage of loss of earning capacity is suggested as 50.

key_passages.label: prosthetic_leg_future_medical
