key_passages.quote: the Tribunal ought to have considered the expenses towards prosthetic leg and the replacement of the same in the coming years. Noticing the age of the applicant as 28 years at the time of accident, this Court is inclined to consider the future medical expenses to the tune of Rs.2,50,000/-.

key_passages.label: outcome
key_passages.quote: the captioned appeal is hereby allowed. appellant - original claimant is held entitled to total amount of compensation to the tune of Rs.11,73,840/- with 9% interest from the date of filing of the claim petition till its actual realization

summary: Original claimant Yogeshkumar Badharsinh Baria, a 28-year-old skilled worker engaged in masonry and centering, suffered amputation of right leg below the knee in a motor accident. The MACT Godhra awarded Rs. 4,68,600 in MACP No. 695 of 2016, applying 35% whole body disability and income of Rs. 4,000 per month, and omitting future medical expenses. On appeal before the Gujarat High Court, the Court held: (i) functional disability for amputation below knee should be 50% per Schedule I Part II ECA 1923, Entries 20 and 21, especially for a masonry worker requiring full physical mobility; (ii) income must be assessed at minimum wages for skilled workers, being Rs. 7,800 per month for the relevant period April-September 2016; (iii) future prospects at 40% are applicable per Pranay Sethi as the claimant was below 40; (iv) multiplier 17 for age 28 confirmed; (v) future medical expenses including prosthetic limb Rs. 2,50,000 must be separately awarded. Applying monthly income Rs. 7,800, 40% future prospects (Rs. 10,920/month), 50% disability (Rs. 5,460/month), multiplier 17, the future loss of income was Rs. 11,13,840. Adding enhanced pain/suffering Rs. 1,00,000, SAT Rs. 25,000, medical Rs. 60,000, actual loss Rs. 93,600, and future medical Rs. 2,50,000, total compensation was enhanced to Rs. 16,42,440.

case_title: Rajesh Kumar Shukla And Another vs. Naseem Ahmed And Others (with connected petitions)
court: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (Pilot Court), Karkardooma Courts, Delhi
judge_or_bench: Sh. G. N. Pandey, MACT Judge

respondents: M/s Sparsh Transport Carrier Pvt. Ltd. (owner of truck UP 27 5376)
United India Insurance Co. Ltd. (insurer of truck)
claimants: Rajesh Kumar Shukla (father of deceased Shaksham, age 27)
Anushka Shukla (minor, age 6, daughter of Sandeep Kumar Shukla)
Meena Shukla (wife of Sandeep Kumar Shukla, age 29)
Vansh Shukla (minor, age 9 months, son of Sandeep Kumar Shukla)
owner_or_driver: M/s Sparsh Transport Carrier Pvt. Ltd. (owner)

core_facts: On 09.06.2015 at about 5:45 hrs, the family was travelling in Wagon-R No. DL 2 CAL 3562 on NH 24 from Delhi to Faizabad, UP.

At Village Kotra, PS Praswa, Sub Division Mohamdi, Lakhimpur Kheri, a speeding truck No. UP 27 5376 owned by M/s Sparsh Transport Carrier Pvt. Ltd. and driven by Naseem Ahmed came from the opposite direction in high speed and in gross violation of lane driving and hit the Wagon-R.

Shaksham Shukla (approximately 5 years old, DOB 17.10.2010) sustained fatal injuries and died; Anushka Shukla (6 years) sustained head injuries with 7 stitches; Meena Shukla (29 years) sustained rib fractures and head injuries; Vansh Shukla (9 months) sustained head injuries and right upper limb weakness.

FIR No. 16/15 registered under Sections 279/337/338/304A/427 IPC at PS Praswa. Respondent No. 3 (United India Insurance Co. Ltd.) confirmed policy No. 0805013114P107786597 was valid from 31.12.2014 to 30.12.2015.
legal_issues: Whether the accident occurred due to rash and negligent driving of truck UP 27 5376 and whether the petitioners suffered fatal injuries/simple and grievous injuries as a result.
Quantum of compensation in cases of death of a young child and injuries of varying severity to surviving family members.
outcome: All four claim petitions allowed. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. directed to pay: Rs. 6,53,334 with 9% interest from date of filing (MACT 14615/15 - death of Shaksham Shukla); Rs. 88,663 with 9% interest (MACT 15128/15 - injuries to Anushka Shukla); Rs. 1,83,444 with 9% interest (MACT 15129/15 - injuries to Meena Shukla); Rs. 26,172 with 9% interest (MACT 15182/15 - injuries to Vansh Shukla).
key_holdings: In motor accident claims, FIR, chargesheet and eyewitness testimony on the standard of preponderance of probability are sufficient to establish negligence of the offending vehicle driver.

For death of a child in a motor accident where no established income exists, compensation is computed using inflation-corrected notional income (Rs. 15,000 p.a. from Second Schedule, multiplied by CII for year of accident divided by base CII 331), deducting 1/3 for personal expenses, applying appropriate multiplier, and adding equal amount for composite non-pecuniary damages.
An insurer of the offending vehicle is liable to pay compensation when the insurance policy was valid at the time of accident and no violation of policy terms is proved.
Loss of wages of an employed person during treatment period and actual medical expenses are separate and cognizable heads of compensation.

key_passages.label: negligence_established
key_passages.quote: Shukla, Meena Shukla and Vansh Shukla sustained fatal injuries / simple and grievous injuries on 09.06.2015 due to rash and negligent driving of offending vehicle bearing No. UP 27 5376 driven by its driver i.e. respondent No. 1.

key_passages.label: standard_of_proof
key_passages.quote: establish their case on the touchstone of preponderance of probability. The standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt could not have been applied.

key_passages.label: child_death_cii_formula
key_passages.quote: The death occurred on 09.06.2015 and therefore the CII (cost inflation index) for the financial year 2015-2016 i.e. Rs. 1,081/- would apply. The age of the deceased child was about 5 years and therefore the calculation is to be made on multiplier of 10.

key_passages.label: insurer_liability
key_passages.quote: Respondent No. 3 is the insurance company which admittedly has issued a valid insurance policy of the offending vehicle. There is no evidence on behalf of respondent No. 3 to show that there was any violation of the rules and terms of policy by the respondent No. 1 & 2.

summary: Four connected MACT petitions filed by members of the Shukla family arising from a road accident on 09.06.2015 on NH 24 at Lakhimpur Kheri when speeding truck UP 27 5376, owned by M/s Sparsh Transport Carrier Pvt. Ltd. and driven by Naseem Ahmed, collided with their Wagon-R car DL 2 CAL 3562. Shaksham Shukla (age 5 years) died of fatal injuries; Anushka Shukla (6 yrs, head injuries), Meena Shukla (29 yrs, rib fractures), and Vansh Shukla (9 months, head injuries) survived with varying injuries. The Tribunal applied the preponderance of probability standard and found negligence established through criminal records, eyewitness testimony, and adverse inference from the driver's non-appearance in the witness box. For Shaksham's death, the Delhi High Court's formula for child deaths was applied: notional income Rs. 15,000 p.a. (Second Schedule) inflation-corrected using CII 1081/331 = Rs. 49,000 p.a.; deducting 1/3 personal expenses gives Rs. 32,666; multiplier 10 for child below 5 years gives pecuniary loss Rs. 3,26,667; adding equal amount for composite non-pecuniary damages, total = Rs. 6,53,334. United India Insurance Co. Ltd., confirmed as insurer with valid policy, was held liable for all amounts across the four petitions.

case_title: Sangeeta Devi W/O Sh. Vinod Kumar Singh vs Mahesh Chand & Ors
court: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (Pilot Court), Karkardooma Courts, Delhi

respondents: Mahesh Chand s/o Sh. Kishori Lal

core_facts: Deceased child Shivam (aged approximately 10 years, born 2005) died on 14.01.2014 after being hit by motorcycle No. DL 3SBY5198 near Annpurna Mandir, Sonia Vihar, Delhi
The motorcycle was driven rashly and negligently at high speed by respondent Mahesh Chand
Shivam was taken to Jag Pravesh Chandra Hospital and then Lok Nayak Hospital where he died on the same day
Claimant is the mother of the deceased child
Respondent did not file a reply or lead evidence despite opportunities
No insurance company was made a party; liability fastened solely on respondent-driver
legal_issues: Whether the deceased died due to rash and negligent driving of vehicle No. DL 3SBY5198 by respondent
Whether claimant is entitled to compensation and on what quantum for death of a child
outcome: DAR petition allowed. Respondent directed to pay compensation of Rs. 5,74,000/- with interest at 9% p.a. from date of filing till realisation.
key_holdings: Compensation for death of a child is computed using the notional income formula laid down by Delhi High Court in MAC Apps. No. 554/2010, with inflation correction using Cost Inflation Index from the base year 1997-98 and age-appropriate multiplier.
For a child aged up to 10 years the multiplier of 10 is applied and an equal amount is added as composite non-pecuniary damages.
Uncontested FIR and criminal record, coupled with absence of any defence evidence, is sufficient to prove rash and negligent driving on a preponderance of probability standard.

key_passages.label: negligence_proof
key_passages.quote: I have gone through the record and documents in respect of the accident caused to the petitioner which is prima facie suggestive of negligence of respondent in driving the vehicle at the time of accident.

key_passages.label: compensation_quantum_child
key_passages.quote: The inflation calculated notional income comes to Rs. 42,553/- (15,000/- x 939/331), rounded off Rs. 43,000/-. After deducting 1/3rd and applying the multiplier of 10, the pecuniary loss to estate is computed as ( Rs. 43,000/- x 1/3 x 10) Rs. 2,86,667/-.

key_passages.label: just_compensation_outcome
key_passages.quote: I accordingly award an amount of compensation of Rs. 5,73,334/- rounded to Rs. 5,74,000/- in favour of the Claimant and against Respondent.

key_passages.label: standard_of_proof
key_passages.quote: strict proof of any accident caused by a particular bus in a particular manner may not be possible to be done by the claimant. The claimants were merely to establish their case on the touchstone of preponderance of probability.

summary: The claimant-mother Sangeeta Devi filed a DAR petition under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, claiming compensation for the death of her 10-year-old son Shivam, who was killed on 14.01.2014 near Annpurna Mandir, Sonia Vihar, Delhi. The deceased was hit by motorcycle No. DL 3SBY5198 driven rashly and negligently by respondent Mahesh Chand. The respondent neither filed a reply nor led evidence, and the criminal record along with the mother's testimony established negligence on a preponderance of probability. On the quantum, the Tribunal applied the formula prescribed by the Delhi High Court for deaths of children: the notional income of Rs. 15,000 p.a. (Second Schedule) was inflation-corrected using the Cost Inflation Index for 2013-14 (CII 939 against base 331), yielding a notional income of Rs. 43,000 p.a. After one-third deduction for personal expenses and applying a multiplier of 10 (appropriate for age group up to 10 years), the pecuniary loss to estate was Rs. 2,86,667. An equal amount was added as composite non-pecuniary damages, yielding total compensation of Rs. 5,74,000. Interest was awarded at 9% p.a. from the date of filing. The award was made solely against the respondent-driver.

case_title: Suman Lata And Ors. vs Madan Mohan Sonkar And Ors.
court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad

appellants: New India Assurance Company Ltd. (F.A.F.O. No. 510 of 2001)
Suman Lata and others (F.A.F.O. No. 509 of 2001)

core_facts: Dr. Kamlesh Kumar, an Eye Surgeon aged 43 years, was killed on 12 August 1996 when a jeep bearing No. P.42-A 0174 hit his scooter No. U.P. 42/1395 from behind near Ayodhya
The jeep was owned by Madan Mohan Sonkar and insured with New India Assurance Company Ltd.; the driver Gaya Prasad held a valid driving licence
MACT-II Additional District Judge, Faizabad awarded Rs. 16,09,000 with 9% p.a. interest by judgment dated 7 August 2001
The insurer filed F.A.F.O. No. 510/2001 challenging the award amount; the claimants filed F.A.F.O. No. 509/2001 seeking enhancement
Monthly salary of deceased at the time of death was Rs. 9,776 (old scale) revised to Rs. 12,593 (5th Pay Commission scale) from 01.01.1996
Tribunal applied multiplier of 10 instead of the correct multiplier of 12 for age 43
legal_issues: Whether the insurer can challenge the quantum of compensation without permission under Section 170 of the MV Act
Whether contributory negligence on the part of the deceased was established
Whether the Tribunal applied the correct multiplier and correctly computed compensation
Whether the rate of interest of 9% per annum was excessive
outcome: Both appeals disposed of with a modification: the rate of interest was reduced from 9% to 7.5% per annum. The award amount of Rs. 16,09,000 was confirmed. The share of minors was directed to be deposited in a nationalised bank in fixed deposits till majority.
key_holdings: When the jeep hit the deceased's scooter from behind, findings of rash and negligent driving negate any case of contributory negligence; no separate finding on contributory negligence is necessary where the facts are self-speaking.
An insurer who has no valid defence under Section 149(2) has no right to challenge quantum of compensation without permission under Section 170 of the MV Act.
Where the Tribunal's formula under Susamma Thomas leads to the same figure as would result from the correct multiplier applied to revised salary, there is no ground for interference.
Interest on compensation may be reduced to 7.5% per annum having regard to prevailing bank rates.

key_passages.label: contributory_negligence
key_passages.quote: when there are the findings in unambiguous and clear terms that the deceased was hit by the jeep from behind, then no question of contributory negligence on the part of the deceased arises and the things being obvious, apparent and self-speaking, there was no question of any contributory negligence on the part of the deceased.

key_passages.label: insurance_liability_section_170
key_passages.quote: the Assurance Company cannot challenge the quantum of compensation without having permission under Section 170 of the Act.

key_passages.label: just_compensation
key_passages.quote: the compensation awarded must be just, fair and reasonable.

key_passages.label: interest_on_compensation
key_passages.quote: we are of the view that the interest should be reduced to 7.5% per annum.

adverse_value: Insurer cannot challenge quantum without Section 170 permission — cuts both ways but limits insurer's appeal rights.
summary: Two First Appeals arose from the same MACT award of Rs. 16,09,000 with 9% interest, passed by MACT-II Additional District Judge, Faizabad, for the death of Dr. Kamlesh Kumar (Eye Surgeon, aged 43) who was knocked down by a jeep from behind while riding his scooter in Ayodhya on 12 August 1996. The insurer (New India Assurance Co. Ltd.) appealed challenging the quantum, while the claimants (widow, minor children and father) appealed for enhancement. The High Court rejected the insurer's contributory-negligence argument because the undisputed finding was that the jeep struck the scooter from behind, making any question of the deceased's negligence self-evidently untenable. The insurer's challenge to the multiplier (10 instead of 12) was also rejected on the ground that the overall compensation figure was correct when the Tribunal's formula was read as a whole — and in any case the insurer had no standing to challenge quantum without Section 170 permission. The claimants' enhancement appeal was dismissed because the compensated amount would not materially change even if the revised pay scale and future prospects were considered. The sole modification was a reduction of the interest rate from 9% to 7.5% p.a. to align with prevailing bank rates.

case_title: Sunil Shreesail Killiket vs Mr. Subbaray and Bajaj Allianz General Insurance Co. Ltd.
court: III Additional Judge and Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Court of Small Causes, Bengaluru (SCCH-18)
judge_or_bench: Lavanya H.N., III Addl. Judge & Member MACT

respondents: Bajaj Allianz General Insurance Co. Ltd. (insurer)
insurer: Bajaj Allianz General Insurance Co. Ltd.

core_facts: On 09.01.2021 at about 5.30 p.m., petitioner Sunil Shreesail Killiket was a passenger in car No. KA-03-AC-5300 near MG Patel Hospital, Indi, Vijayapura when the driver Appu drove it rashly and negligently, causing the car to fall and rotate on the roadside
Petitioner sustained spinal cord injury (C7-T1), underwent surgery (laminectomy and C4-D2 fusion), and was left in wheelchair with 90% whole body disability and 100% functional disability
Medical expenses incurred of Rs. 14,85,260/-; petitioner was 25 years old at the time of accident
Insurer's defence: driver had no valid driving licence; vehicle used without valid permit and fitness certificate
Tribunal found the driver did not possess a driving licence; breach of fundamental condition proved by insurer
Insurer nonetheless directed to pay compensation to the third-party petitioner under the 'pay and recover' principle
legal_issues: Whether the accident was caused by rash and negligent driving of the driver of car KA-03-AC-5300
Whether petitioner is entitled to compensation and at what quantum
Whether insurer is absolved of liability due to driver having no driving licence, or whether pay and recover should be ordered
outcome: Petition allowed in part. Total compensation of Rs. 87,49,500/- awarded against Respondent No. 1 (owner). Insurer directed to pay first under 'pay and recover' principle with liberty to recover from Respondent No. 1. Interest at 6% p.a. on Rs. 68,21,500/- from date of petition till realisation.
key_holdings: A third party petitioner cannot be made to suffer due to the fault of the owner in allowing an unlicensed driver; the insurer must pay the compensation first and recover from the owner under the 'pay and recover' doctrine.
Where functional disability is 100%, future prospects at 40% must be added to notional income for computing loss of future earnings; multiplier of 18 applies for age 25.
Attendant charges are awarded using the multiplier method (Rs. 8,000/month x 12 x 18) for permanently disabled victims who require lifetime care.
Loss of marriage prospects is a compensable head for a victim with 90% whole body disability.

key_passages.label: pay_and_recover
key_passages.quote: But, on the said ground, the petitioner is third party, cannot be made to suffer due to fault of owner when the vehicle is covered with insurance at relevant point of time.

key_passages.label: driving_license_breach
key_passages.quote: riding/driving vehicle on public road without having driveling license it is not only an offense punishable under section 3(1) r/w 181 of MV Act but also fundamental and statutory breach of insurance policy. Hence, the respondent No.2 is not liable to indemnify the respondent No.1 for the loss suffered by him though there was insurance on the date of accident.

key_passages.label: compensation_quantum
key_passages.quote: In all, the petitioner is entitled for the compensation of Rs.87,49,260/- which is rounded to Rs.87,49,500/- (Rupees Eighty Seven Lakh Forty Nine Thousand & Five Hundred only).

key_passages.label: disability_finding
key_passages.quote: the petitioner was found to have sever spastic weakness, which amounts to disability of 90% to whole body. From this it could be said that petitioner unable to do any work including his day to day personal works such as attending nature call on his own without support of anyone.

adverse_value: Insurer proved breach of policy (no driving licence) and was found not liable to indemnify owner, but still directed to pay and recover; this case confirms that proving licence breach does not by itself exonerate the insurer from paying the third party.
summary: Petitioner Sunil Shreesail Killiket (25 years) sustained catastrophic spinal cord injuries on 09.01.2021 when a car driven by an unlicensed driver overturned near Vijayapura, leaving him in a wheelchair with 90% whole body and 100% functional disability. He filed a claim under Section 166 of the MV Act against the vehicle owner and Bajaj Allianz General Insurance Co. Ltd. The Tribunal found rash and negligent driving proved. The insurer established that the driver had no valid driving licence, which constituted a fundamental breach of policy, and was held not liable to indemnify the owner. However, applying the 'pay and recover' principle (Pappu v. Vinod Kumar Lamba; Shamanna v. Oriental Insurance), the insurer was directed to pay the compensation first with liberty to recover from the owner. Compensation totalling Rs. 87,49,500/- was awarded, including Rs. 45,36,000 for future loss of income (notional income Rs. 15,000/month + 40% future prospects x multiplier 18 x 100% disability), Rs. 14,85,260 medical expenses, Rs. 17,28,000 attendant charges, Rs. 3,00,000 loss of marriage prospects, and other heads. Interest awarded at 6% p.a. on the principal sum (excluding attendant charges and future medical expenses).

case_title: New India Assurance Co. Ltd. vs Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharnakeri
court: High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru (Special Full Bench)
judge_or_bench: Hon'ble Mrs. Justice B.V. Nagarathna, Hon'ble Mr. Justice K.N. Phaneendra, Hon'ble Mr. Justice B.A. Patil

appellants: New India Assurance Co. Ltd., Bijapur (by its Divisional Manager)

core_facts: Claimant Yallavva W/O Yamanappa Dharanakeri was travelling as a coolie/gratuitous passenger in Tempo No. KA-28/B-5434 (a goods vehicle) from Tikota to Dhulkhed village for coolie work on 24.04.2006
The tempo's driver drove rashly near Horti village on NH-13, the vehicle turned turtle and the claimant sustained grievous injuries
MACT-V, Bijapur awarded compensation of Rs. 1,000/- with 6% p.a. interest and directed New India Assurance Co. to pay and recover from owner (Respondent No. 2)
The insurer appealed arguing it was not liable since the claimant was a gratuitous passenger in a goods vehicle — a policy breach under Section 149(2)

Learned Single Judge referred two questions to a Full Bench: (I) whether a contractual policy with extra premium makes insurer liable to pay and recover for any breach; (II) whether 'pay and recover' rule applies in view of Section 149 mandate
legal_issues: Whether the Tribunal and High Court have jurisdiction to pass a 'pay and recover' order even when the insurer has proved a breach of policy condition under Section 149(2), or whether only the Supreme Court can do so under Article 142
Whether the distinction between 'Act policy' and 'contractual policy' (extra premium) affects the insurer's liability to pay and recover
What constitutes 'fundamental breach' and how the 'main purpose rule' applies to Section 149 of the MV Act
outcome: Appeal dismissed. Full Bench held that Tribunals and High Courts can pass 'pay and recover' orders even when the insurer has proved a breach of policy under Section 149(2), subject to the exception of fraud or collusion by the victim with the insured. The only circumstance where the insurer can be completely absolved is if the third party/victim was responsible for or complicit in the breach.
key_holdings: Tribunals and High Courts — and not only the Supreme Court under Article 142 — have the power to pass a 'pay and recover' order against an insurer that has proved a defence under Section 149(2) of the MV Act.

A 'fundamental breach' of a policy condition is one which is referable to the cause of the accident; but even a fundamental breach does not automatically absolve the insurer of its liability to pay the third party — it only entitles the insurer to recover from the insured.
The insurer can be completely absolved of liability only where the third party/victim was individually or in collusion with the insured responsible for the breach of a fundamental condition.
The 'main purpose rule' requires that conditions in an insurance policy be interpreted so that no innocent third party suffers for a breach of condition for which they had no responsibility.
A pay and recover order is an exercise of discretion based on facts and circumstances of each case; the court must give appropriate reasons.

key_passages.label: pay_and_recover_tribunal_power
key_passages.quote: Tribunals and High Courts can also pass such an order of pay and recovery but there must be valid reasons to be recorded in absolving liability of the Insurance Company or fastening the liability on the Insurance Company, again by considering the facts and circumstances of each case.

key_passages.label: fundamental_breach_definition
key_passages.quote: a mere breach of any condition, even if it falls under Section 149 (2) of the Act but which is not responsible for the cause of accident, in such an eventuality, the insurance company cannot absolve itself from its liability because under the doctrine of indemnity, the insurer is liable to reimburse the awarded amount to the insured.

key_passages.label: main_purpose_rule
key_passages.quote: the main purpose recognized under the statute is that no third party should suffer despite breach of any condition in the insurance policy between insurer and insured. Though such breach of condition is proved by the insurer against the insured, it should be treated as an inter se dispute between the insurer and the insured and the same should not affect the right of a third party

key_passages.label: answer_to_reference
key_passages.quote: The Insurer is liable to pay the third party and recover from the insured even if there is breach of any condition recognized under Section 149(2), even if it is a fundamental breach (that is breach of condition which is the cause for the accident) and the insurer proves the said breach, in view of the mandate under Section 149(1) of the Act.

key_passages.label: fraud_exception
key_passages.quote: no such order can be passed against the insurer, if, on the facts and circumstances of a case, a finding is given by the court that the third party (injured or deceased) had played any fraud or was in collusion with the insured, individually or collectively, for a wrongful gain to themselves or cause wrongful loss to the insurer.

adverse_value: Insurer directed to pay and recover even when gratuitous-passenger breach was proved; insurer retains pay-and-recover rights but cannot be fully exonerated for third-party claims absent fraud/collusion — limits insurer's ability to use policy breach as complete defence.
summary: In this Special Full Bench judgment of the Karnataka High Court (three judges), the court answered a reference arising from MFA No. 30131/2010 in which the New India Assurance Co. challenged a Tribunal order directing it to pay Rs. 1,000 compensation and recover from the insured for injuries to a coolie (Yallavva) travelling as a gratuitous passenger in a goods vehicle (Tempo KA-28/B-5434) that overturned on 24.04.2006. The insurer argued the breach (gratuitous passenger in goods vehicle) was a fundamental breach under Section 149(2) and that only the Supreme Court under Article 142 could order 'pay and recover.' After exhaustively analysing Sections 146, 147 and 149 of the MV Act, the Full Bench held: (1) Tribunals and High Courts can pass 'pay and recover' orders; this power is not exclusive to the Supreme Court. (2) A 'fundamental breach' is one causally connected to the accident, but even proving such a breach does not completely absolve the insurer vis-à-vis an innocent third party. (3) The 'main purpose rule' — protecting innocent third parties — means the insurer's inter-se dispute with the insured cannot affect the third party's right to compensation. (4) Complete absolution is possible only if the victim/third party was responsible for or in collusion with the insured in causing the breach. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: National Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Ellappa and others
court: High Court of Judicature at Madras

appellants: National Insurance Co. Ltd., Hosur (in all CMAs)
claimants: Ellappa and others (multiple claimants across 11 petitions)

core_facts: On 21.06.1991, a large group of persons was travelling in tempo TN-29 Y-1724 towards Thenkanikottai on Kelamangalam-Parandur road; at about 9.00 a.m. the driver drove rashly and the vehicle capsized near Koottur diversion road, injuring many and killing some
The owner-cum-driver Kuttiappan was carrying paying passengers (52 persons) in the goods vehicle, which is not authorised under the policy
National Insurance Co. Ltd. had insured the vehicle and contested liability on two grounds: (i) goods vehicle not authorised to carry passengers, (ii) driver had no valid driving licence at the time
MACT, Hosur held the insurer liable and fixed quantum of compensation in various amounts across 11 petitions
Full Bench of Madras HC in Nagammal's case (2009-I-CTC-1) had already settled that insurer is not statutorily required to cover liability for passengers in a goods vehicle

Madras HC applied its own Full Bench guidelines (Nagammal) but exercised discretion to pass 'pay and recover' order due to the claimants being poor village residents who had been litigating since 1996
legal_issues: Whether the insurance company is liable to pay compensation to gratuitous passengers travelling in a goods vehicle
Whether a 'pay and recover' direction can be issued against the insurer despite no statutory liability for such passengers
Whether the quantum of compensation awarded by the Tribunal is correct
outcome: All 11 civil miscellaneous appeals disposed of. Common award of the Tribunal as to quantum confirmed. Insurer directed to pay compensation to claimants first and to recover the same from the owner-cum-driver (Kuttiappan/first respondent in MCOPs) by filing execution proceedings directly before the concerned court.
key_holdings: Passengers travelling in a goods vehicle — whether gratuitous or paying — are not covered under the insurance policy and the insurer has no statutory liability to pay them compensation.

Notwithstanding the absence of statutory liability, the court can exercise discretion to direct 'pay and recover' in appropriate cases, particularly where the claimants are poor and have been litigating for years.
The insurer, once directed to pay and recover, can initiate execution proceedings against the insured directly without filing a fresh suit.

key_passages.label: insurance_liability_goods_vehicle_passengers
key_passages.quote: The insurer is not liable to pay compensation to such passenger since the statute has not imposed any duty or liability upon it for that purpose.

key_passages.label: pay_and_recover_discretion
key_passages.quote: In order to shorten the litigation and as the claimants, being the beneficiaries receiving the benefits flowing from the Motor Vehicles Act, a Social Welfare Legislation, are entitled to get their compensation without undergoing cumbersome legal proceedings, a direction of "pay and recover" is inevitable.

key_passages.label: quantum_confirmed
key_passages.quote: As far as the quantum of compensation made available to each of the claimants is concerned, this court does not find any infirmity in the observations of the Tribunal. The common award as to the quantum of compensation is confirmed.

key_passages.label: execution_mode
key_passages.quote: The appellant insurance company is at liberty to institute execution proceedings against the owner of the vehicle/first respondent in the MCOPs directly before the court concerned as per the procedure set out in Nanjappa's case.

adverse_value: Insurer is not statutorily liable for gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles; however, court exercised discretion to pass pay-and-recover order. Insurer-supporting precedent on the statutory non-coverage point, but adverse on the pay-and-recover outcome.
summary: Eleven Civil Miscellaneous Appeals were filed by National Insurance Co. Ltd. challenging MACT awards arising from the capsizing of goods tempo TN-29 Y-1724 on 21.06.1991 near Koottur, in which a large group of persons travelling as passengers sustained injuries and some died. The insurer contested liability on the basis that the passengers were travelling in a goods vehicle without authorisation and that the driver had no valid licence. Following the Full Bench ruling in Nagammal's case (2009-I-CTC-1), the Madras High Court reiterated that persons travelling as passengers in goods vehicles — whether gratuitous or paying — are not covered under the insurance policy and the insurer has no statutory obligation to compensate them. The owner-cum-driver Kuttiappan was held personally liable. However, exercising discretion given the poverty of the claimants and the fact they had been litigating since 1996, the court directed the insurer to pay the compensation first and recover it from the insured by executing the award directly before the executing court without needing to file a fresh suit. The quantum awarded by the Tribunal was confirmed without modification.

case_title: The Manager, New India Assurance Co. Ltd. vs Chennamma and others
court: High Court of Judicature at Madras
judge_or_bench: Hon'ble Mrs. Justice R. Banumathi and Hon'ble Mr. Justice R. Subbiah

appellants: The Manager, New India Assurance Co. Ltd., Chennai
respondents: M/s. Ravi Bricks Pvt. Ltd. (R5 — owner of lorry)
owner_or_driver: unidentified driver of lorry TN-20 Z 3024

core_facts: On 5.10.2002 at 1.45 p.m., deceased Venkata Kondaiya (aged 38 years, Rivetter Grade II at Chennai Port Trust, earning Rs. 10,395/month) was riding his Hero Honda motorcycle TN-22 Y 1596 on Chennai-Minjur Road near Pungambedu bus stand when lorry TN-20 Z 3024 (belonging to 5th Respondent M/s Ravi Bricks Pvt. Ltd.) driven rashly in the opposite direction dashed against the motorcycle; deceased succumbed at Stanley Government Hospital
Claimants (widow, minor children, mother) filed claim petition claiming Rs. 30,00,000/-; MACT, Tiruvallur awarded Rs. 12,89,500/- with pay and recover order against insurer
Insurer's defence: driver held only LMV (light motor vehicle) licence; the lorry was a 'heavy goods vehicle' (GVW 16,200 kg); driver lacked valid licence to drive HGV
Registration Certificate (Ex.P8) confirmed lorry as 'Heavy Goods Vehicle' with GVW 16,200 kg exceeding the 12,000 kg threshold in Section 2(16)
Driver's history sheet (Ex.R1) showed licence for 'light motor vehicle' with an endorsement to drive 'transport vehicle' but no separate endorsement for 'heavy goods vehicle'
Owner remained ex parte before the Tribunal
legal_issues: Whether the lorry TN-20 Z 3024 is a 'heavy goods vehicle' within Section 2(16) of the MV Act
Whether a driver holding an LMV licence with 'transport vehicle' endorsement had valid driving licence to drive a heavy goods vehicle
Whether the insurer's defence of invalid driving licence justifies exoneration or only pay and recover
Whether quantum of compensation awarded by the Tribunal is just and reasonable
outcome: Appeal dismissed. Tribunal's award of Rs. 12,89,500/- confirmed. Insurer directed to pay and recover from 5th Respondent (owner M/s Ravi Bricks Pvt. Ltd.) as per the mode stated in Nanjappan's case. 4th Claimant (Ramulamma) having died, her share to be apportioned equally among remaining claimants.
key_holdings: For a goods vehicle the gross vehicle weight (not unladen weight) determines vehicle classification; a lorry with GVW of 16,200 kg is a 'heavy goods vehicle' under Section 2(16) of the MV Act.
An endorsement to drive 'transport vehicle' on an LMV licence does not authorise driving a 'heavy goods vehicle'; a separate endorsement is required for HGV.

When the driver of a vehicle did not have a valid driving licence to drive that category of vehicle, this constitutes a breach of Section 149(2)(a)(ii); however, as a third-party claim this does not exonerate the insurer — a 'pay and recover' order is appropriate.

In third-party risks cases the insurer has to indemnify the claimant and recover from the insured; the insurer cannot disown liability merely because the driver held a licence for a different category of vehicle.

key_passages.label: heavy_goods_vehicle_classification
key_passages.quote: since the gross vehicle weight of the lorry involved is 16,200 kilograms, we are of the view that the vehicle/lorry involved in the accident is only a "heavy goods vehicle".

key_passages.label: license_endorsement_insufficient
key_passages.quote: endorsement to drive 'transport vehicle' would not amount to valid licence to drive 'heavy goods vehicle'.

key_passages.label: pay_and_recover_third_party
key_passages.quote: the Hon'ble Supreme Court has consistently held that in case of Third Party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so directed, to recover the same from the insured.

key_passages.label: quantum_confirmed
key_passages.quote: The total compensation of Rs.12,89,500/- awarded by the Tribunal is just and reasonable and the same is confirmed. Appellant-Insurance Company is directed to pay the said compensation of Rs.12,89,500/- along with interest at the rate of 7.5% per annum from the date of Claim Petition till the date of realisation to the Claimants and recover the same from the 5th Respondent, owner of the vehicle.

adverse_value: Confirms that insurer who proves LMV-only-licence breach for a HGV still cannot be exonerated from paying third-party claimants; only pay and recover is available. Insurer-friendly on the substantive licence-breach finding but adverse on the remedy.
summary: The widow, minor children and mother of Venkata Kondaiya (Rivetter at Chennai Port Trust, aged 38) challenged a MACT award which directed the insurer (New India Assurance Co. Ltd.) to pay Rs. 12,89,500/- and recover from the lorry owner (M/s Ravi Bricks Pvt. Ltd.) after the lorry TN-20 Z 3024 fatally knocked down the deceased's motorcycle on 5.10.2002. The insurer appealed arguing the driver had only an LMV licence with a 'transport vehicle' endorsement and lacked a specific HGV licence, so it should be fully absolved. The Madras High Court undertook a detailed analysis of Sections 2(16), 2(21) and 2(47) of the MV Act and the Central Government's vehicle-classification notifications. It held that the lorry with a gross vehicle weight of 16,200 kg was unambiguously a 'heavy goods vehicle', and that a 'transport vehicle' endorsement on an LMV licence does not extend to driving an HGV. The breach under Section 149(2)(a)(ii) was thus proved. However, following the consistent Supreme Court position (Swaran Singh, Iyyappan, Laxmi Narain Dhut), the court held that in third-party risk cases the insurer must indemnify first and recover from the insured. The quantum (Rs. 12,89,500/-) and interest (7.5% p.a.) were confirmed unchanged. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Sukumarbai Suryakant Nikam And Ors
court: High Court of Judicature at Bombay, Bench at Aurangabad

appellants: United India Insurance Company Ltd., Latur (through its Authorized Signatory/Divisional Manager)
respondents: Abdul Gazi s/o Abdul Rahim Shaikh (R4 — driver-cum-owner)
owner_or_driver: Abdul Gazi s/o Abdul Rahim Shaikh (driver-cum-owner of Tata Sumo jeep)

core_facts: On 15.04.2012, deceased Suryakant Pandurang Nikam (aged 50) was travelling as a passenger in Tata Sumo jeep No. MH 23/E-3762 on Tandulja-Ambajogai road after attending a marriage ceremony at village Padoli, when driver-cum-owner Abdul Gazi lost control near Amba Sakhar Karkhana petrol pump at about 4.00 p.m.; the vehicle got skid, hit a bridge railing and overturned
Suryakant succumbed to injuries after 17 days of hospitalisation (Ashwini Accident Hospital, YCM College Hospital and Civil Hospital, Latur)
Claimants (widow and two sons) claimed Rs. 7,50,000/-; MACT, Latur awarded Rs. 7,79,800/- with interest against the insurer jointly and severally with owner-driver, with a pay and recover order

Insurance company's defence: the vehicle was a private jeep, but respondent No. 4 (owner) was carrying the deceased for hire or reward (jeep hired by Sheshrao for his son's marriage); this was a wilful fundamental breach of the Act policy (Section 149(2)(a)(ia))
No additional premium was paid for passenger risk; the policy was an Act policy
Tribunal found the breach proved but still directed pay and recover; High Court reversed this
legal_issues: Whether the insurer can be directed to pay compensation under the 'pay and recover' principle when the deceased was a passenger in a private vehicle plied for hire or reward — a breach of the Act policy under Section 149(2)(a)(ia)
Whether a passenger in a private vehicle hired for reward qualifies as a 'third party' for the purpose of Section 147 of the MV Act
Whether the Tribunal or High Court can pass a 'pay and recover' order in such circumstances, or whether this is confined to the Supreme Court under Article 142
outcome: Appeal partly allowed. MACT award set aside to the extent of holding the insurance company liable jointly and severally. Claim as against the insurance company dismissed. Claimants directed to recover compensation solely from opponent No. 1 (driver-cum-owner Abdul Gazi). Insurance company's deposited amount to be returned.
key_holdings: A passenger in a private vehicle plied for hire or reward against the Act policy is not a 'third party' within the meaning of Section 147 of the MV Act; the risk of such occupant is not covered under an Act policy.
Where the risk of the deceased passenger is not covered under the Act policy and the deceased cannot be termed a 'third party', the Tribunal cannot pass a 'pay and recover' order against the insurer.
The insurer must be completely exonerated, not merely subjected to pay and recover, when the deceased's claim falls entirely outside the statutory coverage.

key_passages.label: passenger_not_third_party
key_passages.quote: when the passenger travelling from the vehicle for hire or reward, against the policy condition, cannot be treated as "third party"; then the Tribunal ought not to have passed the order of 'pay and recover' in this case.

key_passages.label: insurer_exonerated
key_passages.quote: the Tribunal has committed error in holding the Insurance Company liable to pay jointly and severally with opponent No. 01 and to that extent, decision of the Tribunal needs to be set aside.

key_passages.label: policy_breach_defence
key_passages.quote: respondent No.1 was carrying passenger on hire and therefore, there was willful fundamental breach of the policy. Insurance company is not liable to pay compensation to the petitioners.

key_passages.label: asha_rani_principle
key_passages.quote: passengers in a private vehicle are not to be treated as "third party". Further the ratio in Asha Rani & Ors is reiterated by another Three Judge Bench of the Apex Court

adverse_value: A claimant travelling in a private vehicle being plied for hire or reward is not a 'third party' and the insurer may be completely exonerated; this judgment is directly adverse to claimants in such scenarios as it removes even the pay-and-recover protection. Insurer can cite this to resist any claim by occupants of privately-owned vehicles used for hire.
summary: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. challenged a MACT award (Latur) directing it to pay Rs. 7,79,800/- compensation jointly and severally with the driver-cum-owner for the death of Suryakant Pandurang Nikam, who was travelling in a private Tata Sumo jeep (MH 23/E-3762) being operated for hire for a marriage ceremony. The insurer proved that the deceased was travelling for hire or reward in a private vehicle — a wilful fundamental breach of the Act policy under Section 149(2)(a)(ia) — and that no additional premium had been paid for passenger coverage. The Bombay High Court (Aurangabad Bench) followed New India Assurance Co. Ltd. v. Asha Rani (AIR 2003 SC 607) and subsequent Supreme Court decisions to hold that occupants of private vehicles plied for hire or reward are not 'third parties' under Section 147 of the MV Act and are not covered by the Act policy. Since the deceased was not a third party, the court held that no 'pay and recover' order could be passed against the insurer, distinguishing cases like Shamanna (which involved an unlicensed driver carrying a genuine third party). The insurer was completely exonerated and the claimants were directed to recover compensation solely from the driver-cum-owner.

case_title: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. vs Minor Mahesh Kanubhai & 2
court: High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad

owner_or_driver: owner of Matador Tempo No. GJ.5T-2312

core_facts: Five consolidated first appeals by United India Insurance Co. Ltd. challenging Claims Tribunal awards directing pay-and-recover
FA 3852/2008: deceased Chandrakantbhai was travelling as gratuitous passenger in a Matador Tempo bearing No.GJ.5T-2312 carrying his goods; driver drove rashly causing death
FA 710-713/2007: tractor No.GAO-6007 accident causing death of Parvatiben Tejabhai and injuries to other claimants who were travelling on the mudguard/tractor
In all cases, insurance policies were 'Act only' policies not covering gratuitous passengers
Claims Tribunals had held insurance companies not liable but directed them to pay compensation and recover from owner (pay-and-recover direction)
Insurance companies challenged the pay-and-recover direction as beyond statutory power
legal_issues: Whether gratuitous passengers in a goods vehicle or other vehicle are 'third parties' within Chapter XI of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988
Whether section 149(4) and (5) can be invoked to issue pay-and-recover directions when victims are gratuitous passengers not covered by 'Act only' policy
Whether Claims Tribunal or High Court under section 173 has power to issue pay-and-recover directions absent statutory backing
Whether prior Supreme Court pay-and-recover directions in such cases were under Article 142 or under section 149 of the Act
outcome: All five appeals allowed. Insurance companies exonerated. Impugned awards modified so that only the driver and owner of the vehicle are liable to pay compensation; insurance companies stand exonerated from such liability.
key_holdings: Gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles are not 'third parties' covered under Chapter XI of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, and an 'Act only' policy does not cover such risk.
Section 149(4) and (5) operate only in respect of liabilities required to be statutorily covered or covered by the policy; they cannot be invoked for gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles.
Neither the Claims Tribunal nor the High Court in section 173 appellate jurisdiction has power to issue pay-and-recover directions where the risk is neither statutory nor covered by the policy.

Supreme Court pay-and-recover directions in earlier cases involving gratuitous passengers (Baljit Kaur, Saju Paul) were exercises of power under Article 142 of the Constitution, not precedents under section 149.

key_passages.label: policy_breach / third_party_liability
key_passages.quote: However, where the policy is an 'Act only' policy and does not cover the risk of gratuitous passengers, section 149 of the Act cannot be invoked.

key_passages.label: pay_and_recover limitation
key_passages.quote: The powers conferred under section 149(4) and (5) of the Act, are the only source of power insofar as the High Court and the Claims Tribunal are concerned, to direct the insurer to pay the compensation and then recover the same from the insured/owner of the vehicle.

key_passages.label: outcome / holding
key_passages.quote: The impugned awards passed by the Claims Tribunal in all the appeals shall stand modified to the extent that instead of the opponents being jointly and severally liable to pay the compensation awarded under the said award, it shall be only the driver and the owner of the vehicle who shall be so liable and the insurance company shall stand exonerated from such liability.

key_passages.label: no statutory power
key_passages.quote: If the case does not fall within the ambit of the said provisions, in the absence of any statutory power being vested either in the High Court or in the Claims Tribunal, the question of issuing such directions would not arise.

adverse_value: Holds that Claims Tribunal and High Court exercising section 173 jurisdiction have no power to direct an insurer to pay and recover for gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles; such directions require Article 142 powers only available to the Supreme Court. Insurers can cite this to challenge pay-and-recover orders passed against them in non-third-party cases.
summary: In five consolidated first appeals before the Gujarat High Court, the central issue was whether, where a Claims Tribunal found an insurance company not liable to indemnify the insured under an 'Act only' policy (because victims were gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles), the Tribunal or High Court could still direct the insurer to first pay compensation and then recover from the owner. The cases involved a Matador tempo accident (FA 3852/2008) and a tractor accident (FA 710-713/2007). The court held that gratuitous passengers in goods vehicles are not 'third parties' under Chapter XI of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. Section 149(4) and (5) operates only for third-party risks and risks required to be statutorily covered. The Claims Tribunal and High Court, exercising powers under sections 166 and 173, have no authority to issue pay-and-recover directions for non-statutory, non-third-party risks. Any such direction by the Supreme Court in prior cases (Baljit Kaur, Challa Bharathamma, Saju Paul) was under Article 142 of the Constitution, not under section 149. Affirming the co-ordinate bench decision in United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Lilaben, the court allowed all appeals, exonerated the insurance companies, and restricted liability to the vehicle owners and drivers.

case_title: Dadapeera S/O Abdul Salam Sab vs Mallesh M S/O Hanumanthappa
court: High Court of Karnataka, Dharwad Bench
core_facts: Accident on 28.07.2011 during agricultural tilling operations at Kamalapura village
Claimant Dadapeera (20-year-old agricultural coolie) was sitting on mud-guard of tractor engine (tractor and trailer KA-35/T-9766) during field tilling
Driver Mallesh M drove the tractor rashly and negligently causing the tractor to turtle; claimant fell and sustained fracture of left femur and left leg
Claims Tribunal (MVC No.300/2013) awarded Rs.84,160/- with interest; held driver and owner liable; exonerated National Insurance Co. Ltd.
Claimant appealed for enhancement of compensation; insurer's exoneration was not challenged by claimant
Full Bench of Karnataka High Court in Gadhilingappa's case had already held person sitting on mud-guard of tractor is not covered under s.147(1) MV Act
legal_issues: Whether a person sitting on the mud-guard of a tractor engine during tilling operations is a 'third party' covered under statutory insurance under section 147(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988

Whether Rule 28 of Rules of Road Regulations, 1989 (prohibiting riding on non-designated part of vehicle) constitutes a defence under section 149(2) entitling insurer to avoid liability or enabling pay-and-recover
Whether compensation awarded by the Tribunal requires enhancement and on what heads
outcome: Appeal partly allowed. Compensation enhanced from Rs.84,160/- to Rs.2,33,680/- with interest at 6% per annum from date of petition till realisation. Insurance company's exoneration upheld. Only owner (Hussain Sab Bavaji) and driver (Mallesh M) are liable to pay the enhanced compensation.
key_holdings: A person sitting on the mud-guard of a tractor is not required to be covered by statutory insurance under section 147(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, as held by the Full Bench of the Karnataka High Court in Gadhilingappa's case.

The defence available to the Insurance Company is violation of Rule 28 of Rules of Road Regulations, 1989 (person sitting on mud-guard), which is not a defence under section 149(2) of the MV Act; therefore pay-and-recover order cannot be made.

Compensation under the heads of loss of income, pain and suffering, loss of amenities, medical expenses, and incidental charges was enhanced; notional income taken as Rs.6,000/- per month and functional disability at 8% (from 20% physical disability) with multiplier of 18.

key_passages.label: third_party_liability / mud-guard exclusion
key_passages.quote: we have no manner of doubt that a liability of a person working either on the ploughing or crushing machines attached to the tractor and who is travelling on the mud-guard of the tractor is not required to be covered by the statutory insurance as contemplated under sub-section (1) of Section 147 of the M.V.Act.

key_passages.label: insurance exoneration
key_passages.quote: the Insurance Company is not liable to indemnify the owner and the Insurance Company is liable to be exonerated for payment of compensation to the claimant.

key_passages.label: pay_and_recover / no power
key_passages.quote: defence available for the Insurance Company is violation of Regulation 28 of Rules of the Road Regulations, 1989, but not as stated under Sub- section (2) of Section 149 of Motor Vehicles Act. Therefore, order of pay and recovery cannot be made.

key_passages.label: outcome / compensation enhanced
key_passages.quote: The judgment and award dated 16.06.2014 passed in MVC No.300/2013 on the file of Member, Motor Accidents Claim Tribunal-II, Bellary, is hereby modified and the claimant is entitled for total compensation of Rs.2,33,680/- along with interest @ 6% p.a., from the date of petition till its realization

adverse_value: Holds that persons sitting on the mud-guard of a tractor are not covered by statutory insurance under section 147(1) MV Act, exonerating the insurer entirely. Also clarifies that violation of Rule 28 of Road Regulations is not a section 149(2) defence and therefore pay-and-recover cannot be ordered even in such breach cases.
summary: A claimant-appellant aged 20 sustained fracture injuries to his left femur and left leg on 28 July 2011 while sitting on the mud-guard of a tractor engine during field tilling at Kamalapura village. The driver lost control, causing the tractor to turtle. The Claims Tribunal (MVC No.300/2013) awarded Rs.84,160/- but exonerated the insurer (National Insurance Co. Ltd.), holding only owner and driver liable. The Karnataka High Court upheld the insurance company's exoneration on the basis of a Full Bench ruling (Gadhilingappa's case) that persons sitting on the mud-guard of a tractor are not covered under section 147(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. The court further held that while the claimant's presence on the mud-guard violated Rule 28 of the Rules of Road Regulations, 1989, this did not constitute a section 149(2) defence and therefore pay-and-recover order could not be made. On quantum, the court enhanced compensation significantly to Rs.2,33,680/-, taking notional income of Rs.6,000/- per month, functional disability of 8% from 20% physical disability, and multiplier of 18, plus adding amounts for pain and suffering, loss of amenities, incidental expenses, and medical expenses. The appeal was partly allowed: insurer exonerated, only owner and driver liable for the enhanced compensation.

case_title: National Insurance Co. Ltd vs Laxmi Narain Dhut
court: Supreme Court of India
judge_or_bench: Dr. Arijit Pasayat and S.H. Kapadia, JJ.
core_facts: Civil Appeal No. 1140 of 2007 and connected appeals by National Insurance Co. Ltd. challenging High Court and Consumer Forum decisions
Multiple High Courts and the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission had applied the Swaran Singh ratio to own-damage claims (first-party insurance disputes) — not third-party claims
In several cases, insurer's defence of fake driving licence was not accepted on the basis that Swaran Singh's liberal approach applies to all motor accident cases
Some cases involved fake licences that had subsequently been renewed, with forums holding the renewal cured the defect
Appellants argued that Swaran Singh applies only to third-party risk cases under section 149, not to own-damage or consumer disputes
legal_issues: Whether the decision in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297 has application to cases other than third-party risk claims under section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988
Whether a fake driving licence that has subsequently been renewed becomes valid so as to bind the insurer under an own-damage policy
Whether purposive interpretation applicable to third-party claims under section 149 extends to own-damage cases
outcome: All appeals allowed. High Courts and Consumer Commissions directed to reconsider matters afresh in light of the principles laid down: Swaran Singh applies only to third-party risk; fake licence renewal cannot cure the defect; purposive interpretation does not apply to section 149 cases.
key_holdings: The decision in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh has no application to cases other than third-party risks under section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988.
Where originally the licence was a fake one, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality; a fake licence cannot be transformed into a genuine one by any subsequent renewal.
In cases of third-party risks the insurer must indemnify the amount and may, if so advised, recover the same from the insured.
The concept of purposive interpretation has no application to cases relatable to section 149 of the Act; the statute is beneficial only qua the third party, not the owner of the offending vehicle.

key_passages.label: third_party_liability / no contractual relation
key_passages.quote: there is no contractual relation between the insurance company and the third party. The liabilities and the obligations relatable to third parties are created only by fiction of Sections 147 and 149 of the Act.

key_passages.label: beneficial statute limited to third party
key_passages.quote: In the background of the statutory provisions, one thing is crystal clear i.e. the statute is beneficial one qua the third party. But that benefit cannot be extended to the owner of the offending vehicle.

key_passages.label: fake_license / renewal cannot cure
key_passages.quote: As a point of law we have no manner of doubt that a fake licence cannot get its forgery outfit stripped off merely on account of some officer renewing the same with or without knowing it to be forged. Section 15 of the Act only empowers any Licensing Authority to "renew a driving licence issued under the provisions of this Act with effect from the date of its expiry". No Licensing Authority has the power to renew a fake licence and, therefore, a renewal if at all made cannot transform a fake licence as genuine.

key_passages.label: outcome / four situations
key_passages.quote:
In view of the above analysis the following situations emerge:
1. The decision in Swaran Singh's case (supra) has no application to cases other than third party risks.
2. Where originally the license was a fake one, renewal cannot cure the inherent fatality.
3 In case of third party risks the insurer has to indemnify the amount and if so advised to recover the same from the insured.
4. The concept of purposive interpretation has no application to cases relatable to Section 149 of the Act.

adverse_value: Limits the protective scope of Swaran Singh to third-party risk cases only; insurers can rely on this to resist paying own-damage claims where a driver held a fake licence. Also confirms that renewal of a fake licence does not validate it, a defence insurers can raise in both third-party and own-damage contexts.
summary: Multiple civil appeals before the Supreme Court addressed a common question: whether the principles of National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh (2004) 3 SCC 297, relating to third-party claims under section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, apply to own-damage claims and Consumer Forum matters. High Courts and the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission had extended Swaran Singh beyond third-party cases, holding insurers liable in own-damage contexts even where the driver had a fake licence or where the licence had been forged and subsequently renewed. The Supreme Court held categorically that Swaran Singh was rendered in the context of section 149, which governs only third-party risk, and has no application to own-damage cases or Consumer Forum disputes. The Court further held that a fake driving licence cannot be cured by any subsequent renewal, as no licensing authority has power to renew a fake licence and transform it into a genuine one. The distinction arises because section 149 creates a statutory fiction between third parties and insurers, while own-damage cases are pure contractual matters between insured and insurer where no such fiction operates. For third-party risks, the insurer must indemnify and may recover from the insured. Purposive interpretation applicable to third-party cases does not apply to own-damage cases under section 149. The High Courts and Commissions were directed to reconsider matters afresh in accordance with these principles.

case_title: S. Iyyapan vs M/S United India Insurance Co. Ltd. & Anr
court: Supreme Court of India
judge_or_bench: Surinder Singh Nijjar and M.Y. Eqbal, JJ.

respondents: M/S United India Insurance Company Ltd.

core_facts: On 23.05.1998 at about 8.30 PM, deceased Charles was riding his bicycle when driver Sivananayaitha Perumal drove a Mahindra van at high speed and dashed against Charles, causing his death
Driver held a valid LMV (light motor vehicle) driving licence but had no specific endorsement for driving the Mahindra van as a commercial vehicle (taxi)
The vehicle was being used as a taxi (commercial vehicle) at the time of accident
Claims Tribunal awarded Rs.2,42,400/- with interest; the insurer challenged the award before the High Court
High Court exonerated the insurer, holding that the driver was not duly licensed to drive a commercial vehicle as he lacked an endorsement for driving commercial vehicles
Owner S. Iyyapan appealed to the Supreme Court against the High Court judgment
legal_issues: Whether an insurance company can disown its liability to pay compensation to a third party on the ground that although the driver held a valid LMV driving licence, there was no endorsement in the licence for driving the light motor vehicle when used as a commercial vehicle (taxi)
Whether a Mahindra Maxi Cab is a 'light motor vehicle' requiring only an LMV licence or a 'commercial vehicle' requiring a separate endorsement
outcome: Appeal allowed. Impugned judgment of the High Court set aside. Insurer held liable to pay the compensation so awarded to the dependants of the victim of the fatal accident.
key_holdings: A Mahindra Maxi Cab is a light motor vehicle; a driver holding a valid LMV licence is entitled to drive it without needing a separate endorsement for use as a commercial vehicle.
An insurer cannot disown its third-party liability on the ground that although the driver held a valid LMV licence, there was no endorsement to drive the LMV when used as a commercial vehicle.

The statutory right of a third party to recover compensation from the insurer cannot be defeated merely by absence of a commercial vehicle endorsement when the vehicle qualifies as a light motor vehicle.

Chapter XI of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 mandates compulsory third-party insurance to ensure that victims of accidents can get compensation; this purpose is defeated if insurers can avoid liability on technical licensing grounds.

key_passages.label: legislative intent / third party insurance
key_passages.quote: The heading "Insurance of Motor Vehicles against Third Party Risks" given in Chapter XI of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 (Chapter VIII of 1939 Act) itself shows the intention of the legislature to make third party insurance compulsory and to ensure that the victims of accident arising out of use of motor vehicles would be able to get compensation for the death or injuries suffered.

key_passages.label: license_breach_defence / insurer cannot disown
key_passages.quote: the insurer cannot disown its liability on the ground that although the driver was holding a licence to drive a light motor vehicle but before driving light motor vehicle used as commercial vehicle, no endorsement to drive commercial vehicle was obtained in the driving licence. In any case, it is the statutory right of a third party to recover the amount of compensation so awarded from the insurer.

key_passages.label: driving_license_validity / LMV licence sufficient
key_passages.quote: admittedly the driver was holding a valid driving licence to drive light motor vehicle. There is no dispute that the motor vehicle in question, by which accident took place, was Mahindra Maxi Cab. Merely because the driver did not get any endorsement in the driving licence to drive Mahindra Maxi Cab, which is a light motor vehicle, the High Court has committed grave error of law in holding that the insurer is not liable to pay compensation because the driver was not holding the licence to drive the commercial vehicle.

key_passages.label: outcome / holding
key_passages.quote: We, therefore, allow this appeal, set aside the impugned judgment of the High Court and hold that the insurer is liable to pay the compensation so awarded to the dependants of the victim of the fatal accident.

summary: The Supreme Court considered whether an insurance company could avoid its statutory third-party liability to pay compensation to a motor accident victim on the ground that the driver of the offending vehicle held a valid light motor vehicle (LMV) licence but had no specific endorsement for driving the vehicle when used as a commercial vehicle (taxi/Mahindra Maxi Cab). The deceased, Charles, was killed on 23 May 1998 when the driver of a Mahindra van drove at high speed and hit his bicycle. The Claims Tribunal awarded Rs.2,42,400/- with interest. The High Court exonerated the insurer, holding that a driver using a vehicle as a commercial taxi without a commercial vehicle endorsement was not duly licensed. The Supreme Court reversed this, holding that the Mahindra Maxi Cab was a light motor vehicle and a driver holding a valid LMV licence was duly authorised to drive it. No separate commercial vehicle endorsement was required when the vehicle qualifies as an LMV. The Court reiterated that Chapter XI of the Motor Vehicles Act mandates compulsory third-party insurance specifically to ensure victims receive compensation, and the insurer could not disown its statutory liability on technical licensing grounds. The insurer was held fully liable to pay the award; recovery from the insured remains available in the event of an actual policy breach.

case_title: Satto & Ors vs New India Assurance Co Ltd
court: High Court of Delhi at New Delhi

appellants: Satto (mother of deceased Naresh Kumar son of Kashmira)
Harpal Singh (father of deceased Naresh Kumar @ Setu)
New India Assurance Co Ltd (in some appeals)

core_facts: Accident on night of 11-12 September 2005 on Outer Ring Road, Delhi; Tempo No. UP-12K-5797 was travelling loaded with guava (fruit) when driver Sunil Kumar drove at high speed, causing the vehicle to overturn after a tyre burst
Five claim petitions: deaths of Naresh Kumar @ Setu (aged 18, son of Harpal Singh) and Naresh Kumar son of Kashmira (aged 21), plus injuries to three others
Insurance company proved that driver Sunil Kumar held only a Light Motor Vehicle (Non-Transport) licence and was driving a goods vehicle (commercial vehicle) — breach of policy conditions established
Insurance company did not challenge liability in three injury cases; challenged only in death cases (MAC APPs 138/2011, 143/2011, 744/2011)
Claims Tribunal had granted recovery rights to insurer and held insurer liable to pay despite proven breach; claimants appealed for enhancement of quantum
Key factual dispute: whether deceased were gratuitous passengers or owners/representatives of goods being transported
legal_issues: Whether the two deceased were travelling as gratuitous passengers or as owners/representatives of goods (guava) in the tempo, which determines their status as third parties covered under the MV Act
Whether the insurance company's statutory liability to satisfy a third-party award survives despite proven breach of policy condition (driver's licence breach)
Whether pay-and-recover direction is appropriate where insurer proves conscious breach of policy by the insured
Quantum of compensation: whether addition of 50% future prospects is permissible for self-employed or temporary workers
outcome: MAC APPs 30/2012 and 138/2011 (Harpal Singh): compensation enhanced to Rs.4,38,000/-. MAC APPs 744/2011 and 143/2011 (Satto): compensation enhanced to Rs.3,75,000/-. Insurance company held liable to pay with recovery rights against owner (Mohd. Qayum) and driver (Sunil Kumar). No addition for future prospects as deceased were self-employed/temporary workers.
key_holdings: Evidence established that the two deceased were travelling as owners/representatives of goods (guava) and not as gratuitous passengers; the insurance company could not avoid its liability to them as third parties.

The insurance company's statutory liability to satisfy a third-party award is not defeated by a proven breach of policy conditions; it must pay the compensation and can recover from the insured/tortfeasor.
No addition towards future prospects is permissible for self-employed or temporarily employed workers (following Reshma Kumari three-Judge Bench).
The owner and driver who did not appeal the recovery rights granted by the Tribunal remain bound by that finding.

key_passages.label: third_party_liability / owners of goods not gratuitous passengers
key_passages.quote: the Insurance Company cannot shy away from its liability to pay the compensation to the legal representatives of the two deceased as it is proved that the deceased Naresh Kumar @ Setu was travelling as owner of the goods whereas the deceased Naresh Kumar son of Kashmira was travelling as representative of the owner (Ajay Pal) of the goods.

key_passages.label: pay_and_recover / statutory liability survives breach
key_passages.quote: there is no manner of doubt that the liability of the Insurance Company to satisfy the award in the first instance is statutory; it is bound to satisfy the same and will be entitled to recover the amount of compensation paid from the driver and the owner Sunil Kumar and Mohd. Qayum (Respondents No.2 and 3 in MAC APPs.138/2011 and 143/2011) in execution of this very judgment without having recourse of independent civil proceedings.

key_passages.label: future_prospects / no addition for self-employed
key_passages.quote: Since the deceased was not in permanent or regular employment, he would not be entitled to any addition towards future prospects. The loss of dependency thus comes to ` 3,78,000/- (`4500/- x 1/2 x 12 x 14).

key_passages.label: outcome / compensation enhanced
key_passages.quote: The overall compensation thus comes to `4,38,000/-. The compensation stands enhanced from `4,24,000/- to `4,38,000/-. The enhanced compensation of `14,000/- shall carry interest @ 7.5% per annum as awarded by the Claims Tribunal.

adverse_value: Holds that no future prospects addition is permissible where the deceased was self-employed or in temporary employment (following Reshma Kumari). Insurers and defendants can cite this to restrict compensation in cases where the deceased was not in permanent salaried employment.
summary: Four connected appeals arose from a tempo accident on the night of 11-12 September 2005 in Delhi when the driver lost control after a tyre burst, killing two passengers and injuring three others. The insurance company (New India Assurance Co. Ltd.) proved that the driver held only a Light Motor Vehicle (Non-Transport) licence but was driving a commercial goods vehicle — an established breach of policy conditions. The central issues were: (1) whether the two deceased were gratuitous passengers or owners of goods, and (2) whether the insurer remained liable despite proven breach. The Delhi High Court held that evidence proved both deceased were travelling as owners/representatives of goods (guava) and were not mere gratuitous passengers, so the insurer could not avoid liability on that ground. As regards the licence breach, the court confirmed that the insurance company's statutory obligation to pay third-party compensation survives a proven policy breach; the insurer pays and recovers from the owner/driver. On quantum, following Reshma Kumari (three-Judge Bench), no addition towards future prospects was permitted for self-employed or temporary workers. Compensation for Harpal Singh's son was enhanced to Rs.4,38,000/- and for Satto's son to Rs.3,75,000/-, with recovery rights preserved for the insurer against the owner and driver.

case_title: K.G. Srinivasamurthy vs Habib Khathun And Ors.
court: High Court of Karnataka
judge_or_bench: R.V. Raveendran and V.G. Sabhahit, JJ.

appellants: K.G. Srinivasamurthy (owner of lorry in MVC 140/1994)
claimants: Habib Khathun (mother of deceased Inthu Pasha, MVC 140/1994)
insurer: unnamed insurance company (respondent in MFA 5566/1999 and MFA 3557/1998)
owner_or_driver: K.G. Srinivasamurthy (owner of Canter lorry KA 18-240)

core_facts: Case 1 (MVC 177/1997, M.F.A. 5566/1999 by insurer and 690/2000 by claimant): Minor girl Suma (3 years old, right leg amputated above knee, 80% permanent disability) was hit by lorry MYT 6600 on 13.01.1997 while standing by the roadside; driver's licence had expired on 28.11.1996 and was renewed only on 17.01.1997 — 50-day gap; insurer appealed against Tribunal's joint liability finding

Case 2 (MVC 140/1994, M.F.A. 3557/1998 by owner): Inthu Pasha (20 years, pillion rider on motorcycle) died on 19.01.1994 when hit by Canter lorry KA 18-240 owned by K.G. Srinivasamurthy; driver's licence had expired 05.07.1993 and was renewed 24.02.1994 — 7-month 20-day gap; Tribunal dismissed claim against insurer; owner K.G. Srinivasamurthy appealed
In both cases, insurer's defence was that drivers had no valid (effective) driving licence on the date of accident due to licence expiry
Insurance policy condition in both cases used the word 'and' (not 'or') connecting 'not duly licensed' and 'disqualified'
Both drivers had been licensed since the early 1980s and had renewed consistently, except for the gaps on the accident dates
legal_issues: Whether mere expiry of a driving licence at the time of accident — without disqualification — constitutes a breach of the insurance policy exclusion clause under section 149(2)(a)(ii) of the MV Act

Whether the insurance company's statutory liability to third parties is defeated by the driver's failure to renew the licence, where the licence exclusion clause uses 'and' (not duly licensed AND disqualified) rather than 'or'
Whether the non-renewal of a driving licence as on the date of the accident amounts to a fundamental breach justifying the insurer's total avoidance of liability
Enhancement of compensation in both cases
outcome: M.F.A. No. 5566/1999 (insurer's appeal in MVC 177/1997) dismissed; insurer remains jointly liable with owner. M.F.A. No. 690/2000 (claimant's appeal) partly allowed; compensation enhanced to Rs.3,50,000/- with interest at 9% p.a. Cross-objection No. 23/2000 allowed in part (interest rate aspect). M.F.A. No. 3557/1998 (owner's appeal in MVC 140/1994) allowed; insurer held jointly and severally liable with owner; compensation enhanced to Rs.1,95,000/- with interest at 9% p.a. No recovery order made since insurer failed to prove breach.
key_holdings: The insurance company's liability to satisfy an award against a third party is a statutory liability not inhibited by policy conditions; breach of policy conditions cannot bind the third party.

Mere expiry of a driving licence and failure to renew it as on the date of accident — without the driver being disqualified — does not amount to breach of the exclusion clause where the exclusion clause uses 'and' to connect 'not duly licensed' and 'disqualified'.

Where the breach alleged is not a factor that contributed to causing the accident, it is not a fundamental breach; the exclusion clause must be read down to serve the main purpose of the policy, i.e., to indemnify the insured.
In both cases, the insurance company failed to prove willful breach of policy conditions and therefore cannot recover the amount paid from the insured.

key_passages.label: third_party_liability / statutory liability not inhibited by policy conditions
key_passages.quote: it is clear that the liability of the insurance company to satisfy the award passed against third party is a statutory liability and the same is not inhibited by any of the conditions imposed in the policy and any breach of conditions imposed in the policy would not bind the third party and the insurance company is bound to satisfy the award against the third party

key_passages.label: driving_license_validity / expiry not a breach
key_passages.quote: mere fact that the driver of the offending vehicle had not got his driving licence renewed on the date of the accident and got it renewed subsequently would not amount to breach of condition of the policy as it cannot be said that there was violation of the condition of the exclusion clause.

key_passages.label: fundamental_breach / exclusion clause read down
key_passages.quote: Where the breach alleged is not a factor which has contributed to the causing of the accident, the said breach would not be a fundamental breach so as to afford a ground to the insurer to avoid liability altogether and the exclusion clause must be read down so as to serve the main purpose of the policy, i.e., to indemnify the insured.

key_passages.label: outcome / holding
key_passages.quote: we hold that the insurance company has failed to prove that there was breach of conditions of the policy and that, it is absolved of its liability to pay the compensation as per the terms of the policy and hold that the insurance company in both the cases is liable with the owner jointly and severally to pay the compensation awarded in these appeals.

summary: A Division Bench of the Karnataka High Court consolidated four appeals arising from two separate motor accident cases. In MVC No. 177 of 1997, a minor girl Suma had her right leg amputated above the knee after being hit while standing by the roadside; in MVC No. 140 of 1994, Inthu Pasha (20 years) died as a pillion rider on a motorcycle. In both cases, insurers argued that the drivers lacked valid driving licences on the accident date as licences had expired and were renewed only thereafter (50-day gap in the first case; 7-month gap in the second).
