The court held comprehensively: (1) the insurance company's liability to satisfy a third-party award is statutory and is not defeated by policy conditions; (2) mere expiry of a driving licence without disqualification does not constitute a breach of the exclusion clause, particularly where the clause uses 'and' (requiring both unlicensed and disqualified) rather than 'or'; (3) where the breach does not contribute to causing the accident, it is not a fundamental breach and the exclusion clause must be read down; and (4) the insurers in both cases failed to prove willful breach, so no recovery could be ordered. The insurer's appeal in the first case was dismissed; the owner's appeal in the second case was allowed with insurer held jointly liable. Compensation was enhanced to Rs.3,50,000/- and Rs.1,95,000/- respectively with interest at 9% per annum.

case_title: United India Insurance Company Limited vs V. Vijayakumar
court: High Court of Judicature at Madras
judge_or_bench: R. Banumathi, J. and G.M. Akbar Ali, J.

appellants: United India Insurance Company Limited, Salem
respondents: V. Vijayakumar (rep. by his mother V. Kalamani)

statutes: Tamil Nadu Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 Rule 35
Tamil Nadu Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989 Rule 36
core_facts: Accident on 07.07.2002: claimant V. Vijayakumar (22 years, B.Com graduate, working as accountant at Rs.4,500/month) was walking on road near Annur Bus Stand when Tourist Maxi Cab (Mahendra van TN 27 L 3638) driven by 3rd respondent Marimuthu dashed into him
Claimant sustained severe head injuries — diffuse axonal injury and corpus callosum involvement; admitted to KMCH ICU for 5.5 months; on ventilator 46 days; tracheostomy performed
At time of trial, claimant was totally paralysed, non-communicative, in vegetative existence; permanent disability assessed at 95%
Driver (3rd respondent) had only LMV licence (No.1407/97) valid up to 05.06.2016 but had no authorisation (badge) to drive a transport vehicle (Tourist Maxi Cab)
R.W.1 (Junior Assistant from Motor Vehicles Inspector's office) testified that 3rd respondent was not granted any authorisation to drive transport vehicle nor allotted a badge number
Claims Tribunal awarded Rs.19,59,895/- including Rs.8,20,800/- for permanent disability and Rs.9,37,095/- for medical expenses; held insurer jointly and severally liable
Insurer appealed challenging both liability and the quantum as excessive
legal_issues: Whether the insurer discharged its burden of proving that the driver was not duly licensed to drive the transport vehicle (Tourist Maxi Cab) and thereby proved a breach of policy conditions under section 149(2)(a)(ii)
Whether, upon proving breach of policy conditions, the insurer is absolved of liability or whether pay-and-recover (insurer pays claimant then recovers from owner) should be directed
Whether the compensation of Rs.19,59,895/- awarded by the Tribunal is excessive or just and reasonable
outcome: Appeal partly allowed. Quantum of Rs.19,59,895/- with 9% interest per annum confirmed as just and reasonable. Award modified: insurance company is not jointly and severally liable but must pay the compensation to the claimant (1st respondent) and then recover the same from the insured (owner C. Marimuthu and driver). Insurer entitled to file execution petition against respondents 3 and 4 in the same proceedings.
key_holdings: The insurance company discharged its burden of proving that the 3rd respondent (driver) had only an LMV licence and lacked the specific authorisation (badge) required to drive a transport vehicle (Tourist Maxi Cab), establishing a breach of policy conditions under section 149(2)(a)(ii).

Absence of badge/authorisation for transport vehicle proved by R.W.1's evidence that no badge was allotted and by the absence of endorsement in the driving licence; the Tribunal erred in fastening statutory liability on the insurer.

Despite the insurer proving breach of policy conditions, a pay-and-recover order is the appropriate remedy: the insurer must pay compensation to the innocent claimant and can then recover from the insured/owner.

Total compensation of Rs.19,59,895/- including Rs.8,20,800/- for permanent disability (Rs.4,500 x 12 x 16 x 95/100) and Rs.9,37,095/- for medical expenses with interest at 9% per annum is just, reasonable, and not excessive given the 95% disability and vegetative existence.

key_passages.label: driving_license_validity / breach proved
key_passages.quote: The absence of any endorsement in the driving licence as to the issuance of authorisation to drive the transport vehicle and non-mention of allotment of badge number clearly shows that the 3rd Respondent was not in possession of a valid driving licence and that he was not duly licensed to drive the transport vehicle and there was violation of Policy conditions.

key_passages.label: pay_and_recover / direction despite breach proved
key_passages.quote: The 3rd Respondent had a licence, but not a valid one. As there was violation of conditions of policy, Tribunal was not right in fastening the statutory liability upon the Insurance Company. Since there was violation of policy conditions the Tribunal ought not to have fastened the statutory liability upon the Insurance Company. Keeping in view the nature of injuries sustained by the claimant and that the claimant is now reduced to vegetable existence, the only just and reasonable course would be to direct the Insurance Company to pay compensation to the 1st Respondent – Claimant and recover it from the owner for his breach of the policy conditions.

key_passages.label: pay_and_recover / insurer must pay and recover
key_passages.quote: we are of the view that the Appellant - insurer must pay the amount to the claimant - 1st Respondent and then recover the same from the insured and to that extent the award passed by the Tribunal has to be modified.

key_passages.label: outcome / quantum confirmed
key_passages.quote: the quantum of compensation of Rs.19,59,895/- awarded by the Tribunal in M.C.O.P.No.428 of 2003 on the file of the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (Principal Subordinate Judge), Coimbatore is confirmed. The award passed by the Tribunal holding that the Appellant Insurance Company is jointly and severally liable to pay the compensation along with Respondents No.3 and 4 – driver and owner of the vehicle is modified and it is held that the Appellant Insurance Company must pay the compensation amount to the 1st respondent – Claimant along with interest at 9% per annum and then recover the same from the insured

adverse_value: Holds that an insurer who proves that the driver lacked specific transport vehicle authorisation (badge) has established a breach of policy conditions under section 149(2)(a)(ii); the insurer escapes joint-and-several liability and obtains recovery rights against the owner/driver through a pay-and-recover modification.
summary: A Madras High Court Division Bench heard an appeal by United India Insurance Company Limited challenging both liability and quantum in an award of Rs.19,59,895/- for a severe road accident. On 7 July 2002, V. Vijayakumar (22 years, B.Com graduate, accountant earning Rs.4,500/month) sustained severe head injuries when the driver of a Tourist Maxi Cab (Mahendra van) drove rashly and hit him while walking near Annur Bus Stand. The driver was convicted. The claimant suffered diffuse axonal injury, became totally paralysed, entered vegetative existence (95% permanent disability), and spent 5.5 months in ICU on ventilator. The insurer proved that the driver held only an LMV licence without the specific transport vehicle badge/authorisation required under Tamil Nadu Motor Vehicles Rules. The court accepted this defence: the driver was not duly licensed for the transport vehicle (tourist maxi cab), establishing violation of policy conditions under section 149(2)(a)(ii). However, applying the Kamla/Swaran Singh doctrine, the court modified the award so that the insurer must pay compensation to the claimant and then recover from the owner/insured. The quantum of Rs.19,59,895/- (including Rs.8,20,800/- for permanent disability and Rs.9,37,095/- for medical expenses) with 9% interest was maintained as just and reasonable given the severity of injuries.

case_title: Tarachand Raosaheb Chaudhari vs The Oriental Insurance Co Ltd
court: Maharashtra State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Mumbai, Bench at Aurangabad
judge_or_bench: Milind S. Sonawane (Presiding Member) and Nagesh C. Kumbre (Member)

respondents: MD India Health Insurance TPA Private Ltd.

core_facts: Multiple appellants availed the Corona Rakshak Policy from Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. and paid premiums.

Each appellant was diagnosed COVID-19 positive by RTPCR during the policy period and admitted to a Covid care centre declared by Aurangabad Municipal Corporation for more than 72 hours on medical advice.
Oriental Insurance repudiated all claims on the ground that the Covid centres were quarantine centres and not hospitals under clause 3.6 of the policy.
District Consumer Commission, Aurangabad dismissed all original consumer complaints.
Appellants challenged the dismissal orders before the Maharashtra State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission in First Appeal Nos. 619 to 623 of 2022.
legal_issues: Whether a Covid care centre declared by Aurangabad Municipal Corporation qualifies as a hospital under clause 3.6(vi) of the Corona Rakshak Policy.
Whether repudiation of insurance claims on the ground that Covid centres are not hospitals constitutes deficiency in service by the insurer.
Whether appellants satisfied the eligibility criteria of being Covid-positive and hospitalized for more than 72 hours on medical advice during the policy period.
outcome: All five first appeals partly allowed. District Commission orders quashed. Oriental Insurance directed to pay Rs. 2,50,000/- under Corona Rakshak Policy with interest at 8% p.a. from the respective dates of repudiation plus Rs. 10,000/- for mental agony and litigation costs in each case.
key_holdings: A Covid care centre designated by the government or Municipal Corporation for Covid-19 treatment qualifies as a hospital under clause 3.6(vi) of the Corona Rakshak Policy.
Repudiation of insurance claims solely on the ground that a Municipal Corporation-declared Covid centre is not a hospital constitutes deficiency in service by the insurer.
An insured who was corona positive and hospitalized for more than 72 hours on medical advice of a qualified practitioner is entitled to the full sum insured under the Corona Rakshak Policy.

key_passages.label: policy_clause_3.6vi
key_passages.quote: For the purpose of this policy any other set-up designated by the government as hospital for the treatment of Covid-19 shall also be considered as hospital.

key_passages.label: deficiency_in_service_holding
key_passages.quote: the MIT Boys Hostel declared by Aurangabad Municipal Corporation as a Covid centre comes within the purview of clause 3.6 (vi) of policy and repudiation of claim on the said ground is deficiency in service on the part of respondent no.1.

key_passages.label: entitlement_holding
key_passages.quote: Appellant was Corona positive and hospitalized for more than 72 hours as per the advice of qualified medical practitioner and therefore entitled for benefits under the Corona Rakshak Policy.

key_passages.label: operative_clause
key_passages.quote: If during the policy period the insured person is diagnosed with COVID and hospitalized for more than 72 hours following medical advice of a duly qualified medical practitioner. The insurance company shall pay the agreed sum insured towards the coverage mentioned in the policy schedule.

summary: This combined judgment of the Maharashtra State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (Aurangabad Bench), delivered on 21 October 2024, decides five first appeals (FA Nos. 619-623/2022) challenging dismissals of consumer complaints against Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. for repudiating claims under the Corona Rakshak Policy. Each appellant tested COVID-19 positive during the policy period, was referred by the Aurangabad Municipal Corporation's Medical Officer to a designated Covid care centre (MIT Boys Hostel, Samajkalyan Boys Hostel, or Government Engineering College Covid Centre), and was admitted for more than 72 continuous hours on medical advice. The insurer repudiated all claims arguing the Covid centres were quarantine centres, not hospitals under clause 3.6 of the policy, and that no active line of treatment was given. The District Consumer Commission had dismissed the original complaints. On appeal, the State Commission held that clause 3.6(vi) of the Corona Rakshak Policy expressly includes any government-designated setup for Covid-19 treatment as a hospital, that the Municipal Corporation-declared Covid centres fell within this definition, and that the insurer's repudiation was deficiency in service. Each appellant, having satisfied the twin conditions of confirmed Covid-positive diagnosis and hospitalization exceeding 72 hours on medical advice, was held entitled to Rs. 2,50,000/- with 8% p.a. interest from the date of repudiation plus Rs. 10,000/- for mental agony and costs.

case_title: Bhagyashree Santosh Galande vs The Oriental Insurance Co Ltd
court: Maharashtra State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, Mumbai, Bench at Aurangabad
judge_or_bench: Milind S. Sonawane (Presiding Member) and Nagesh C. Kumbre (Member)

respondents: MD India Health Insurance TPA Private Ltd.

core_facts: Multiple appellants availed the Corona Rakshak Policy from Oriental Insurance and paid premiums ranging from Rs. 2,580/- to Rs. 5,185/-.
Each appellant was diagnosed Covid-positive by RTPCR during the policy period and admitted to a Covid centre declared by Aurangabad Municipal Corporation for more than 72 hours on medical advice.
Oriental Insurance repudiated claims asserting Covid centres were quarantine centres and not hospitals under policy clause 3.6, and that there was no active line of treatment during hospitalization.
District Consumer Commission, Aurangabad dismissed the consumer complaints in CC Nos. 334, 335, 374, 375, and 336 of 2021 on 26.07.2022.
Appellants filed First Appeal Nos. 619-623 of 2022 before the Maharashtra State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission.
legal_issues: Whether a Covid care centre declared by the Aurangabad Municipal Corporation constitutes a hospital within the meaning of clause 3.6(vi) of the Corona Rakshak Policy.
Whether the insurer's repudiation of claims on the ground that Covid centres are not hospitals constituted deficiency in service.
Whether the conditions of the operative clause (Covid-positive diagnosis plus hospitalization exceeding 72 hours on medical advice) were satisfied.
outcome: All five appeals partly allowed. District Commission orders dated 26.07.2022 quashed. Oriental Insurance directed to pay Rs. 2,50,000/- per claimant under Corona Rakshak Policy with 8% p.a. interest from the respective repudiation dates plus Rs. 10,000/- for mental agony and costs.
key_holdings: A government-designated Covid care centre run under municipal authority with medical practitioners and qualified nursing staff qualifies as a hospital under clause 3.6(vi) of the Corona Rakshak Policy.
Repudiation of a claim when the insured was demonstrably Covid-positive and hospitalized for more than 72 hours on medical advice amounts to deficiency in service.
The District Commission erred in dismissing the complaints by ignoring evidence that appellants met the eligibility criteria under clause 2 and 4.1 of the Corona Rakshak Policy.

key_passages.label: policy_clause_3.6vi
key_passages.quote: For the purpose of this policy any other set-up designated by the government as hospital for the treatment of Covid-19 shall also be considered as hospital.

key_passages.label: deficiency_in_service_holding_case621
key_passages.quote: the Samajkalyan Boys Hostel Covid centre declared by Aurangabad Municipal Corporation as a Covid centre comes within the purview of clause 3.6 (vi) of policy and repudiation of claim on the said ground is deficiency in service on the part of respondent no.1.

key_passages.label: entitlement_holding
key_passages.quote: Appellant was corona positive and hospitalized for more than 72 hours as per the advice of qualified medical practitioner and therefore entitled for benefits under the Corona Rakshak Policy.

key_passages.label: covid_cover_clause_4.1
key_passages.quote: Lump sum benefit equal to 100% of the sum insured shall be payable on positive diagnosis of Covid, requiring hospitalization for a minimum continuous period of 72 hours. The positive diagnosis of Covid shall be form a government authorized diagnostic centre.

summary: This combined judgment of the Maharashtra State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (Aurangabad Bench), dated 21 October 2024, contains five appeal judgments (FA Nos. 619-623 of 2022) against the District Consumer Commission's dismissal of complaints under the Corona Rakshak Policy issued by Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. Each appellant was RTPCR-confirmed Covid-positive and admitted to a Municipal Corporation-declared Covid care centre in Aurangabad for hospitalization exceeding 72 hours on medical advice. The insurer repudiated all claims under clause 3.6 of the policy, contending Covid centres were quarantine facilities rather than hospitals with active treatment. The State Commission examined clause 3.6(vi), which includes any government-designated setup for Covid-19 treatment as a hospital, and held that Municipal Corporation-declared Covid centres with qualified medical staff squarely fell within this definition. The insurer's repudiation was found to be deficiency in service. All claims were allowed for Rs. 2,50,000/- each with 8% p.a. interest from the date of repudiation and Rs. 10,000/- towards mental agony and costs. The District Commission's orders were quashed. This judgment confirms that Covid-era pandemic care centres with government designation and qualified staff meet the policy definition of hospital under similar insurance products.

case_title: M/S Crown Consultants (P) Ltd. vs The Oriental Insurance Company Ltd.
court: National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, New Delhi
judge_or_bench: Justice R.C. Jain (Presiding Member) and Anupam Dasgupta (Member)
statutes: Securities and Exchange Board of India Act
core_facts: Complainant M/s Crown Consultants (P) Ltd., a stockbroker and NSE member, suffered a loss of Rs. 43,05,032/- in share purchase transactions on behalf of client Babu Lal Sethia during 01-03 May 1996 after being allegedly deceived by an unidentified person impersonating Sethia on telephone.

The complainant lodged an insurance claim on 30.06.1996 under an NSE-negotiated policy with Oriental Insurance covering member stockbrokers against specified perils including deception as to identity of any person.

Oriental Insurance repudiated the claim on three grounds: (i) claim filed more than 30 days after crystallisation of loss on 07.05.1996; (ii) member-constituent agreement not executed on stamp paper as per NSE/SEBI rules; (iii) client codes not entered contemporaneously in trades as per NSE rules.
The complainant argued the loss crystallised only on 01.06.1996 after exhaustive enquiries at Barmer, and the NSE regulations cited were not in force in May 1996.
The National Commission found the complainant's conduct inconsistent with genuine deception and failed the burden of establishing the insured peril under Section 1(c) of the policy.
legal_issues: Whether the insurance claim was filed within 30 days of discovery of loss as required by the Certificate of Insurance.
Whether the complainant discharged the burden of proving that the loss was caused by the insured peril (deception as to identity under Section 1(c) of the policy).
Whether the insurer's repudiation of the claim on the stated grounds constituted deficiency in service under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986.
Whether the doctrine of utmost good faith (uberrima fides) was breached by the complainant.
outcome: Original complaint dismissed as totally devoid of merit or good faith. No deficiency in service found on the part of the insurer in repudiating the insurance claim.
key_holdings: The burden of proving that a loss was caused by the insured peril rests on the assured; the complainant failed to discharge this burden in respect of the alleged deception.
A contract of insurance is governed by the doctrine of utmost good faith (uberrima fides); the complainant's conduct showed lack of even ordinary good faith throughout.
The claim was filed well beyond the 30-day period from the date of discovery/awareness of the loss; the insurer committed no deficiency in service in treating the delay as uncondonable.

A stockbroker's failure to follow NSE regulatory requirements in executing large trades on behalf of a new client without adequate margin is inconsistent with the due diligence required for a valid insurance claim.

key_passages.label: repudiation_grounds_insurer
key_passages.quote: Claim was lodged on 1.7.96 i.e. more than 30 days after the incident and crystallisation of the loss on 7.5.96 and not immediately.

key_passages.label: uberrima_fides_principle
key_passages.quote: Good faith forbids either party by concealing what he privately knows, to draw the other into a bargain from his ignorance of that fact, and his believing the contrary.

key_passages.label: adverse_conduct_finding
key_passages.quote: ample evidence of lack of even ordinary good faith, leave alone utmost good faith in the conduct of the complainant.

key_passages.label: final_holding
key_passages.quote: we find no deficiency in service on the part of the Opposite Party no. 1, Insurance Company in repudiating the complainants insurance claim and dismiss the complaint as being totally devoid of merit or good faith.

summary: This original complaint (Complaint Case No. 121 of 1999) before the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, decided on 31 May 2011, concerns a stock-broking firm's claim for indemnification of Rs. 43,05,032/- under an NSE-negotiated insurance policy covering stockbrokers against various risks including deception as to the identity of persons placing orders. Crown Consultants alleged that an unidentified caller impersonated client Babu Lal Sethia and placed large share purchase orders during 01-03 May 1996, resulting in a loss after prices fell. The insurer repudiated the claim citing delayed filing (30 days from loss), non-execution of member-constituent agreement on stamp paper, and non-entry of client codes at the time of trading. The Commission conducted a thorough factual examination and found the complainant's narrative of deception implausible and internally inconsistent when compared across the first information report, the complaint filed three years later, and affidavits filed after twelve years. The Commission held that the doctrine of utmost good faith pervades an insurance contract from formation through claim, that the complainant breached NSE regulations by trading for Nahata without a separate member-constituent agreement, and that the delay in filing was uncondonable. The complaint was dismissed entirely, with no deficiency in service found on the insurer's part.

case_title: Smt. Kamla Devi vs Government Of NCT Of Delhi And Anr.
court: High Court of Delhi
core_facts: Uday Singh, an electrician from Wazirpur, Gurgaon, died on 20.04.1996 in a bomb blast at Arjun Guest House, Paharganj, Delhi, caused by a terrorist who assembled an improvised explosive device (RDX) in the building.
Sixteen other persons also died in the blast. The terrorist was a member of a Jammu and Kashmir terrorist organisation and died in the explosion.
The Government of NCT of Delhi paid an ex-gratia amount of Rs. 50,000/- to the petitioner Kamla Devi (widow), which she regarded as grossly inadequate.

Petitioner filed a writ petition under Article 226 seeking a writ of mandamus directing respondents to pay Rs. 10 lakhs or adequate compensation for the State's failure to protect the life of her husband under Article 21 of the Constitution.
At the time of death, Uday Singh was 29 years old, earning Rs. 3,000/- per month, leaving behind wife Kamla Devi and infant son Mukesh (aged 4 months).
legal_issues: Whether the State is liable to pay compensation in public law under Article 226 for the death of a citizen caused by a terrorist act due to failure of State intelligence and protective duty under Article 21.
Whether compensation for crime victims can be awarded in writ jurisdiction without relegating the claimant to civil courts.
What is the appropriate methodology for computing compensation for loss of dependency and non-pecuniary loss in a public law claim.
outcome: Writ petition allowed. State directed to pay Rs. 4,36,500/- (after adjusting ex-gratia of Rs. 50,000/-) with simple interest at 7% p.a. from 20.04.1996 (date of explosion) till date within four weeks. The compensation comprised standard conventional sum of Rs. 97,700/- (inflation-adjusted) and dependency compensation of Rs. 3,88,800/- computed using the multiplier method.
key_holdings: The State owes a duty to protect the life and liberty of innocent citizens under Article 21 and when it fails to prevent terrorism resulting in death, it is liable to compensate the victim's family under public law jurisdiction.
Compensation for crime victims can be awarded by High Courts under Article 226 without relegating them to civil courts; such public law compensation is in addition to private law tort remedies.

Compensation comprises two parts: a standard conventional sum for non-pecuniary losses (revised periodically for inflation using CPI-IW) and dependency compensation computed by the multiplier method using the Second Schedule of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 as a guide.
The standard conventional sum for non-pecuniary losses for the year 1996 was held to be Rs. 97,700/- (inflation-corrected from Rs. 50,000/- set in Lata Wadhwa for 1989).

key_passages.label: public_law_compensation_principle
key_passages.quote: The Court, where the infringement of the fundamental right is established, therefore, cannot stop by giving a mere declaration. It must proceed further and give compensatory relief, not by way of damages as in a civil action but by way of compensation under the public law jurisdiction for the wrong done, due to breach of public duty by the State of not protecting the fundamental right to life of the citizen.

key_passages.label: state_liability_for_terrorism
key_passages.quote: So, compensation is payable to the petitioner by the State for the death of Uday Singh for the breach of the constitutional guarantee of Article 21 that ''no person shall be deprived of his life .. except according to procedure established by law''.

key_passages.label: multiplier_method_description
key_passages.quote: the multiplier method involves the ascertainment of the loss of dependency or the multiplicand having regard to the circumstances of the case and capitalizing the multiplicand by an appropriate multiplier.

key_passages.label: final_order
key_passages.quote: it is directed that the Respondents shall, within a period of four weeks from today, pay to the petitioner (for herself and her minor son, Mukesh) an amount of Rs 4,36,500/- Along with simple interest thereon @ 7% for the period 20.4.1996 (i.e., the date of the explosion) till date.

summary: This writ petition (decided 10 September 2004 by the Delhi High Court) was filed by Kamla Devi, widow of Uday Singh who died in the Paharganj bomb blast of 20 April 1996 caused by a terrorist. Uday Singh was 29 years old and earned Rs. 3,000/- per month at the time of death. The petitioner sought Rs. 10 lakhs compensation from the State for failing to prevent the terrorist attack in violation of the constitutional guarantee under Article 21. The court held that the State, having failed to prevent terrorism resulting in the death of an innocent citizen, is liable to pay compensation in public law jurisdiction under Article 226. Rejecting the view that petitioners must pursue private law tort remedies, the court adopted a two-tier compensation formula drawing on D.K. Basu, Lata Wadhwa, and the Motor Vehicles Act Second Schedule: a standard conventional sum for non-pecuniary loss (revised to Rs. 97,700/- using CPI-IW inflation adjustment from the 1989 Lata Wadhwa benchmark of Rs. 50,000/-) plus dependency compensation using the multiplier of 18 (applicable to age 29) yielding Rs. 3,88,800/-. After adjusting the ex-gratia of Rs. 50,000/- already paid, the State was directed to pay Rs. 4,36,500/- with 7% simple interest from the date of death. The judgment is an important precedent on the methodology of inflation-adjusted conventional sums and crime-victim compensation under public law.

case_title: A.V. Janaki Amma And Ors. vs Union Of India (Uoi) And Ors.
court: High Court of Andhra Pradesh

respondents: Col. M.N. Nath (Senior Advisor, Gynaecology, Military Hospital Secunderabad)
Brig. S.V. Vatve (Commandant, Military Hospital Secunderabad)
Director General of Armed Forces Medical Services

core_facts: Smt. Savithri, wife of Major P. Gopalakrishna (a Commissioned Officer in the Indian Army), died on 16.02.1997 after surgery at Military Hospital, Secunderabad.
A cystectomy surgery was performed on 26.11.1996 by Col. M.N. Nath (Obstetrician and Gynaecologist); a surgical mop was negligently left inside Savithri's abdomen during the operation.
Despite persistent post-operative symptoms including fever and wound discharge, Savithri was not referred to a specialist and was prematurely discharged.
On 01.01.1997, Savithri was taken to Apollo Hospital where exploratory laparotomy revealed the mop; she ultimately died on 16.02.1997 from septicemia and multi-organ failure.

A Court of Inquiry confirmed the negligence and recommended disciplinary action against Col. M.N. Nath and censure against Brig. S.V. Vatve; the findings were accepted by the General Officer Commanding.
legal_issues: Whether respondent Nos. 2 and 3 (doctors at Military Hospital) were negligent in treating Savithri and whether Union of India and other respondents are vicariously liable.
Whether petitioners are entitled to compensation in public law remedy under Article 226 of the Constitution for violation of Savithri's fundamental right to life under Article 21.
outcome: Writ petition allowed. Union of India directed to pay Rs. 3,00,000/- apportioned as Rs. 50,000/- each to petitioners 1 and 4, and Rs. 1,00,000/- each to petitioners 2 and 3. Medical expenses of Rs. 2,99,241/- at Apollo Hospital were separately reimbursed by the President of India. Petitioners given liberty to file civil suit, with any civil damages to be adjusted against the public law award.
key_holdings: Principle of res ipsa loquitur applies where a surgical mop is left inside a patient's abdomen; the respondent doctors were grossly negligent.

When a fundamental right to life under Article 21 is violated by the negligence of a public authority's employees, the State is vicariously liable and compensation is awardable in public law under Article 226.

Public law compensation for violation of Article 21 is a palliative remedy in addition to private law tort remedies; it is based on strict liability and the defence of sovereign immunity is inapplicable.
The Court of Inquiry's findings of gross negligence, when produced before the court and accepted by the appropriate superior authority, constitute strong evidence of medical negligence.

key_passages.label: court_of_inquiry_finding
key_passages.quote: The wife of Major Gopalakrishna, Mrs. A.V. Savithri died due to the complications arising out of leaving a surgical mop in her abdomen during the surgery for ovarian cyst conducted at the Military Hospital, Secunderabad, on 26 November 1996.

key_passages.label: res_ipsa_loquitur_application
key_passages.quote: This Court, having gone through the detailed proceedings before the Court of Inquiry running into 114 pages, is of considered opinion, the principle of res ipso loquitor must be applied to the facts of this case.

key_passages.label: public_law_compensation_basis
key_passages.quote: It is no more res integra that for violation of fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India, public authorities, officials and State are liable to pay compensation.

key_passages.label: compensation_order
key_passages.quote: this Court is of the considered opinion that a Mandamus should go to first respondent to pay an amount of Rs. 3,00,000/- (Rupees three lakhs only). I make it clear that this amount is not by way of punitive damages or is it towards pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages.

summary: This writ petition (decided 23 October 2003 by the Andhra Pradesh High Court) arises from the death of Smt. Savithri, wife of Major P. Gopalakrishna, due to medical negligence at Military Hospital, Secunderabad. During surgery for an ovarian cyst on 26 November 1996, Col. M.N. Nath (Senior Advisor, Gynaecology) left a surgical mop inside Savithri's abdomen. Despite post-operative complications including persistent fever and wound discharge, she was not referred to a specialist and was prematurely discharged. When admitted to Apollo Hospital in January 1997, the mop was discovered; she died on 16 February 1997 from septicemia and multi-organ failure. A Court of Inquiry assembled in November 1997 confirmed gross negligence, attributing blame to Col. M.N. Nath for leaving the mop, concealing the information, and failing to take corrective measures, and to the Commandant for not investigating adequately. The court applied res ipsa loquitur and held the doctors grossly negligent. On the public law remedy, the court surveyed landmark decisions from Rudul Shah to D.K. Basu, holding that violation of Article 21 through State medical negligence attracts compensatory relief in writ jurisdiction. The Union of India was directed to pay Rs. 3,00,000/- apportioned among petitioners and was permitted to recover from the negligent doctors. Petitioners were also left free to pursue civil remedies, with any civil award to be adjusted.

case_title: Mrs. M. Rathnamma and Others vs ICICI Lombard General Ins. Co. Ltd. and Another
court: IX Additional Small Causes Court and Additional MACT, Bangalore (SCCH-7), M.V.C. No. 2107/2015
judge_or_bench: Smt. Indira Mailswamy Chettiyar, B.Com., LL.B.(Spl), L.L.M., IX Addl. Small Causes Judge and Member MACT-7

respondents: ICICI Lombard General Ins. Co. Ltd.
insurer: ICICI Lombard General Ins. Co. Ltd. (Policy No. 3004/TM00253774/4/00/000, valid 02.09.2014 to 01.09.2015)
owner_or_driver: Manager Partner, M/s. Megha Travels (R) (owner of Bus KA-51-C-114)

core_facts: On 01.04.2015 at about 10.15 p.m., M. Eshwarappa (aged 32, Security Guard earning Rs. 11,970.55 per month) was walking on the extreme left edge of Bangalore Main Road near Chandu Motors, Singasandra.

Bus bearing Registration No. KA-51-C-114, owned by M/s. Megha Travels and insured by ICICI Lombard, driven rashly and negligently at high speed, dashed into the deceased and fled the spot, leaving the bus near Madiwala Traffic Police Station.
Deceased was shifted to LIVE 100 Hospital where he was declared dead; post mortem confirmed cause of death as injuries to head and spinal cord.
Electronic City Traffic Police registered FIR and filed charge sheet against the driver for offences under IPC s.279, 304A and MV Act s.134(a), (b) and 187.
Insurer ICICI Lombard contested the claim raising defences of invalid driving licence, absence of permit and fitness certificate, but did not produce any evidence on its behalf.
legal_issues: Whether the accident occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the offending bus and whether the deceased died of injuries sustained therein.
Whether the insurer's defences of invalid driving licence and permit/fitness certificate violations were proved.
What is the just compensation payable to the dependants of the deceased including application of future prospects and appropriate multiplier.
outcome: Petition partly allowed. ICICI Lombard directed to pay Rs. 25,95,346/- with interest at 9% p.a. from the date of petition till payment. Insurer's defences (invalid licence, no permit/fitness) rejected as not proved. Father (petitioner No. 3) held not entitled to dependency but recognized as legal representative. Amount to be shared in ratio 50:20:10:20 among petitioners 1-4.
key_holdings: Eye-witness testimony corroborated by FIR, complaint, charge sheet, spot panchanama, MVI report, inquest and post mortem report conclusively established rash and negligent driving by the bus driver as the cause of death.

The insurer failed to produce any evidence to substantiate its specific defences of invalid driving licence or absence of permit/fitness certificate; violation of policy terms by the owner was accordingly not proved.

For a deceased aged 32 years in permanent salaried employment, future prospects are computed by adding 50% of actual income per the Rajesh v. Rajbir Singh formula; with 3 dependants, 1/3rd of total income is deducted as personal expenses, and a multiplier of 16 is applied.
A father cannot be considered a dependant upon his son for the purposes of motor accident compensation.

key_passages.label: negligence_finding
key_passages.quote: due to very high speed, rash and negligent manner of driving of the offending Private Mini Bus bearing Registration No.KA-51-C-114 by its driver itself, the said road traffic accident was taken place, wherein, the deceased succumbed to the fatal injuries on the way to the Hospital

key_passages.label: insurer_defence_rejected
key_passages.quote: The violation of the terms and conditions of the admitted Insurance Policy by the Respondent No.2 is not proved by the Respondent No.1. Under such circumstances, the Respondent No.1 being an Insurer and the Respondent No.2 being a R.C. Owner of the offending Private Mini Bus bearing Registration No.KA-51-C-114 are jointly and severally liable to pay the above said compensation and interest to the Petitioners.

key_passages.label: father_not_dependent
key_passages.quote: the father cannot be considered as a dependant upon the son.

key_passages.label: compensation_award
key_passages.quote: The Petitioners are entitled for compensation of Rupees 25,95,346/- with interest at the rate of 9% p.a. from the date of the petition till the date of payment, from the Respondent No.1.

adverse_value: The Tribunal held that a father cannot be considered a dependant upon a son, which could be cited to exclude fathers from the class of dependants in compensation claims for male deceased breadwinners.
summary: This MACT award (M.V.C. No. 2107/2015, dated 19 October 2016) concerns the death of M. Eshwarappa, a 32-year-old security guard earning Rs. 11,970.55 per month, who was fatally struck by a privately operated mini bus (KA-51-C-114) while walking on the extreme left edge of Bangalore Main Road on 01 April 2015. The bus driver fled the scene after the impact. The owner M/s. Megha Travels remained ex-parte. ICICI Lombard, the insurer, contested the claim raising defences of invalid driving licence and absence of permit and fitness certificate, but produced no evidence. The Tribunal, relying on the eye-witness account of P.W.2, corroborated by FIR, charge sheet, spot sketch, MVI report and post mortem, held rash and negligent driving conclusively proved. All insurer defences were rejected for want of evidence. Following Rajesh v. Rajbir Singh (2013) for future prospects (50% addition for age below 40), Sarla Verma for multiplier (16 for age 32) and deduction (1/3rd for personal expenses with 3 dependants), the Tribunal computed loss of dependency at Rs. 22,98,346/-. Additional heads included consortium (Rs. 1,00,000/-), loss of care and guidance for minor child (Rs. 1,00,000/-), funeral expenses (Rs. 25,000/-), loss of love and affection (Rs. 25,000/-), transportation of body (Rs. 7,000/-) and loss of estate (Rs. 40,000/-). Total compensation: Rs. 25,95,346/- at 9% interest.

case_title: Nazar Singh vs State Of Punjab And Others
court: High Court for the States of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh

owner_or_driver: Nazar Singh (driver, Punjab Roadways bus PBM-6964)

core_facts: Petitioner Nazar Singh, a driver employed by Punjab Roadways, was driving bus PBM-6964 on 12.02.1985 when it met with an accident in village Mander area, resulting in two deaths and two injuries.

The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT), Ludhiana, by award dated 02.06.1986 held the petitioner negligent and the employer Punjab Roadways paid Rs. 3,10,427.95/- in compensation to the accident victims.

Punjab Roadways issued a show cause notice in 1992 seeking recovery of Rs. 2,12,000/- with 9% interest from the petitioner-driver, and passed an order dated 24.02.1994 directing recovery of Rs. 3,10,427.95/- without conducting any departmental inquiry.

The bus was not insured; the State of Punjab had not established a statutory compensation fund as required by the proviso to Section 146(3) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 as a precondition for exempting State transport vehicles from mandatory insurance.

In the proceedings before the MACT, Punjab Roadways had itself contested the claim supporting the driver's plea that he was not negligent, only for the employer to later seek full recovery from the same driver.
legal_issues: Whether the employer-State can recover compensation paid to accident victims from the employee-driver solely on the basis of the MACT award without conducting a departmental inquiry affording the driver a meaningful opportunity of being heard.

Whether the State of Punjab's failure to maintain a statutory compensation fund under the proviso to Section 146(3) of the MV Act, while exempting its vehicles from insurance, bars it from recovering compensation from the driver.
Whether the MACT award by itself constitutes sufficient indictment of the driver to justify recovery proceedings against him.
outcome: Both writ petitions allowed. Recovery order dated 24.02.1994 (Annexure P-3) quashed. State impressed upon to either insure its vehicles or establish and maintain a statutory compensation fund under Section 146 MV Act. State told it may recover loss from errant employees only after following proper departmental inquiry procedure with effective opportunity of hearing.
key_holdings: The MACT award, standing alone, cannot form the basis of recovery of compensation from the driver-employee; a prior departmental inquiry with effective opportunity of hearing is mandatory before any such recovery can be ordered.

Vicarious liability of the State to pay compensation awarded by the MACT is qua the accident victims (claimants) and not qua the employee-driver; the State cannot bypass its own statutory obligations and shift its liability entirely to the driver.

The State of Punjab was in violation of its statutory duty under Section 146(3) of the MV Act by exempting its buses from insurance without establishing and maintaining the mandatory compensation fund, and cannot take shelter from this violation to recover from the driver.

Issuance of a show cause notice followed by an order without considering the driver's reply does not satisfy the requirement of affording an effective opportunity of being heard; such an order has no legal significance.

key_passages.label: section_146_3_proviso
key_passages.quote: When owner of a motor vehicle is statutorily obligated to obtain an insurance for the vehicle to cover with the third party risk, exemption from this statutory obligation of obtaining an insurance cover, is permissible inter-alia to the State, subject to the condition of establishing and maintaining a fund to meet liabilities such as the present one, towards legal heirs of the deceased or to the victims injured in the accident caused by its vehicles while any vehicle of the State was being in use.

key_passages.label: natural_justice_requirement
key_passages.quote: neither any inquiry was held nor liability to pay the demanded sum had been fixed by any objective method or criteria.

key_passages.label: mact_award_not_sufficient_basis
key_passages.quote: Award of the Tribunal ipso facto could not have formed the basis of recovery of the amount from the petitioner-driver of compensation paid to the victims of the accident by the respondent-employer.

key_passages.label: vicarious_liability_clarification
key_passages.quote: The State is vicariously liable for acts done by its employees but vicarious liability to pay compensation awarded of the State is qua the claimants and not qua the employees, viz, drivers.

summary: This common judgment of the Punjab and Haryana High Court (dated 21 December 2013) decides CWP Nos. 12064 of 1994 (Nazar Singh) and 2373 of 1995 (Iqbal Singh), both challenging orders by Punjab Roadways seeking to recover from driver-employees the compensation amounts paid pursuant to MACT awards arising from bus accidents. In the lead case, Nazar Singh drove Punjab Roadways bus PBM-6964 in 1985 when it met with an accident killing two persons; the MACT held him negligent and the employer paid Rs. 3,10,427.95/-. Without holding any departmental inquiry and without meaningfully considering the driver's reply to the show cause notice, Punjab Roadways ordered recovery of the entire amount from the driver in 1994. The court quashed the recovery orders on two grounds. First, the State of Punjab exempted its buses from compulsory insurance under Section 146(3) MV Act without establishing the mandatory statutory compensation fund; having failed its own statutory obligation, the State could not pass its financial liability to the driver. Second, the MACT award was made on a preponderance-of-evidence standard not equivalent to a criminal conviction or departmental inquiry; the employer must hold a proper departmental inquiry with natural justice principles before recovering from an employee. The court directed that recovery from errant drivers is permissible only after following appropriate punishment rules and giving effective hearing, and impressed upon the State the obligation to insure its vehicles or establish the required statutory fund.

case_title: Jagdish Rai vs State of Punjab and Others
court: High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh

respondents: Assistant Excise and Taxation Commissioner, Muktsar

statutes: Punjab Civil Service (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1970 Rule 5
Punjab Civil Service (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1970 Rule 10
core_facts: Petitioner Jagdish Rai was a government driver employed with the Assistant Excise and Taxation Commissioner, Muktsar
On 4.10.1991, while driving government Jeep No. PAR-782 from Fazilka to Ferozepur, an accident occurred resulting in death of Constable Ranjit Singh
FIR registered under Section 304; petitioner was acquitted in criminal trial on 27.2.1999
Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Ferozepur awarded compensation of Rs. 2,49,600/- against petitioner and respondents jointly and severally under Sections 166 and 140 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988
State paid the full compensation without filing an appeal; petitioner also did not challenge the award
On 26.11.1998, respondent No. 3 directed recovery of Rs. 83,200/- (1/3rd share) from petitioner's salary at Rs. 2,700/- per month without issuing prior notice or conducting any inquiry
legal_issues: Whether recovery from a government employee's salary can be effected without following the mandatory procedure under Punjab Civil Service (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1970
Whether acquittal in criminal proceedings absolves the driver of liability for contribution to the compensation award
Scope of vicarious liability of the State Government as employer for the negligent act of its driver
outcome: Writ petition allowed. Order dated 26.11.1998 directing salary recovery quashed. Respondents at liberty to proceed in accordance with law after following mandatory procedure under Punjab Civil Service Rules.
key_holdings: Recovery from a government employee's salary for pecuniary loss caused by negligence is a minor penalty under Rule 5(iii) of the Punjab Civil Service (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1970, requiring prior notice and opportunity of hearing under Rule 10
Acquittal in criminal proceedings does not absolve a driver from civil liability for compensation under the Motor Vehicles Act
The State as employer has vicarious liability when its driver causes injury to a third party while driving in the course of employment

key_passages.label: vicarious_liability
key_passages.quote: But once it is found and established that vehicle was being used for the business of the employer, then the employer will be held vicariously liable even for the lapse, omission and negligence of his driver to whom the vehicle had been entrusted for being driver for the business of the employer.

key_passages.label: disciplinary_procedure
key_passages.quote: no order imposing any of the penalties specified in Rule 5 (i) to (iv) could be passed except after informing the employee concerned of the proposal to take action against him and giving him a reasonable opportunity of making representation.

key_passages.label: holding
key_passages.quote: The aforesaid procedure in the present case admittedly has not been followed. Therefore, I am of the considered view that order dated 26.11.1998 (P-1) is liable to be set aside.

key_passages.label: minor_penalty_rule
key_passages.quote: (iii) recovery from his pay of the whole or partly of any pecuniary loss caused by him to the Government by negligence or breach of orders.

summary: This writ petition under Article 226 was filed by a government driver challenging an order directing recovery of Rs. 83,200 from his salary. The petitioner had been involved in a motor vehicle accident on 4.10.1991 resulting in the death of Constable Ranjit Singh while driving a government Jeep in official duty. Though acquitted in criminal proceedings on 27.2.1999, the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal awarded Rs. 2,49,600 against the petitioner and others jointly and severally. After the State paid the compensation, it sought recovery of the petitioner's one-third share from his salary, issuing a direction without prior notice or inquiry as required by Rule 10 of the Punjab Civil Service (Punishment and Appeal) Rules, 1970. The Court examined the Supreme Court's principles on vicarious liability of government employers in motor accident cases, and held that such salary recovery constitutes a minor penalty under Rule 5(iii) of the Rules, which mandatorily requires notice, opportunity to make representation, and a recorded finding before imposition. Since the mandatory procedure was not followed, the recovery order was quashed and the State was directed to re-proceed in accordance with law.

case_title: Monnet Ispat & Energy Ltd vs C.C.E., Raipur
court: Customs Excise & Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, New Delhi
core_facts: Monnet Ispat manufactured sponge iron and other iron and steel products chargeable to central excise duty under Chapter 72 and availed Cenvat credit under Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004
Department issued show cause notice dated 3.11.2006 seeking to deny service tax credit of Rs. 4,36,650 and impose penalty under Rule 15 of Cenvat Credit Rules

Assistant Commissioner allowed credit of Rs. 3,98,142 but disallowed Rs. 38,510 for five categories of services including marine inland transit insurance, money insurance, personnel accident insurance, follow-up installation services, and telephone services at GM residence and guest house
Commissioner (Appeals) vide order dated 9.10.2007 upheld the Assistant Commissioner's order in full

Appellant contended that the disallowed services fall within the definition of 'input service' under the Cenvat Credit Rules and that transit insurance for capital goods is covered when inward transportation is expressly covered
legal_issues: Whether marine inland transit insurance for captive power plant machinery during inward transport qualifies as an input service eligible for Cenvat credit
Whether insurance of money in transit from factory to bank qualifies as an input service
Whether follow-up services for installation of captive power plant qualify as business auxiliary input services
Whether accident insurance for contract workers (for whom the principal employer has vicarious liability under the Factory Act) qualifies as an input service
Whether telephone services installed at the General Manager's residence and company guest house qualify as input services
outcome: Appeal partly allowed. Cenvat credit held eligible for marine inland transit insurance, money insurance in transit, follow-up installation services for captive power plant, and accident insurance for factory personnel including contract workers. Credit denied and penalty upheld for telephone services at GM's residence and company guest house.
key_holdings: When inward transportation of capital goods is specifically covered by the definition of input service, transit insurance during inward transport of those capital goods is also covered
Insurance of money in transit from factory to bank is part of the business activity and is covered by the definition of input service
Follow-up services for installation of captive power plant are business auxiliary services eligible for Cenvat credit as they relate to setting up or modernisation
Accident insurance for contract workers engaged in the factory is eligible where the principal employer has vicarious liability under the Factory Act
Telephone services at the GM's residence and guest house are not eligible as no nexus with manufacturing activity was demonstrated

key_passages.label: transit_insurance_holding
key_passages.quote: When inward transportation of input or capital goods is specifically covered by the definition of input services, the insurance during inward of the transport of capital goods would also be covered.

key_passages.label: money_in_transit_holding
key_passages.quote: I therefore, hold that service of insurance of money in transit is covered by the definition of Input Service.

key_passages.label: personnel_insurance_holding
key_passages.quote: I hold that appellants are eligible for Cenvat credit of service tax on the insurance premium for the insurance of the personnel working in the factory.

key_passages.label: outcome_order
key_passages.quote: the rest of the order upholding the cenvat credit demand by denying cenvat credit in respect of marine inland transit insurance, money insurance for money in transit from bank to factory to & fro, follow up services in connection with installation of plant & machinery of captive power plant and insurance of personnel working in the factory for accident or loss and upholding the penalty on the Appellant, is set aside.

summary: This excise appeal before CESTAT was filed by Monnet Ispat & Energy Ltd. against denial of Cenvat credit under the Cenvat Credit Rules, 2004 for five categories of services. The Assistant Commissioner and Commissioner (Appeals) had disallowed credit of Rs. 38,510 for: marine inland transit insurance for captive power plant machinery transported from BHEL's premises to the appellant's factory; money insurance for cash in transit between factory and bank; follow-up services for installation of the captive power plant; accident insurance for personnel including contract workers; and telephone services at the General Manager's residence and company guest house. The Tribunal held that transit insurance for capital goods is covered by the definition of input service since inward transportation is expressly included. Money-in-transit insurance was held to be a normal prudent business activity covered as input service. Follow-up installation services qualified as business auxiliary services for setting up. Accident insurance for contract workers was held eligible on account of the principal employer's vicarious liability under the Factory Act. However, telephone services at non-factory premises with no demonstrated nexus to manufacturing were rightly denied. The appeal was accordingly allowed in part and the penalty qua the denied credit upheld.

case_title: K. Surappa vs V. Venkatesha Reddy and Others
court: High Court of Karnataka
statutes: Representation of the People Act s.160
Representation of the People Act s.161
core_facts: Petitioner K. Surappa, a police constable, was travelling in bus No. MYY 3122 belonging to first respondent V. Venkatesha Reddy for election duty on 7.3.1971
Bus was requisitioned by the Deputy Commissioner under Section 160 of the Representation of the People Act for transporting election officials and boxes
The bus dashed against a roadside tree and capsized due to rash or negligent driving of the driver, causing compound fracture of both bones of petitioner's left leg and a simple fracture

Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal dismissed the claim holding: (a) master-servant relationship between owner and driver was temporarily suspended during requisition, and (b) State had sovereign immunity for tortious acts in exercise of sovereign function
Insurer also contended that commandeering of vehicle for election purposes was outside the policy cover
No evidence was adduced by the owner that he was not required to pay the driver's wages during the requisition period
legal_issues: Whether requisitioning of a vehicle under Section 160 of the Representation of the People Act suspends the master-servant relationship between the vehicle owner and his driver
Whether the vehicle owner is vicariously liable for the driver's negligence when the vehicle is requisitioned by government for election purposes
Whether the insurer can avoid liability on the ground that the vehicle was commandeered for election purposes falling outside the policy cover
Whether the State can claim sovereign immunity for tortious acts of the driver during a sovereign function
outcome: Appeal allowed with costs. Judgment and award of Tribunal rejecting claim set aside. Petitioner awarded Rs. 20,000 with 12% interest per annum from date of filing petition to date of payment. Insurer (fifth respondent) liable for Rs. 5,000 with proportionate costs and interest; balance payable by owner (first respondent).
key_holdings: Mere requisitioning of a vehicle by government under Section 160 of the Representation of the People Act does not suspend or extinguish the master-servant relationship between the vehicle owner and his driver

When a vehicle along with its driver is effectively given on hire for a temporary period, the driver does not cease to be the employee of the owner; the relationship only ends if the hirer also controls the method of driving, not merely the destination
The insurer's defence that commandeering for election purposes took the vehicle outside the policy cover was rightly rejected by the Tribunal under Section 96(2) of the Motor Vehicles Act
The question of the State's sovereign immunity was rendered unnecessary to decide once owner's vicarious liability was established

key_passages.label: master_servant_relationship
key_passages.quote: The mere fact that the vehicle ' is requisitioned by the Deputy Commissioner under the above statutory provision, does not lead to the inference that the driver of the vehicle ceased to be the employee of the owner nor does it indicate that the owner ceased to have interest in the vehicle.

key_passages.label: vicarious_liability_holding
key_passages.quote: the driver continued to be employee of the first respondent and that the first respondent is vicariously liable for the rash or negligent driving of the bus by the driver.

key_passages.label: insurer_liability
key_passages.quote: The only objection which has been raised by the insurer with regard to its liability namely that as the vehicle had been commandeered for election purposes it is not liable to pay the compensation has been rightly negatived by the Tribunal.

key_passages.label: compensation_awarded
key_passages.quote: awarding him Rs. 20,000/- together with costs and current interest at 12% per annum from the date of the filing of the petition till date of payment.

adverse_value: Insurer's liability limited to Rs. 5,000 per endorsement No. 13 in the policy despite total compensation of Rs. 20,000; the endorsement limiting third-party liability was accepted, with the balance payable by the owner.
summary: This appeal was filed by K. Surappa, a police constable, seeking compensation for injuries sustained in a motor vehicle accident on 7.3.1971 when a bus requisitioned by the Deputy Commissioner for election duty capsized due to rash and negligent driving. The Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal had dismissed the claim on two grounds: that the requisition temporarily suspended the master-servant relationship between the bus owner and driver, and that the State enjoyed sovereign immunity for tortious acts during a sovereign function. The insurer also pleaded that commandeering placed the vehicle outside the policy cover. The Karnataka High Court reversed all these findings. Applying the principle from Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, the Court held that mere requisitioning under statute does not sever the employer-employee relationship; the burden rests heavily on the owner to prove transfer of the servant and no such evidence was led. The Court further noted that Section 160 of the Representation of the People Act only contemplated requisitioning the vehicle and not the driver's services. The insurer's defence was rejected under Section 96(2). The claimant was awarded Rs. 20,000 with 12% interest, with the insurer bearing Rs. 5,000 per the policy endorsement and the owner the balance.

case_title: Ajay Alias Vishal Veeru Devgan vs The Artists Planet & Ors
court: High Court of Delhi at New Delhi
statutes: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 Order XXXIX Rule 1
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 Order XXXIX Rule 2
Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021
core_facts: Plaintiff Ajay Devgn is an acclaimed Bollywood actor with a career spanning over four decades, recipient of multiple National Film Awards and the Padma Shri

Plaintiff holds registered trademarks for his name 'Ajay Devgn'/'Ajay Devgan'/'Ajay Veeru Devgn' and variations under various classes, and has personality rights over his name, voice, likeness and image

Identified infringing defendants include: a website offering fake appearance/performance bookings, sellers of unauthorized merchandise, a YouTube channel creating deepfake content, Facebook pages posting AI-generated images in unsavoury scenarios, and pornographic websites posting face-morphed content

Defendant No. 7 (Google LLC/YouTube) impleaded on account of its 'Your content & third-party training' policy allowing creators to use videos for AI-model training, posing risk of propagating defamatory content

Defendants are using plaintiff's name, image and persona for commercial gain through unauthorized merchandise sales, deepfakes, AI-generated advertisements and pornographic content without plaintiff's consent
The Court noted that some infringing posts dated back to June 2025 and the plaintiff had not availed the IT Intermediary Rules grievance mechanism before approaching the court
legal_issues: Whether plaintiff's personality and publicity rights have been infringed by unauthorized use of his name, image, voice and likeness for commercial gain
Whether AI-generated deepfake content and face-morphed pornographic material violate the plaintiff's personality rights
Whether ex-parte ad-interim injunction should be granted against infringing defendants
Whether social media intermediaries must take down infringing content when uploaders fail to comply
Whether plaintiffs are required to first exhaust IT Intermediary Rules mechanism before seeking court-ordered takedowns
outcome: Ex-parte ad-interim injunction granted against all identified infringing defendants. Directions issued to take down infringing content within 72 hours. Social media intermediaries (YouTube/Google, Meta, X) directed to act if uploaders fail to comply. ISPs directed via MeiTY/DoT to block infringing domains. Court issued prospective observation that plaintiffs bypassing IT Intermediary Rules mechanism for certain categories of posts may be denied ex-parte injunctions in future.
key_holdings: Celebrity status grants the plaintiff proprietary rights over his personality and associated attributes including name, likeness, voice and image
Plaintiff's personality traits are protectable elements of personality rights and he is entitled to injunction against their use for commercial gain without authorisation
Plaintiff is prima facie entitled to protect himself against morphed and distorted AI-generated content that portrays him in a repugnant manner

Complainants who approach the court without first availing the statutory IT Intermediary Rules mechanism for certain categories of infringing content may be held not entitled to ex-parte ad-interim injunction

key_passages.label: celebrity_status_finding
key_passages.quote: this Court is of the prima facie view that the Plaintiff is a well-known face in India who has gained immense goodwill and reputation over a course of a successful career and has acquired a celebrity status in India.

key_passages.label: personality_rights_holding
key_passages.quote: prima facie, the Plaintiff's personality traits and/or parts thereof, including the Plaintiff's name, likeness, voice, and image are protectable elements of the Plaintiff's personality rights. The Plaintiff is entitled to seek injunction against the use of his personality rights by third parties for selling merchandise for their commercial gains, without his authorisation.

key_passages.label: deepfake_protection
key_passages.quote: the Plaintiff is prima facie entitled to protect himself against morphed and distorted content created with the use of AI technology which portrays the Plaintiff in a repugnant manner, subjecting him to humiliation and ridicule.

key_passages.label: it_intermediary_rules_observation
key_passages.quote: if henceforth a complainant/plaintiff approaches the Court without availing the statutory mechanism provided under the IT Intermediary Rules, the said party may be held to be not entitled to an ex-parte ad-interim injunction, and the Court will direct the party to first avail its remedy under the aforesaid Rules.

summary: Bollywood actor Ajay Devgn filed this commercial suit (CS(COMM) 1269/2025) seeking permanent injunction and interim relief against 17 defendants infringing his personality, publicity, trademark, and copyright rights. The infringement took multiple forms: unauthorized merchandise bearing his name and image, deepfake videos, AI-generated pornographic content, impersonation on social media, and commercial exploitation of his persona without consent. The plaintiff holds registered trademarks for variations of his name and asserts personality rights under Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution, moral rights under Sections 38-38B of the Copyright Act, and statutory trademark rights. The Court granted ex-parte ad-interim injunction against identified infringing defendants, directing takedown of infringing content within 72 hours, and ordered social media intermediaries (YouTube/Google, Meta/Facebook, X) to take action if uploaders failed to comply within the granted time. ISPs were directed via MeiTY and DoT to block infringing domains. The Court also issued a significant prospective observation that plaintiffs who bypass the IT Intermediary Rules grievance mechanism for certain categories of content before approaching the court risk being denied ex-parte ad-interim injunctions in future proceedings.

case_title: New Balance Athletics Inc. vs Ashok Kumar & Ors.
court: High Court of Delhi at New Delhi
statutes: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 Order VIII Rule 10
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 Order I Rule 10
core_facts: New Balance Athletics Inc. is a US-based footwear company using the trademark 'NEW BALANCE' since 1951 and 'NB' device marks since the 1970s, with registrations in India
Defendants Indramani Sahu and Jagabandhu Sahoo operated website www.luxurytag.in which openly sold counterfeit footwear bearing the plaintiff's marks
The website explicitly described itself as 'India's first online store to sell replica of all kind (Since 2015)' and admitted selling products 'which look similar to the originals'
A representative of the plaintiff placed a test order in February 2023 and confirmed the product received was a fake/counterfeit
Main contesting defendants (Nos. 1 and 11) were served but failed to appear or file any written statement despite service on 08.09.2023 and 02.09.2023 respectively
Other defendants (proforma defendants) had either complied with court directions or had their right to file written statements closed
legal_issues: Whether the defendants' sale of counterfeit footwear bearing the plaintiff's registered trademarks constitutes trademark infringement under Section 29(2)(c) and 29(3) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999
Whether the triple/quadruple identity test (same marks, goods, consumers, and channels) is satisfied
Whether defendants' self-admission of selling replica/counterfeit products is sufficient proof of infringement
Whether actual litigation costs can be awarded as a remedy for counterfeiting
outcome: Suit decreed in favour of plaintiff against defendant nos. 1 and 11. Permanent injunction granted. Actual costs of Rs. 14,51,670/- (including court fees of Rs. 2,01,000 and Local Commissioner's fee of Rs. 1,00,000) awarded jointly and severally payable within 8 weeks.
key_holdings: Where defendants use marks identical to plaintiff's registered trademarks on identical goods sold to identical consumers through identical channels, the triple/quadruple identity test under Section 29(2)(c) read with 29(3) is satisfied and likelihood of confusion is presumed
Defendants' explicit self-admissions on their website of selling replica/counterfeit products constitute sufficient proof of infringement and passing off
Where contesting defendants fail to file a written statement despite service, the plaintiff's submissions stand admitted under Order VIII Rule 10 of the CPC
Counterfeiting is a serious economic offence that erodes brand value and misleads consumers, warranting strict treatment and award of actual costs

key_passages.label: self_admission_of_counterfeiting
key_passages.quote: Perusal of the above clearly shows that defendant nos. 1 and 11 have made categorical statements admitting sale of replica/fake/counterfeit products.

key_passages.label: triple_identity_test
key_passages.quote: the triple identity test, which envisages identity of marks, goods and consumers and availability of the goods through identical sources and outlets, is satisfied in the present case. One may even say the quadruple identity test stands satisfied.

key_passages.label: infringement_and_passing_off
key_passages.quote: The statements as aforenoted, on the Impugned Website, which can be found in plain view, for the consumers to observe, is sufficient admittance on its own by the said defendants, and prima facie amounts to the acts of infringement and passing off of the plaintiff

key_passages.label: actual_costs_awarded
key_passages.quote: In view of the above and on account of a clear case of counterfeiting and infringing activity being made out against defendant nos. 1 and 11, the present is a fit case for awarding actual costs in favor of the plaintiff and against defendant nos. 1 and 11.

summary: New Balance Athletics Inc., the American footwear company holding registered trademarks 'NEW BALANCE' and 'NB' in India, filed this commercial suit against operators of a rogue website www.luxurytag.in that openly sold counterfeit footwear bearing the plaintiff's marks. The website explicitly described itself as selling replicas 'which look similar to the originals.' The plaintiff's identities of the infringing defendants were established through discovery from proforma defendants, revealing Indramani Sahu as operator and Jagabandhu Sahoo as the UPI payment beneficiary. Despite service in September 2023, the contesting defendants failed to appear or file written statements, allowing the Court to invoke Order VIII Rule 10 CPC and treat the plaintiff's submissions as admitted. The Court found that the triple/quadruple identity test under Section 29(2)(c) read with 29(3) of the Trade Marks Act was satisfied: identical marks, identical goods (footwear), identical consumer base, and identical channels of distribution. The defendants' own website statements constituted clear admissions of selling counterfeit products. Following the coordinate bench's ruling in Puma SE v. Brijendra Singh that counterfeiting is a serious economic offence, the suit was decreed with a permanent injunction and actual litigation costs of Rs. 14,51,670 awarded jointly and severally against the infringing defendants.

case_title: Azuga Inc & Anr vs Azuga Telematics LLC & Ors
court: High Court of Delhi at New Delhi
statutes: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 Order XXXIX Rule 1
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 Order XXXIX Rule 2
core_facts: Plaintiff No. 1 Azuga Inc. is a California-based GPS fleet tracking and management company acquired by Bridgestone Americas Inc. in September 2021; Plaintiff No. 2 is its Indian engineering subsidiary based in Bangalore
Plaintiff No. 1 holds registered trademark 'AZUGA' in India (Registration No. 6422638) since at least 2012, as well as registrations in the US, Germany, Mexico and the EU
Defendant No. 1 Azuga Telematics LLC, founded in 2022 in Jamshedpur, provides identical GPS fleet tracking and management services using the name 'AZUGA TELEMATICS' and a similar logo

Defendant No. 3 (Senthil Kumar) is a former employee of Plaintiff No. 2; Defendant No. 2 (Aman Kumar) was listed as domain registrant but voluntarily appeared and denied active involvement with Defendant No. 1

Despite cease and desist notice in January 2023, Defendant No. 1 only altered its logo while continuing to use the full 'AZUGA' mark; defendants also copied plaintiff's website UI assets and product photographs on an 'as-is' basis
Pre-litigation mediation before Delhi High Court Legal Services Committee resulted in non-starter report dated 27.05.2025 as defendants failed to appear
legal_issues: Whether defendants' adoption of the trade name 'AZUGA TELEMATICS' incorporating the plaintiff's registered trademark 'AZUGA' for identical GPS fleet tracking services constitutes trademark infringement under Section 29(5) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999
Whether copying of website UI assets and product photographs constitutes copyright infringement under the Copyright Act, 1957
Whether ex-parte ad-interim injunction should be granted pending the suit
outcome: Ex-parte ad-interim injunction granted. Defendant Nos. 1 and 3 restrained from using the 'AZUGA' mark or any deceptively similar mark including the tradename 'AZUGA TELEMATICS' for GPS fleet tracking services, and from copying plaintiff's copyright-protected website images. Defendant No. 4 (BigRock) directed to lock and suspend Defendant No. 1's domain https://azugatelematicsllc.com/.
key_holdings: Adoption of the name 'AZUGA' in identical services as that of the plaintiff's by defendants (including a former employee), prima facie appears mala fide

Defendants' use of a deceptively similar mark is likely to mislead the public into believing an association with the plaintiffs, causing confusion and diluting the distinctive character of the AZUGA brand
Defendants copying website images on an 'as-is' basis constitutes infringement of plaintiff's copyright in the product photographs
Prima facie case established; balance of convenience lies in plaintiff's favour and irreparable harm established

key_passages.label: mala_fide_adoption
key_passages.quote: the Defendants adoption of the name 'AZUGA' in the identical services as that of the Plaintiffs, prima facie appears mala fide to the Court.

key_passages.label: confusion_and_dilution
key_passages.quote: Given the well-established recognition of the Plaintiffs' trademarks, Defendants use of a deceptively similar mark is likely to mislead the public into believing an association with the Plaintiffs, thereby causing confusion and diluting the distinctive character and identity of the Plaintiffs' AZUGA brand.

key_passages.label: prima_facie_case
key_passages.quote: In the view of the above, the Plaintiffs have made out a prima facie case for the grant of ad-interim injunction, balance of convenience lies in favour of the Plaintiffs and irreparable harm will be caused to the Plaintiffs, in case the restraint is not granted.

key_passages.label: injunction_direction
key_passages.quote: Defendant Nos. 1 and 3, their partners, if any, officers, servants, agents, distributors, stockists and representatives are restrained from importing, manufacturing, warehousing, selling and/or offering for sale, advertising, directly or indirectly dealing, in any manner in any product/services including GPS Fleet Tracking / Management related product/services bearing marks either identical or deceptively similar to the Plaintiffs' registered trademark 'AZUGA'

summary: California-based Azuga Inc. and its Indian subsidiary Azuga Telematics Private Limited (acquired by Bridgestone in 2021) filed this suit against Azuga Telematics LLC, a Jamshedpur-based GPS fleet management startup founded in 2022, for trademark infringement and copyright infringement. The plaintiff holds registered trademark 'AZUGA' in India since 2012 and reported global revenues of USD 83 million in 2024. The defendants, allegedly connected to former employees of the plaintiff, adopted the near-identical trade name 'AZUGA TELEMATICS' for identical GPS fleet tracking services and copied the plaintiff's website UI assets and product photographs on an 'as-is' basis. Despite cease and desist notices and an attempted pre-litigation mediation (which the defendants failed to attend), the infringement continued. Defendant No. 2 appeared voluntarily through video conferencing, denied active involvement with Defendant No. 1, and offered to cooperate. The Court, finding prima facie evidence of mala fide adoption of the mark, likelihood of confusion, and copyright infringement in the copied website images, granted an ex-parte ad-interim injunction restraining Defendant Nos. 1 and 3 from using the 'AZUGA' mark for GPS fleet tracking services and directed the domain registrar (BigRock) to lock and suspend the defendants' domain.

case_title: Intel Corporation vs S.P. Gupta and Others
court: High Court of Delhi at New Delhi
core_facts: Intel Corporation (USA, incorporated 1968) is the world's leading developer and manufacturer of microprocessors; it has used the mark 'INTEL' since inception and holds trademark registrations in India in Classes 9 and 18

In November 2005 the plaintiff discovered that defendant entities (Intel Gas Gadgets P. Ltd., Intel Gas Guards P. Ltd., and Intel Safety Devices), all promoted by S.P. Gupta, were using 'INTEL' as part of their trading names and domain name www.intelgasgadgets.com for LPG regulators, valves and accessories
Despite cease and desist letters in November 2005, December 2005 and March 2006, defendants did not respond, prompting the plaintiff to file suit in May 2006
No interim injunction was granted during the pendency of the suit; evidence was recorded and completed by April 2016
