During pendency of the suit, the mark 'INTEL' was declared a well-known trademark by the Trade Marks Registry under Section 2(zg) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999

S.P. Gupta passed away during proceedings; his legal heirs (sons including Punit Gupta) informed the court through counsel that the three entities had ceased business and would not contest if plaintiff waived damages
legal_issues: Whether defendants' use of 'INTEL' as part of their corporate trading names, trademarks and domain name constitutes trademark infringement
Whether defendants are passing off their goods as those of the plaintiff
Whether the suit suffers from delay and laches
outcome: Suit decreed for permanent injunction in terms of prayers (i) and (ii) of the plaint. All other reliefs not pressed. Intel Gas Gadgets (P) Ltd. directed to change its name within three months. Decree sheet to be drawn accordingly.
key_holdings: The mark 'INTEL' has been declared a well-known trademark within the meaning of Section 2(zg) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 by the Trade Marks Registry
Use of the mark 'INTEL' as a trademark and/or part of trading style by the defendants constitutes infringement as also passing off the defendants' products as those of the plaintiff
Where the lis no longer exists between the parties and the defendants are willing to suffer permanent injunction, the suit can be decreed in terms of the prayer clause without proceeding to trial

key_passages.label: well_known_trademark
key_passages.quote: during the pendency of the suit, the mark 'INTEL' has, in fact, been declared a well-known trademark within the meaning of Section 2(zg) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 by the Trade Marks Registry in the well-known mark list published by the Registrar of Trademarks.

key_passages.label: infringement_and_passing_off
key_passages.quote: it is clear that the trademark 'INTEL' has been registered by the Plaintiff in several classes. The use of the mark 'INTEL' as a trademark and/or part of trading style would constitute infringement as also passing off the Defendants' products as that of the Plaintiff.

key_passages.label: lis_no_longer_exists
key_passages.quote: it is clear that the lis no longer exists between the parties and the Defendants are willing to suffer permanent injunction in terms of the prayer clause 37(i) & (ii) in the plaint for permanent injunction.

key_passages.label: decree
key_passages.quote: Under these circumstances, the suit of the Plaintiff is decreed in terms of the paragraph 37 (i) & (ii) of the plaint. All other reliefs are not pressed for.

summary: Intel Corporation (USA) filed this trademark infringement suit in 2006 against three Indian entities controlled by S.P. Gupta—Intel Gas Gadgets P. Ltd., Intel Gas Guards P. Ltd., and Intel Safety Devices—that used 'INTEL' as part of their corporate names, trademarks, and domain name for manufacturing and selling LPG regulators, adaptors, valves, and related accessories. Despite cease and desist notices from November 2005 onwards, the defendants did not respond. No interim injunction was granted during the prolonged proceedings. Evidence was recorded by April 2016. Notably, during the pendency of the suit, the Trade Marks Registry declared 'INTEL' a well-known trademark under Section 2(zg) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999. After S.P. Gupta's death, his legal heirs instructed counsel that the three entities had ceased business operations and were willing to suffer permanent injunction provided no damages were pursued. The plaintiff agreed not to press for damages or other reliefs. The Court noted that the lis had effectively ceased and decreed the suit for permanent injunction in terms of the prayer clauses. The registered company among the defendants was additionally directed to change its name within three months through the Registrar of Companies.

case_title: M/S. Mandvi Co-Op Bank Ltd. vs Nimesh B. Thakore
court: Supreme Court of India
judge_or_bench: Hon'ble Mr. Justice Aftab Alam, Hon'ble Mr. Justice Tarun Chatterjee
statutes: Negotiable Instruments (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2002
core_facts: Mandvi Co-Op Bank Ltd. and other complainants had filed complaints under s.138 NI Act for dishonoured cheques
Multiple writ petitions and s.482 CrPC applications were filed before the Gujarat High Court by accused and complainants raising procedural questions about s.145 NI Act
High Court framed two questions: (A) scope of accused's right under s.145(2) to call witness for examination, and (B) retrospective applicability of s.145 to pending cases
High Court also held that accused could give evidence on affidavit analogously to the complainant under s.145(1)
Seven appeals arose before the Supreme Court from the High Court judgment
legal_issues: Whether the accused's right under s.145(2) to summon a witness is limited to cross-examination or extends to a fresh examination-in-chief
Whether s.143 to s.147 inserted by the 2002 Amendment Act operate retrospectively to pending cases
Whether the accused can give evidence on affidavit like the complainant under s.145(1)
outcome: Appeal from SLP (Crl.) No. 3915/2006 (by the bank against giving accused the right to tender affidavit evidence) allowed; High Court direction permitting accused to give evidence on affidavit set aside. Remaining six appeals by accused dismissed. Accused's right under s.145(2) is limited to cross-examination; provisions are procedural and retrospective.
key_holdings: When summoned on the application of the accused under s.145(2), the witness's affidavit already on record constitutes examination-in-chief; the accused is limited to cross-examination of the deponent.
Sections 143 to 147 inserted by the 2002 Amendment are procedural, not substantive, and apply retrospectively to cases pending on the date they came into force (February 6, 2003).

Section 145(1) confers the right to give evidence on affidavit only on the complainant; the High Court erred in reading into the statute a similar right for the accused; courts cannot add words to a statute.

key_passages.label: scheme_of_sections_143_to_147
key_passages.quote: sections 143 to 147 were inserted in the Act by the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2002 to do away with all the stages and processes in a regular criminal trial that normally cause inordinate delay in its conclusion

key_passages.label: accused_right_limited_to_cross_examination
key_passages.quote: on being summoned on the application made by the accused the deponent of the affidavit (the complainant or any of his witnesses) can only be subjected to cross-examination as to the facts stated in the affidavit.

key_passages.label: retrospective_application
key_passages.quote: the provisions of sections 143 to 147 do not take away any substantive rights of the accused. Those provisions are not substantive but procedural in nature and would, therefore, undoubtedly, apply to the cases that were pending on the date the provisions came into force.

key_passages.label: holding_accused_cannot_give_affidavit_evidence
key_passages.quote: we have no hesitation in holding that the High Court was in error in taking the view, that on a request made by the accused the magistrate may allow him to tender his evidence on affidavit

summary: The Supreme Court of India considered seven appeals arising from a Gujarat High Court judgment that addressed the procedure for dishonoured cheque trials under Section 145 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, as amended by the Negotiable Instruments (Amendment and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 2002. The Court resolved three issues. First, whether a person summoned under Section 145(2) at the instance of the accused must depose in examination-in-chief before cross-examination. The Court held that the affidavit already on record constitutes examination-in-chief and the accused is limited to cross-examination only. Second, whether Sections 143 to 147 apply retrospectively to cases pending on February 6, 2003, the date of insertion. The Court affirmed these provisions are procedural and therefore retrospective. Third, whether the accused can give evidence on affidavit like the complainant. The Court reversed the High Court, holding that Section 145(1) expressly confers this right only on the complainant, and courts cannot read in words not present in a statute even if the omission appears inadvertent. The judgment emphasises the legislative scheme of Sections 143 to 147 as a special code for expeditious disposal of cheque dishonour cases, cautioning against procedural interpretations that would convert efficiency measures into tools for delay. The appeal by the bank was allowed; the six appeals by accused persons were dismissed.

case_title: Sh. Yashpal Chaudhrani & Ors. vs State (Govt. Of NCT Delhi) & Anr.
court: High Court of Delhi at New Delhi

respondents: HDFC Bank Ltd. (R-2 in first four matters)

core_facts: Four FIRs (Nos.45, 47, 53, 54/2003) were registered against petitioners by Special Cell, Delhi Police for credit card cloning and fraud using skimmed data; charge-sheets filed in December 2003 and October 2004
A fifth case (FIR No.454/2013) arose from creation of fake social media IDs and obscene calls, charge-sheeted under IT Act s.66-A and s.67
All five cases had barely progressed in 10-15 years; charges were not formally framed in all cases

Credit card fraud accused negotiated a settlement of Rs.12 lakh with HDFC Bank through court-annexed mediation (Patiala House Courts) in 2018; IT Act case settled for Rs.2 lakh through Delhi HC Mediation Centre
Petitioners filed five Crl.MC petitions under s.482 CrPC seeking quashing of the FIRs and proceedings based on these settlements
legal_issues: Whether criminal proceedings for serious economic offences (credit card fraud) can be quashed under s.482 CrPC on the basis of private settlement through mediation
Whether criminal cases involving offences of mental depravity (IT Act obscenity) can be quashed on settlement
Whether courts may refer criminal cases to mediation without first assessing the quashability of the offences involved
What guidelines should govern courts and mediation centres when dealing with criminal cases involving non-compoundable or serious offences
outcome: All five petitions under s.482 CrPC dismissed. Quashing of criminal proceedings in credit card fraud cases and IT Act obscene calls case refused. Comprehensive guidelines issued directing courts to assess quashability before referring criminal cases to mediation, and requiring mediators to undertake preliminary scrutiny of permissibility. Four fraud cases directed to be heard on day-to-day basis.
key_holdings: Economic offences affecting the financial and economic well-being of the State and its banking institutions cannot be quashed on private settlement under s.482 CrPC, regardless of the complainant's willingness.

Offences involving mental depravity (such as obscene calls and IT Act violations) fall outside the category of cases quashable on settlement, especially where the court had previously declined to quash the same proceedings.
Before referring a criminal case to mediation, the court must first assess whether a settlement reached through such process could lawfully be acted upon to terminate the criminal proceedings.
Mediators must undertake a preliminary scrutiny of the criminal case to determine whether the settlement being facilitated is permissible in law before brokering any agreement.

key_passages.label: mediation_referral_must_assess_quashability
key_passages.quote: This Court is of the firm view that before making a reference to mediation in the context of criminal case, the court must consider as to whether a settlement reached by such effort would be acceptable for the criminal process to be brought to an end.

key_passages.label: heinous_offences_not_quashable_on_settlement
key_passages.quote: Heinous and serious offences involving mental depravity or offences such as murder, rape and dacoity cannot appropriately be quashed though the victim or the family of the victim have settled the dispute. Such offences are, truly speaking, not private in nature but have a serious impact upon society.

key_passages.label: economic_offences_exception
key_passages.quote: Economic offences involving the financial and economic well-being of the state have implications which lie beyond the domain of a mere dispute between private disputants.

key_passages.label: outcome_all_petitions_dismissed
key_passages.quote: Thus, all the five petitions are liable to be dismissed. Ordered accordingly.

summary: The Delhi High Court consolidated five petitions under Section 482 CrPC seeking quashing of criminal cases on the basis of mediation settlements. Four petitions (Crl.MC 5765, 5768, 5785, 5805/2018) related to FIRs registered in 2003 against accused persons for credit card cloning and fraud using skimmed data, cases that had barely progressed in fifteen years. The fifth petition (Crl.MC 5995/2018) concerned FIR 454/2013 for creation of fake social media IDs and obscene calls under the IT Act. In each case, the accused had reached settlements through court-annexed mediation centres and sought quashing thereafter. The Court declined to quash any of the five proceedings. Reviewing the jurisprudence from Gian Singh, Narinder Singh, Parbatbhai Aahir and related cases, the Court held that economic offences involving credit card fraud affect the financial well-being of the State and public trust in banking; they are not private in nature and cannot be quashed on settlement. The obscene calls offence equally involves mental depravity and falls outside quashable categories. The Court issued comprehensive guidelines directing that before referring criminal cases to mediation, courts must assess whether the offences involved are quashable in law; mediators must conduct preliminary scrutiny before facilitating settlement; and vetting must occur before formal execution of any settlement. The four fraud cases were directed to proceed on day-to-day basis under monitoring of the Sessions Judge.

case_title: Company Of Management For Baranagar Jute Factory vs Atis Dipankar Chowdhuri
court: High Court at Calcutta

appellants: Committee of Management for Baranagar Jute Factory (Petitioner No.1)
respondents: Atis Dipankar Chowdhuri (Manager, Recovery, State Bank of India)

core_facts: Baranagar Jute Factory was a borrower of the State Bank of India; a winding-up proceeding was initiated and the High Court formed a Committee of Management under a court-approved scheme to run the factory and repay debts by instalments

The Committee issued cheque No.776924 dated 29-8-90 on Union Bank of India (Ezra Street) in favour of SBI; the cheque was returned on 11-9-90 with remark 'exceeds arrangement' and again on 23-11-90 with remark 'refer to drawer'

SBI wrote to Union Bank confirming insufficient balance, issued a demand notice dated 4-12-90, and the Committee's reply dated 11-12-90 acknowledged receipt but denied liability and raised objections without paying
SBI filed a complaint before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Calcutta under s.138 read with s.141 NI Act; cognizance was taken and proceedings began as criminal case No. C/46/1991

Petitioners filed a criminal revision challenging the prosecution on three grounds: timeliness of notice after second presentation, need for court's leave before prosecuting a court-created committee, and whether the Committee qualifies as a 'company' under s.141
legal_issues: Whether the bank's failure to give demand notice after the first dishonour and its choice to re-present the cheque bars a prosecution under s.138 NI Act
Whether prosecution of a Committee of Management appointed by the High Court requires prior leave of the court (analogous to prosecution of a court-appointed receiver)
Whether a Committee of Management constituted by court order qualifies as a 'company' under the explanation to s.141 NI Act, enabling vicarious liability
outcome: Criminal revision allowed. The prosecution against the Committee of Management and its signatory quashed. Proceedings in criminal case No. C/46/1991 under s.138/141 NI Act before the CMC Calcutta set aside; accused petitioners discharged from bail bonds. The court held prosecution was bad for want of prior leave of court and that the Committee of Management is not a 'company' under s.141.
key_holdings: A second presentation of a dishonoured cheque within the validity period is not prohibited by s.138 NI Act; the payee retains the right to give demand notice and initiate prosecution after the second dishonour.

A Committee of Management appointed by the High Court under a court-approved scheme is akin to a court-appointed receiver and cannot be prosecuted without prior leave of the court; prosecution without such leave is bad.

A Committee of Management constituted by court order is not a 'company' or body corporate or association of individuals within the meaning of the explanation to s.141 NI Act; no vicarious liability can be fastened on such a committee under that section.

key_passages.label: second_presentation_permissible
key_passages.quote: there is no prohibition in Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act that a returned cheque cannot be presented again.

key_passages.label: prior_leave_of_court_required
key_passages.quote: the prosecution in this case without the prior leave of the Court has been bad.

key_passages.label: committee_not_a_legal_entity
key_passages.quote: the Committee of Management constituted by the High Court has no legal status as such to represent the aggregate of the individuals like a firm or any body corporate.

key_passages.label: outcome_prosecution_quashed
key_passages.quote: The proceedings of criminal case No. C/46/1991 under Section 138/141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act pending in the Court of the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Calcutta, are hereby quashed. The accused petitioners are discharged after being released from their bail bonds.

summary: The Calcutta High Court allowed a criminal revision challenging prosecution under Sections 138 and 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The petitioners were a Committee of Management of Baranagar Jute Factory, formed by High Court order under a court-approved scheme to manage the insolvent company, and its authorised signatory. The Committee had issued a cheque favouring the State Bank of India (creditor), which was dishonoured twice. SBI served a demand notice after the second dishonour and filed a complaint. The petitioners raised three objections. On the first objection, the Court rejected the argument that the bank's choice to re-present the cheque without sending notice after the first dishonour extinguished the right to prosecute; it held that re-presentation within the validity period is permissible and notice after the second dishonour is valid. On the second objection, the Court held that the Committee of Management, being a creation of the Court equivalent to a receiver, required prior leave of the court before it could be prosecuted; prosecuting without such leave rendered the action bad. On the third objection, the Court held that the Committee of Management is not a 'company', body corporate, firm, or association of individuals as defined in the explanation to Section 141 NI Act, and cannot suffer imprisonment, making vicarious prosecution under that section unavailable. The criminal revision was allowed and the prosecution quashed.

case_title: Ashokbhai Shankar Chaudhary & 1 vs Jayendra Virendra Sharma & 1
court: High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad
statutes: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 Order 39 Rule 1
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 Order 39 Rule 2
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 Order 43 Rule 1(r)
core_facts: Suit property (Revenue Survey No.544/3, 19260 sq.ft.) was owned in ½ undivided share each by the plaintiff and defendant No.1, who were cousins

On 07.03.2007, defendant No.1 entered into a sale agreement to sell his ½ share to the plaintiff for Rs.15 lakhs; plaintiff paid part consideration of Rs.1,50,000 by cheque and claimed to have been put in possession of the entire property

Defendant No.1, despite a public notice by him cancelling the sale agreement dated 16.02.2010 (citing plaintiff's failure to pay balance by 29.12.2009), sold his ½ share to defendants 2 and 3 by Registered Sale Deed dated 28.10.2010 for Rs.32 lakhs
Defendants 2 and 3 had published a public notice for title clearance on 02.03.2010 before execution of their sale deed

Plaintiff filed Special Civil Suit No.263 of 2010 for specific performance and filed two injunction applications (Exh.5 and Exh.37); the trial court granted both applications directing status quo on title and possession
legal_issues: Whether defendants 2 and 3 are bona fide purchasers without notice of the prior sale agreement under Section 19 of the Specific Relief Act so as to be protected from specific performance
Whether time was the essence of the sale agreement dated 07.03.2007 such that failure to pay balance consideration by 29.12.2009 entitled defendant No.1 to terminate the agreement
Whether the appellate court should interfere with a discretionary interim injunction order when no arbitrariness or perversity is shown in the trial court's exercise of discretion
outcome: Both Appeal from Orders (AFO No.196 and 197 of 2014) dismissed. Interim injunction directing status quo on title and possession upheld. Civil applications also dismissed. Defendants 2 and 3 cannot claim bona fide purchaser protection at this stage; time was not the essence of the contract.
key_holdings: Defendants 2 and 3 cannot be characterised as bona fide purchasers under Section 19-B of the Specific Relief Act at this stage as they had notice of the prior sale agreement from a public notice before executing their sale deed.
In contracts relating to immovable property, time is ordinarily not the essence of contract and failure to pay balance consideration before a specified date does not render the contract terminable.

An appellate court should not interfere with a trial court's discretionary order on injunction unless the discretion was exercised arbitrarily, capriciously or perversely, or the court ignored settled principles.

key_passages.label: no_bona_fide_purchaser_protection
key_passages.quote: it cannot be inferred that the defendant Nos.2 and 3 are the bona fide purchasers as provided under Section 19-B of the Specific Relief Act so as to non-suit the plaintiff at threshold.

key_passages.label: time_not_essence_of_contract
key_passages.quote: Normally, in the contract relating to immovable property, time cannot be essence of contract and the time stipulated in performance even if expressly read and shown to be the essence required to be read as not being essence of contract

key_passages.label: appellate_court_limited_scope
key_passages.quote: the Appellate Court cannot interfere with the exercise of discretion of the Court of first instance and substitute its own discretion except, where the discretion has been shown to have been exercised arbitrarily, capriciously or perversely or where the Court had ignored the settled principles of law regulating grant or refusal of interlocutory injunctions.

key_passages.label: outcome_appeals_dismissed
key_passages.quote: no case is made out to interfere with the findings recorded by the learned trial Judge in the impugned order and, therefore, present appeals deserve to be dismissed and are accordingly dismissed.

summary: The Gujarat High Court dismissed appeals filed by defendants 2 and 3 against an interim injunction order granted in a specific performance suit (Special Civil Suit No.263 of 2010). The plaintiff and defendant No.1 were co-sharers of the suit property. Defendant No.1 had agreed to sell his ½ share to the plaintiff under a sale agreement dated 07.03.2007, receiving part payment. Before the injunction application was heard, defendant No.1 sold his ½ share to defendants 2 and 3 by registered sale deed dated 28.10.2010 for Rs.32 lakhs. The trial court granted status quo on title and possession. Defendants 2 and 3 challenged the injunction claiming bona fide purchaser protection under Section 19 of the Specific Relief Act, and arguing that the plaintiff's failure to pay the balance consideration by 29.12.2009 had extinguished the sale agreement. The High Court held that defendants 2 and 3 could not claim bona fide purchaser status as they had notice of the prior sale agreement through a public notice before executing their purchase deed. It also held that in immovable property contracts, time is ordinarily not the essence of the contract and failure to pay by a specified date does not automatically terminate the agreement. Applying the limited scope of Order 43 Rule 1(r) CPC, the appellate court declined to substitute its discretion for that of the trial court in the absence of arbitrariness or perversity. Both appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Chinnasamy vs K. Viswanathan (died) and Others
court: High Court of Judicature at Madras

respondents: K. Viswanathan (died, LRs brought on record as Respondents 5-7: Nallammal, Malarkodi, Senthilkumar)

core_facts: Plaintiff claimed to have entered into a sale agreement (Ext.A.1) dated 01.05.1992 to purchase agricultural property belonging to defendants 1 to 3 for Rs.75,000 total, paying Rs.50,000 and receiving possession in continuation of his prior tenancy; balance of Rs.25,000 payable within 11 months
Defendants 1 to 3 denied Ext.A.1 and alleged it was fabricated; on 24.09.1992, the second defendant sold the suit property to the fourth defendant by sale deed (Ext.B.1)
Defendants 1 to 3 failed to enter the witness box; trial court compared signatures under s.73 Evidence Act, found Ext.A.1 genuine, and decreed specific performance

First Appellate Court also found Ext.A.1 genuine but dismissed the suit on the ground that the plaintiff had not proved readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract under s.16(C) Specific Relief Act
Plaintiff filed second appeal before Madras HC on five substantial questions of law, including burden of proof of bona fide purchase and readiness/willingness
legal_issues: Whether a plaintiff is entitled to specific performance when both courts concurrently found the sale agreement genuine but the plaintiff failed to prove readiness and willingness under s.16(C) of the Specific Relief Act
Whether the burden of pleading and proving the bona fide purchaser exception under s.19(b) of the Specific Relief Act lies on the subsequent purchaser or on the plaintiff seeking specific performance
Whether the first Appellate Court could dismiss the suit on the ground of readiness and willingness when the fourth defendant had not raised this defence and the vendors had been set ex-parte
outcome: Second appeal dismissed. Judgment and decree of the first Appellate Court (III Additional District Judge, Krishnagiri) dated 12.07.2000 in A.S.No.34 of 1999 reversing the trial court decree upheld. Plaintiff's failure to prove readiness and willingness to perform the contract under s.16(C) Specific Relief Act was determinative; suit for specific performance dismissed.
key_holdings: A decree for specific performance is a discretionary relief and the plaintiff must satisfy the conscience of the court that he deserves it; the genuineness of the agreement alone does not entitle the plaintiff to a decree.

Section 16(C) of the Specific Relief Act casts a statutory burden on the plaintiff to plead and prove readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract throughout the relevant period; failure to discharge this burden is fatal to the suit.

Even if the subsequent purchaser fails to plead the bona fide purchaser defence under s.19(b) of the Specific Relief Act, the plaintiff who seeks equitable relief of specific performance must still prove that the subsequent purchaser had notice of the original agreement.

key_passages.label: specific_performance_is_discretionary
key_passages.quote: The decision to this case is rooted in the fundamental guiding principal that a decree for specific performances a discretionary relief, and that he who claims specific enforcement of an agreement should satisfy the conscience of the court that he deserves it.

key_passages.label: section_16c_obligation_on_plaintiff
key_passages.quote: Section 16(C) of the Specific Relief Act as it stood then, when the suit was laid, mandates that the party seeking specific enforcement shall plead and prove his readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract.

key_passages.label: burden_remains_on_plaintiff_despite_defendants_failure_to_plead
key_passages.quote: even if the fourth defendant had pleaded so, yet, he cannot prove the negative, for the burden will still be on the plaintiff. Since the plaintiff seeks a relief in equity, he has to walk the extra distance to satisfy the Court's conscience that he is entitled to obtain a decree for specific performance.

key_passages.label: outcome_second_appeal_dismissed
key_passages.quote: This Court does not find any perversity in the findings of the first Appellate Court, though the reasons for arriving at the same finding may have a mild variance. All the substantial questions of law fails. This Court does not find any merit in the appeal.

summary: The Madras High Court dismissed a second appeal in a specific performance suit. The plaintiff, a tenant of agricultural property, claimed to have entered into a sale agreement (Ext.A.1) dated 01.05.1992 paying Rs.50,000 out of Rs.75,000 total consideration and receiving possession. Defendants 1 to 3 (vendors) denied the agreement and sold the property to the fourth defendant by registered sale deed (Ext.B.1) on 24.09.1992. The trial court, finding defendants 1 to 3 failed to contest their signatures in Ext.A.1, decreed specific performance. The first Appellate Court concurrently found Ext.A.1 genuine but dismissed the suit, holding the plaintiff had not proved readiness and willingness to perform his part of the contract. The Madras High Court upheld this finding. Applying Section 16(C) of the Specific Relief Act as it stood at the time of suit, the Court affirmed that a decree for specific performance is a discretionary equitable relief requiring the plaintiff to plead and prove readiness and willingness throughout. The Court further held that even if the fourth defendant failed to plead the bona fide purchaser defence under Section 19(b) of the Specific Relief Act, the plaintiff still bore the burden of demonstrating the fourth defendant had notice of Ext.A.1, as he seeks equitable relief and must walk the extra distance to satisfy the court's conscience. Finding no perversity in the first Appellate Court's findings, all five substantial questions of law failed and the second appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Smt. Iravva K Purantar vs S. Venkatesh and Kendra Upadyayara Sangha (Regd.)
court: High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru
judge_or_bench: Hon'ble Mr. Justice S.R. Krishna Kumar

appellants: Smt. Iravva K Purantar (non-party to original suit; subsequent purchaser of suit property)

statutes: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 Order 41 Rule 27
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 Order 41 Rule 28
core_facts: Respondent No.1/plaintiff instituted O.S.No.3810/2010 against respondent No.2/defendant-Sangha for specific performance of an unregistered lease-cum-sale agreement dated 10.10.1986 in respect of a site property

The Sangha's written statement alleged it had separately allotted and alienated the very same site to the appellant (Smt. Iravva K Purantar) under a registered lease-cum-sale agreement dated 17.09.1987 and had issued a possession certificate dated 17.03.1988
The defendant-Sangha neither cross-examined the plaintiff's witness (PW.1) nor led any oral or documentary evidence in support of its defence
Trial court, on the basis of uncontroverted evidence of PW.1, decreed the suit for specific performance in favour of the plaintiff by judgment and decree dated 15.12.2015

Appellant (not arrayed as a party to the suit despite the Sangha's own written statement disclosing her claim) filed a Regular First Appeal with a delay of 677 days, along with applications for condonation of delay, permission to appeal, impleadment as additional defendant, and production of additional documents (registered lease-cum-sale agreement dated 17.09.1987, possession certificate, sale deed dated 19.03.2012, katha documents)
legal_issues: Whether a non-party to a specific performance suit who has a competing claim to the suit property (acknowledged in the defendant's own written statement) is a proper and necessary party entitled to be impleaded as additional defendant and to prefer an appeal
Whether the delay of 677 days in filing the appeal by a person who had no knowledge of the suit can be condoned as caused by bonafide reasons
Whether additional documents showing the competing claim (registered lease-cum-sale agreement, sale deed) should be received on record under Order 41 Rule 27 CPC
outcome: Regular First Appeal allowed. Impugned judgment and decree dated 15.12.2015 in O.S.No.3810/2010 set aside. Matter remitted to trial court for reconsideration afresh. Appellant impleaded as additional defendant No.2; additional documents received on record; delay of 677 days condoned; liberty granted to all parties to lead evidence and cross-examine witnesses.
key_holdings: A non-party to a specific performance suit may be a proper and necessary party, and is entitled to prefer an appeal, where the suit property is the very property in which she claims rights under a competing registered agreement, and the defendant's written statement acknowledges the alienation in her favour but the defendant defaulted in contesting the suit.

Delay in filing an appeal by a non-party who had no knowledge of the pendency of the suit and whose competing agreement was registered (unlike the plaintiff's unregistered agreement) constitutes bonafide reason and unavoidable circumstance warranting condonation.

Where a non-party with competing rights is impleaded and additional evidence is necessary for adjudication, the proper course under Order 41 Rule 28 CPC is to set aside the impugned decree and remit the matter to the trial court for fresh consideration.

key_passages.label: non_party_as_proper_and_necessary_party
key_passages.quote: While it is true that in a suit for specific performance, a non-party to the contract would ordinarily not be construed or treated as a proper and necessary party, in the light of the specific assertion on the part of the Sangha in the written statement, that the suit was liable to be dismissed

key_passages.label: delay_condoned_bonafide_reasons
key_passages.quote: being satisfied that the delay in preferring the present appeal, has been satisfactorily explained. I.A.No.1/2018 is hereby allowed and the delay in preferring the appeal is hereby condoned.

key_passages.label: matter_remitted_for_fresh_trial
key_passages.quote: remitted back to the trial Court for reconsideration afresh in accordance with law.

key_passages.label: outcome_appeal_allowed
key_passages.quote: Appeal is hereby allowed. II. Impugned judgment and decree dated 15.12.2015 is hereby set aside.

summary: The Karnataka High Court allowed a Regular First Appeal filed by a non-party to a specific performance suit. Respondent No.1/plaintiff had instituted O.S.No.3810/2010 against respondent No.2/defendant (Kendra Upadyayara Sangha, Regd.) for specific performance of an unregistered lease-cum-sale agreement dated 10.10.1986 relating to a site property. The Sangha's written statement admitted it had allotted and alienated the same property to the appellant under a registered lease-cum-sale agreement dated 17.09.1987, but the Sangha neither cross-examined the plaintiff's witness nor led any evidence. The trial court decreed specific performance in the plaintiff's favour. The appellant, who had not been made a party to the suit despite the Sangha's own admission, filed an appeal with a delay of 677 days, seeking impleadment, additional documents on record (including her registered lease-cum-sale agreement, possession certificate and sale deed), and condonation of delay. The High Court held that the delay was due to bonafide reasons since the appellant had no knowledge of the suit and her agreement was a registered document. It found the appellant to be both a proper and necessary party, allowed all interlocutory applications, and set aside the impugned decree. The matter was remitted to the trial court for fresh consideration with the appellant impleaded as additional defendant No.2, with liberty to all parties to adduce evidence.

case_title: Kum. H. Supriya vs S. Krishnappa and Others
court: High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru
judge_or_bench: Hon'ble Mr. Justice S.R. Krishna Kumar

appellants: Kum. H. Supriya (Defendant No.3 in O.S.No.7/2018)

statutes: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 Order 6 Rule 17
core_facts: O.S.No.7/2018 was instituted by respondent No.1/plaintiff before the Senior Civil Judge and JMFC, Holenarasipura, for specific performance of a sale agreement dated 14.09.2018 relating to immovable property, against defendant Nos.1, 2 and 3

The plaintiff had adduced evidence and cross-examination of PW1 (plaintiff's witness) was at an advanced stage when the petitioner/defendant No.3 filed I.A.No.VIII under Order 6 Rule 17 read with s.151 CPC seeking amendment of the written statement

The proposed amendment incorporated additional paragraph No.17a after paragraph 17, relating to certain subsequent events including the pendency of O.S.No.59/2021 before the Senior Civil Judge, Holenarasipura

The plaintiff opposed the amendment application; the trial court rejected I.A.No.VIII by impugned order dated 17.11.2025 on the ground that the petitioner had not exercised due diligence in not seeking the amendment earlier
Petitioner/defendant No.3 challenged the rejection order by Writ Petition No.37035 of 2025 under Article 227 of the Constitution
legal_issues: Whether a defendant's application to amend a written statement to incorporate subsequent events that occurred after institution of the suit (including pendency of another suit) can be rejected on the ground of lack of due diligence
Whether refusal of such amendment occasions failure of justice when the subsequent events could not have been pleaded at the time of filing the written statement
outcome: Writ petition allowed. Impugned order dated 17.11.2025 rejecting I.A.No.VIII in O.S.No.7/2018 set aside. I.A.No.VIII under Order 6 Rule 17 CPC allowed. Liberty granted to respondent No.1/plaintiff to file rejoinder/reply to the amended written statement. Trial court directed to dispose of the suit within one year from receipt of copy of this order.
key_holdings: An application to amend a written statement to incorporate subsequent events that arose after the institution of the suit cannot be refused on the ground of lack of due diligence, since such events obviously could not have been pleaded at the time of filing the original written statement.

Refusal of an amendment relating to subsequent events occasions failure of justice warranting interference under Article 227 of the Constitution, particularly when the plaintiff suffers no prejudice as she can file a rejoinder to the amended written statement.

key_passages.label: subsequent_events_cannot_be_refused_for_lack_of_due_diligence
key_passages.quote: the proposed amendment relates to certain subsequent events that are alleged to have occurred after institution of the suit including institution of O.S.No.59/2021, which obviously could not have been pleaded by the petitioner- defendant No.3

key_passages.label: no_prejudice_to_plaintiff
key_passages.quote: since the plaintiff would have an opportunity to file rejoinder/reply to the amended written statement, no prejudice can be said to have been caused to the plaintiff if the proposed amendment was allowed

key_passages.label: failure_of_justice_warranting_interference
key_passages.quote: the impugned order passed by the trial Court refusing NC: 2026:KHC:7501 HC-KAR amendment has occasioned failure of justice warranting interference by this Court in the present petition.

key_passages.label: outcome_petition_allowed
key_passages.quote: The petition is hereby allowed.

summary: The Karnataka High Court allowed a writ petition under Article 227 of the Constitution filed by defendant No.3 in a specific performance suit (O.S.No.7/2018) pending before the Senior Civil Judge and JMFC, Holenarasipura. The underlying suit was filed by the plaintiff for specific performance of a sale agreement dated 14.09.2018 relating to immovable property. After the plaintiff had led evidence and cross-examination of PW1 was underway, the petitioner/defendant No.3 filed I.A.No.VIII under Order 6 Rule 17 read with Section 151 CPC to amend the written statement by adding a paragraph incorporating certain subsequent events including the pendency of another suit, O.S.No.59/2021, arising after institution of the present suit. The trial court rejected the amendment on the ground that the petitioner had not exercised due diligence by not seeking the amendment earlier. The High Court set aside this order, holding that an amendment to incorporate events that arose after institution of the suit could not be refused on the ground of lack of due diligence since those events could not have been pleaded in the original written statement filed in 2018. Following the principles in LIC v. Sanjeev Builders, Dinesh Goyal v. Suman Agarwal, and a co-ordinate bench ruling, the Court found that refusal of the amendment occasioned failure of justice. No prejudice to the plaintiff was found as the plaintiff could file a rejoinder. I.A.No.VIII was allowed and the trial court was directed to dispose of the suit within one year.
